or emendations of the Drug-sellers, or

✱ The first book concerns simple medicines <note>Medicines made of a single natural ingredient</note>, in which the errors

✱ The second book contains the Corrections to the Antidota-

✱ The third book concerns the method of healing bodies through

✱ The fourth book embraces the cures and remedies for the principal

# To the most illustrious and in every respect most learned, and above all to be revered, Lord François de Tournon, Bishop of the Church of Bourges <note>original: "Bituricē."</note>, Primate of Aquitaine, and Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Symphorien Champier <note>original: "Symphorianus Campegius"</note> of Lyon, Chief Physician <term>Archiatros: a Greek-derived title for a high-ranking or royal physician</term> to the Prince of Lorraine,

->Sends Hearty Greetings.<-

<margin>
Jean
Champier.
Jean
Petit.
</margin>

<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial 'C' depicting two nude putti (cherubic infants) grasping and climbing through stylized vines and foliage.</image-desc>**WHEN I WAS** silently, deeply, and for a long time reflecting within myself, most Reverend Prelate, that it is the mark not only of an immoderate man, but also of an envious and malevolent one to remain idle when he might benefit the human race—and to hide or conceal those things which he himself has attained by divine gift—I wished no longer to leave these works, which I have composed with great diligence, to struggle against moths and bookworms. I wrote these while I was with you, together with my nephew Jean Champier and with Jean Petit of Valensole, a doctor, both men most learned in the Apolline art <note>The "Apolline art" refers to medicine, as Apollo was the god of healing.</note>. At that time, you were suffering from a quartan fever <term>quartana: a form of malaria where the fever recurs every fourth day</term>, which was acting violently upon every part of your body...

He recalls composing the work while tending to the Cardinal's severe quartan fever alongside his nephew and Jean Petit.</summary>

-># Dedicatory Epistle<-

was raging most fiercely. And although you consulted very many most excellent **Physicians**, you could be released from that disease by the help of none of them; although those men, most prudent in affairs, passed over nothing which belonged to the art of medicine. At last, it pleased you to experience what the industry of your **Champier** <note>Latin: Campegius; the author refers to himself in the third person</note> might avail in that matter. Having been summoned, I therefore betook myself to you: I found you surrounded by a circle of Physicians who were by no means of the common sort. With them, we investigated the hidden causes of this disease; and therein we consumed one or two hours (with many words exchanged back and forth).

But that more lingering disease, whose roots could not be so easily plucked out, delayed us there for several days. And since we considered that something should always be done, while others wore away the time with unlearned stories, and others played at **Latrunculi** <note>A strategy board game similar to chess or draughts played in Ancient Rome and the Renaissance</note> for the sake of their spirits, I preferred, according to my custom, to revolve something concerning our studies in my mind: which, afterwards committed to letters, might go forth for the common utility of students. And so, at that time, we undertook a serious commentary; and it seemed best to us in the first place

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle to Symphorien Champier (Symphorianus Campegius), focusing on the relationship between noble lineage and personal virtue.</meta>

# To Master Symphorien Champier

<margin>
Philip. Alexander.
Caesar. Octavius.
Pyrrhus.
</margin>
...that I might prove my spirit and my loyalty to you—to you, I say, the living image of virtue. It was not without the best of reasons that you were promoted to such excellent honors; indeed, you are a great ornament to those honors, rather than they being an ornament to you. But who could wonder that you are so greatly devoted to virtue, which is (as they say) baked into the very roots of your lineage? It is certainly a great help toward virtue to be born of good and famous parents. For young men who possess any natural talent are accustomed to emulate the dignity of their ancestors so that they do not seem to degenerate, and they aspire to the happiness of their fathers' praises. Thus the name of Philip spurred on Alexander; thus the fame of Julius Caesar excited Octavius. Thus, finally, Pyrrhus <note>The son of Achilles, also known as Neoptolemus.</note> was courageous because of the image of his father, Achilles. <note>original: "Pyrrhus Achilleides erat animosus imagine patris." A reference to Ovid or similar classical sentiment regarding hereditary bravery.</note>

You also, most distinguished father, although you embrace and love virtue under the guidance of God and nature and by your own striving efforts, are nevertheless moved in no small way by the images of your ancestors. To equal their character and virtue is as difficult as it is beautiful and most praiseworthy. Truly, you have not only equaled your ancestors, but by daring and by doing, you have grown and brought them even greater luster. And although concerning you and your ancestors...

<summary>The author praises Symphorien Champier for upholding his family's noble reputation, arguing that great ancestors serve as a catalyst for a son's own virtuous achievements.</summary>
<keywords>Symphorien Champier, virtue, nobility, lineage, Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar, Augustus Octavius, Pyrrhus, Achilles, emulation of ancestors</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
# Dedicatory Letter

It would be the mark of an arrogant man to speak at length when the abundance of material makes it impossible to finish a formal oration; however, it would be the mark of an ungrateful man to remain silent. Therefore, I shall briefly use this letter to embrace what I have discovered among hidden but reliable authors concerning the founders of the city of Tournon <note>original: "Turnonis"</note> and your own ancestors. This most noble family of Tournon arose, therefore—as has been passed down to memory by the most celebrated writers—from Merovech and Chlodio, the ancient Kings of the Franks. 
<margin>The founders of the city of Tournon, and the House of Tournon.</margin>
<margin>Merovech and Chlodio, Kings of the Franks.</margin>
<margin>Dionysius of Halicarnassus. Herodotus.</margin>
<margin>Tyrrhenus.</margin>
The Citadel of Tournon, however, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus records in his first book (citing Herodotus), was constructed by Tyrrhenus: who, coming to the northern region, settled and dwelt there. He built the most noble cities which still exist today: the city of Tours <note>original: "Turonensem urbem"</note> in Gallia Aquitanica, and Tournon in Gallia Lugdunensis on the banks of the Rhône. 
<margin>The city of Tours. Tournon. Myrsilus.</margin>
<margin>Tyrrhenus. Atys.</margin>
Myrsilus, indeed a serious author, writes to this same effect. Some suspect the origin of the Tyrrhenians to be from the Lydians. And a little later he says: Tyrrhenus, the son of Atys, coming into the northern region, held the whole middle portion of it from its very sources. And because Myrsilus asserted that the Tyrrhenians were of the greatest antiquity, he proves by this that the Umbrians—considered the most ancient people of Italy—are actually younger than they.
<margin>Myrsilus. Umbrians.</margin>

<summary>This dedicatory letter traces the noble lineage of the House of Tournon to the Merovingian kings and attributes the city's architectural origins to the mythical figure Tyrrhenus, citing classical historians to establish antiquity.</summary>
<keywords>House of Tournon, Merovech, Chlodio, Tyrrhenus, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Myrsilus, genealogy, Gallia Lugdunensis, Rhône River, Umbrians</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page's introduction of the Merovingian and Tyrrhenian origins of the House of Tournon, Champier now expands on these classical and mythical genealogies, citing Pliny and the then-popular pseudo-historical works attributed to Berosus to link the family to the god Janus and the defeated Rutuli of Italy.</meta>

Fo. V.
### Lord Symphorianus Campegius <note>Also known as Symphorien Champier (1471–1539), a prominent French physician and humanist who often wrote about local history and genealogy.</note>

<margin>Pliny.</margin>
This is also asserted by Pliny in Book 3, Chapter 15. Therefore, older than these were their ancestors, 
<margin>The Janigenae Gauls.</margin>
the Janigenae Gauls <note>original: "Galli ianigenæ"; a term used by Renaissance humanists to claim that the Gauls were descended from the god Janus</note>, who built the city of Tours and the city of Tournon during the Golden Age.
<margin>Titus.</margin>
Titus was the son of Tyrrhenus, and Volturrhenus was the son of Titus. 
<margin>Berosus the Chaldean. Janus. Iapetus. Atlas. Cameses. Ion. Italus. Osiris. Egyptian Hercules. Atys.</margin>
Berosus the Chaldean <note>Champier is referencing the "Antiquities" of Berosus, a famous 15th-century forgery by Annius of Viterbo that provided mythical origins for European nations</note> records that Janus had three sons: Iapetus, Atlas the Great, and Cameses. To Atlas the Great was born Ion, the father of Italus; and to Cameses was born Osiris, the father of the Egyptian Hercules. This Hercules was the father of Atys, who was the father of Tyrrhenus, by whom the city of Tours and the Citadel of Tournon were constructed. 
<margin>The Rutuli.</margin>
However, other authors not to be disregarded affirm that the House of Tournon drew its origin from the Rutuli. 
<margin>Livy. Turnus. Lavinia. Aeneas.</margin>
For according to the testimony of Livy, in the early days after the city <note>Rome</note> was founded, Turnus, King of the Rutuli—to whom Lavinia had been betrothed before the arrival of Aeneas—took it poorly that a stranger was preferred over him. He brought war against both Aeneas and Latinus. The Rutuli were defeated and, 
<margin>The Etruscans.</margin>
losing confidence in their affairs, they fled to the flourishing wealth of the Etruscans. 
<margin>Tournon.</margin>
Therefore, after Turnus was overcome, and while the Rutuli were searching for more delightful places in Gaul, they came to the spot where the most flourishing city of Tournon now stands. Having seen the pleasantness and convenience of the location, they built that city, and these authors maintain that Tournon was named after Turnus.

<summary>This page presents two mythical origins for the city of Tournon: one tracing its foundation to a lineage descending from Janus and the Egyptian Hercules, and another linking it to King Turnus and the Rutuli who fled Italy after their defeat by Aeneas.</summary>
<keywords>Symphorien Champier, Tournon-sur-Rhône, Tours, Janus, Tyrrhenus, Berosus the Chaldean, King Turnus, Rutuli, Aeneas, French origins, Renaissance genealogy</keywords>

# Dedicatory Letter

This does not seem to have been said without cause; for in that place, several very ancient ruins are visible, serving as a great testament to its antiquity. There are also those who claim 
<margin>Marcomir, King of the Franks.</margin>
<margin>The Trojans.</margin>
that Tournon was built by Marcomir, King of the Eastern Franks, whose lineage is traced back to the Trojans, and specifically to Aeneas <note>During the Renaissance, it was a popular "national myth" to claim that the French (Franks) were descended from Trojan refugees, mirroring the Roman origin story in the Aeneid</note>. However, the most widely accepted authors maintain that Marcomir was not the original founder, but rather the restorer of the city. Indeed, the City of Tournon has attained no common praise and glory, not only for its antiquity or the pleasant climate of the location (which nature seems to have provided), but also for its most excellent and wise men, who are found there in great number. For it is established both 
<margin>Saint Justus.</margin>
<margin>Saint Viator.</margin>
by the Annals of Lyons <note>original: "Lugdunēfiū"; referring to the city of Lyon, France</note> and by the brilliant histories of other writers that Justus and Viator, bishops of the Church of Lyons, traced their origin from the House of Tournon and have been numbered among the saints <note>original: "in Deorum numerum relatos"; literally "enrolled in the number of the gods," a classical Latin idiom Champier uses to describe Christian canonization</note>. 
<margin>Saint Justus died in Egypt.</margin>
<margin>The Church of Saint Justus in Lyons was built by the Tournon family.</margin>
That Saint Justus of Tournon was a man of wondrous holiness and possessed a prophetic spirit; he died in Egypt, but his body, along with the relics of his assistant, the blessed Viator, was brought back to Lyons by devout citizens. They were entombed with the honor they deserved in the Basilica <note>The Collegiate Church of Saint-Just in Lyon, which was a major religious center in the Middle Ages</note> that was built by your ancestors. From this House of Tournon...

### By Master Symphorianus Campegius. Folio VI.

The head of the family who holds power is usually called Justus <note>The name "Justus" (or Just) was traditional for the lords of the House of Tournon</note>. Concerning the leaders and others most skilled in military matters, those vigorous men of the Tournon family who were of great service to the kingdom of France, it is better to remain silent than to say too little, especially since the brevity of a letter does not permit it. But it will be enough to remember your brother, Justus of Tournon, 
<margin>Pavia, the Marshal of Chabannes. The Count of La Trémoille.</margin>
a high-souled man, who at Pavia <note>original: "Ticinum"; referring to the Battle of Pavia in 1525, a major conflict in the Italian Wars</note> together with the Marshal of France from Chabannes <note>Jacques de La Palice, a famous French military leader</note>, a vigorous man, and with the most illustrious Count of La Trémoille, fell in battle—not conquered, but exhausted by conquering—and was found far from his own men among the corpses of the enemy. At Naples <note>original: "Parthenope"</note> indeed, a little 
<margin>Naples. The sons of Justus of Tournon, Antoine and Jean.</margin>
later, two sons of the same Justus fell in war, most vigorous men and very famous among the French. But no more concerning these. For it would be the mark of a madman to wish to furrow the Aegean Sea in a worthless vessel <note>A classical metaphor meaning that Champier feels his writing skills are too "small" or inadequate to fully describe the "vast ocean" of the family's glory</note>. Yet I could not entirely pass over in silence at least a small part of the praise for such a noble family that has deserved so well of me, regarding their most magnificent deeds.

Therefore, look into what we dedicate to you regarding the **errors of the barbarian and Mohammedan doctors** <note>Champier refers here to the medical writings of Arab and Persian physicians like Avicenna and Rhazes. As a Renaissance humanist, he sought to "purify" medicine by returning to original Greek and Roman sources</note>. For they are not contained in very many pages, so that they might not detain your very busy time with a longer discourse. When you do this, I hope it will happen that [not]...

<meta>Continuity: Following the conclusion of his dedicatory letter to the House of Tournon, where he honored their military sacrifices at the Battle of Pavia and in Naples, Champier transitions to the primary subject of his work: a scholarly history and classification of medical schools of thought.</meta>

# On the Sects of Physicians

...lest the memory of me utterly fade away in your mind. Farewell, be happy, and may you live happily through the years of Nestor <note>Nestor was the legendary king in Homer’s Iliad famed for his extreme old age and wisdom</note>; continue to hold us in your affection, and admit us among those most devoted to you.

->The Champier Tradition on the Sects of Physicians. First Division.<-

And since mention has been made of the sects <note>The word "sect" here refers to a school of thought or a specific philosophical approach to medicine</note> of physicians, it does not seem inappropriate to me to bring them forward here into the light. They are currently divided into three parts: some are Greeks, others Arabs, and the third are Latins; and thus there is a threefold form of healing.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial G containing a scene with two figures, possibly putti, in a wooded landscape.</image-desc>The Greeks followed various paths of healing. To Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BCE)</note>, it seemed that the original causes of disease lay in the spirit or breath <note>original: "spiritu siue flatu"</note>, which he calls the father and grandfather of all diseases. To Herophilus <note>An Alexandrian physician (c. 335–280 BCE) who was one of the first to perform scientific dissections</note>, every defect seemed to reside in the fluids <note>original: "humidis"; referring to the theory of bodily humors</note>. But to Asclepiades <note>A Greek physician who practiced in Rome (c. 124–40 BCE) and rejected the humoral theory</note>, it was pleasing to think that the origin of ailments was that if flowing corpuscles <note>original: "corpuscula"; Asclepiades believed the body was composed of "atoms" or particles</note> should halt within invisible pores, they would block the path and obstruct the passages. For Erasistratus <note>An Alexandrian physician (c. 304–250 BCE) often credited as the father of physiology</note> contended that food is ground down <note>original: "atteri"; a mechanical view of digestion</note> in the stomach. Hippocrates favored the idea that food is "cooked" <note>original: "concoqui"; the concept of "coction" or metabolic heat</note> by heat, which Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 CE), whose writings dominated Western medicine for over a millennium</note> confirms. Many...

<summary>This page introduces Champier’s classification of medical history into Greek, Arabic, and Latin traditions, while summarizing the divergent physiological theories of major ancient Greek physicians regarding the causes of disease and digestion.</summary>
<keywords>Medical Sects, Hippocrates, Herophilus, Asclepiades, Erasistratus, Galen, physiology, digestion, humoral theory, corpuscular theory</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page's introduction to the Greek sects (specifically Hippocrates, Herophilus, and Asclepiades), this page continues the hierarchy of Greek influence before transitioning to the Arabic and Latin medical traditions.</meta>

VII
### The Champier Tradition.

...there were physicians among the Greeks; but in the controversy of writings, the better ones are to be imitated, and **Galen** and **Hippocrates** were the first and highest. If leaders are to be followed, I consider **Hippocrates** the leader of all, and **Galen** is to me as Hector was to Paris <note>original: "Hector Paridi." In the Iliad, Hector was the noble protector and man of action, while his brother Paris was often seen as the cause of the conflict; Champier suggests Galen is the strong defender and essential executor of Hippocrates' foundational principles.</note>.

I hold that **Galen** and **Hippocrates** were the first and highest; that one must always weigh their opinions, not merely count them; that these Greeks were the inventors, while the Arabs were the aggregators <note>A term implying they compiled and synthesized existing knowledge rather than discovering new natural principles</note>; that the Greeks were observers of nature and the works of art, while the others were observers of the books written by those Greeks. This is not to detract from their reliability: for **Avicenna** made himself the interpreter of Galen, and for **Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and physician</note>, the words of Galen are held as reason itself: Galen holds the same place for him as **Pythagoras** held among his own disciples <note>Referring to the "Ipse dixit" (He himself said it) authority where the master's word is final and beyond question.</note>.

### Division Eight.

Neither the body without the soul, nor the soul without the body, can be healthy in life. For this reason, many diseases of the body are incurable...

...they are; because nature, which is the mistress of bodily medicine, is a crippled thing in comparison with God. The efforts of natural physicians are also sometimes weak: because, according to Hippocrates of Cos <margin>Hippocrates, 1st Aphorism</margin>,
> "Life is short, but the art is long, the opportunity fleeting, and experience deceptive." <note>original: "Vita brevis, ars vero longa, tempus acutum, experimentum fallax." This is the most famous opening line in the history of medicine, emphasizing the difficulty of mastering the medical craft within a single lifetime.</note>
We perceive the disease of the body less in another [than in ourselves]; yet we perceive the vice of the soul more in others, and even more so in ourselves. Hence that saying of Persius <note>A Roman satirical poet known for his difficult, Stoic-influenced verse</note>:
> "That no one, no one tries to descend into himself. But instead looks at the knapsack on the back of the person walking ahead." <note>original: "Ut nemo in sese tentat descendere, nemo. Sed precedenti spectat mantica tergo." This refers to Aesop's fable where humans carry their own faults in a bag behind them, while staring at the bag of others' faults hanging in front.</note>
Nor should anyone say that the art of Physicians is concerned only with the body itself. For indeed, Phoebus <note>Apollo, the Greek and Roman god of both healing and truth</note> (as is read in the letters of Hippocrates) judged that the healing of the soul and the body should come together as one; whence among the Egyptians, the Priests and Physicians were the same people.

<note>The decorative initial 'A' begins the next section on the divinity of the soul.</note>
The soul, being divine, is purified by the divine mysteries of Theology; therefore, diseases arise no less from the vice of the soul than from that of the body (according to Plato). Whereby it happens that the same Plato, in his *Charmides* <note>A Socratic dialogue concerning temperance</note>, advises that the body should not be treated without the soul, just as the eyes should not be treated without the head. From this, I discover that it was once observed among the Egyptian priests that there was one and the same faculty...

<summary>This page argues that medicine must treat both the body and the soul, citing Hippocrates, Plato, and the traditions of Ancient Egypt to show that physical health is inseparable from spiritual well-being.</summary>
<keywords>Hippocrates, Plato, Persius, psychosomatic medicine, Egyptian priesthood, medical philosophy, Aphorisms, Charmides, Apollo</keywords>

--- Page 27 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page concludes the discussion from Division Eight regarding the spiritual roots of illness and begins Division Nine, which focuses on the historical figures of Euphorbus and Antonius Musa as paragons of the medical profession.</meta>

-> The Campegius Tradition. Leaf 13. <-

[the soul] is occupied with medicines, music, and mysteries. Therefore, before we come to the cure, we must first determine whether the infirmity arises from the body or from the soul. For one must begin from the causes, just as the death of a tree is to be sought not in the branches, but in the root. God is the Physician of souls, and His works are perfect. No disease of the soul is incurable; hence Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, a Roman Stoic philosopher</note> says:
> "The way to good morals is never too late." <note>original: "Nunquam sera est ad bonos mores via." This quote from Seneca's tragedy *Thyestes* emphasizes that moral reformation is possible at any age.</note>
In the view of Plato, virtue is the health of the soul, while vice is its sickness; virtue is a good habit, while vice is a bad one.

### A Comparison of the Physician Brothers, Euphorbus and Antonius Musa. Division Nine.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'F' inside a square border, featuring a landscape with a central tree and foliage.</image-desc>
**F**elicitous indeed was the pairing of these two brothers, who while they lived so greatly illustrated the human condition, and both performed deeds that posterity will forever praise and remember. The one <note>Referring to Antonius Musa</note> restored health to the Prince <note>Emperor Augustus (r. 27 BCE – 14 CE)</note>, whom all throughout the world then willingly obeyed; at that time, nothing was more fortunate for the sake of peace and glory than the Emperor's recovery. The other <note>Referring to Euphorbus</note> offered us a more certain hope of health for many diseases by the discovery of a remedy that was new and unknown until that day. <note>Euphorbus discovered the medicinal properties of the succulent plant *Euphorbia*, which was named after him by his patron, King Juba II of Mauretania.</note> And will anyone wonder at what Homer sang:
> "A man who is a physician is worth many other men." <note>original: "Pro multis inter homines Medicum hominem censeri oportere." A reference to the Iliad (XI.514), where Homer highlights the vital social value of the healer during wartime.</note>
Praiseworthy...

<summary>This page argues that healing must begin at the "root" (the soul) before treating the body and introduces the famous medical brothers Euphorbus and Antonius Musa as historical examples of the profession's dignity.</summary>
<keywords>holistic medicine, Seneca, Plato, Antonius Musa, Euphorbus, Augustus, Homer, soul vs body, medical history</keywords>

## The Campegius Tradition on the Sects of Physicians.

...[they are called] by the poets the "Castors" <note>A reference to the Dioscuri (Castor and Pollux), the twin brothers of Greek and Roman mythology often used as a symbol of brotherly devotion</note>, who, while living by their own virtue, had temples built for them and altars erected. Sacred rites were instituted, and divine honors increased their fame and glory. 

But all those ancient honors are not to be compared to the praises of the physician brothers, Euphorbus and Antonius Musa, for what the one achieved in Roman history and the other in the history of medical materials <note>original: *medicæ materiæ*, referring to *Materia Medica*, the study of the medicinal properties of plants and substances</note>. For those mythological honors have long since perished; but these medical achievements—so long as the name of Roman dignity and fortune is preserved, and as long as it remains necessary to cure men of diseases—will grow with daily increases of praise. 

The Romans, and indeed all the nations in the whole world, once owed the health of Augustus Caesar <note>The first Roman Emperor (r. 27 BCE – 14 CE)</note> to the physician Antonius Musa. When the Emperor's liver was damaged by catarrhs <note>original: *distillationibus*, a medical term of the time referring to a flow of fluid or "rheum" from the head to other organs</note> and he was reduced to despair, he necessarily underwent a contrary and hazardous <note>original: *ancipitem*, meaning "two-edged" or "perilous"</note> method of healing. Because hot poultices were providing no benefit, he was compelled to be cured by cold treatments on the authority of the physician we have mentioned. 

Juba, the King of Mauritania <note>Juba II (c. 48 BCE – 23 CE), a scholar-king and client of Rome</note>, also owes his health to Euphorbus, the brother of Musa. Beyond this recovery, the King celebrated the discovery made through the man's diligence on Mount Atlas: the *Euphorbium* tree <note>The *Euphorbia resinifera*, a succulent plant whose potent resin was highly valued in ancient medicine</note>, whose sap would be used for medicine by all nations throughout the whole world.

<summary>This page concludes a comparison between the mythological Castor and Pollux and the historical brothers Antonius Musa and Euphorbus, highlighting their medical services to Emperor Augustus and King Juba II.</summary>
<keywords>Antonius Musa, Euphorbus, Augustus Caesar, Juba II, Euphorbium, medical history, cold water cure, Mount Atlas, Materia Medica</keywords>

# Letter of Master Symphorien to Master Geoffrey

<margin>Aristarchus’s mark <note>original: "Aristarchi virgula." Aristarchus of Samothrace was an ancient critic known for using a "virgula" or small mark to identify errors or suspect passages in manuscripts.</note></margin>

<margin>The Arabs and the barbarians: however, not all are to be rejected.</margin>
Yet, I do not think that the Arabs, the <term>Carthaginians</term> <note>original: "Poenos." For even among these, there are many things that I judge highly worthy of approval. For in this way, students will easily distinguish what is "pure" from what is "dark" <note>literally "white" and "black"</note> in them. <margin>Errors of the Arabs.</margin>

Thus, it seemed truly most difficult to me [to bring them together] into a body...

## ¶ Jean Reynier to the candid reader.

This little book contains what a thousand massive volumes hold.
What is sought in many, this little book possesses.
If the vast number of medical books does not cause you weariness,
Then this small book will suffice.
And besides the fact that this single small work encompasses 
The same as many thousands of books:
It explains the foul errors of the <term>North Africans</term> <note>original: "Poenorum." Likely referring to North African medical writers within the Arabic tradition, such as Constantinus Africanus.</note> and the Arabs before your eyes—
Errors through which not a few men have perished.
It also learnedly reveals which <term>vein should be opened</term> <note>A reference to phlebotomy or bloodletting, a primary medical treatment in the 16th century.</note>:
An act that will recall many from the <term>Stygian waters</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the River Styx was the boundary to the underworld; to be recalled from it is to be saved from the brink of death.</note>.
It is not easy to say whether it is more useful to the <term>pharmacist</term> <note>original: "pharmacopolae." A seller of drugs or medicines.</note>
Or the physician: it teaches every medicine.
Which are good, which are bad, which can provide health,
Which cause harm, and indeed, each is placed in its proper order.
After you have read this little book with an attentive ear,
You will say immediately, "I have become an <term>Hippocrates</term> <note>The ancient Greek physician regarded as the "Father of Medicine."</note>."
Therefore, candid reader, give thanks to the author.
If you wish to know who he is, he is Symphorianus.
He is that Symphorianus who, like a victor, is able to recall 
Those who are half-dead back to the upper air.
He is that Symphorianus who binds the threads of the <term>Fates</term> <note>original: "Parca." The three goddesses (Moirai) who spun, measured, and cut the thread of human life. The poem suggests Champier can "rewind" the thread of life.</note> against their will,
And returns the wool to the empty distaff.
He is that Symphorianus who is permitted to subvert the law of fate,
And because of whom <term>Charon’s</term> <note>The ferryman who transported souls across the River Styx to the land of the dead.</note> boat is lighter.
Whom both the dire plague and harmful diseases fear.
Whom the Stygian and <term>Tartarean</term> <note>Referring to Tartarus, the deepest abyss of the underworld in classical mythology.</note> lakes fear.

## On Musk, Chapter VII.

<margin>Musk is different from moss.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "Q" featuring a portrait of a man in profile within the circular body of the letter.</image-desc>
What occurs for us regarding the words *moss* and *musk* <note>original: "musco & moscho"</note>: in which only a single letter is changed and an aspiration <note>The letter "h," which in classical grammar represents a breathing sound or "aspiration."</note> is added, yet they indicate things that are entirely different and of a different kind. For indeed, the Latin word for moss <note>original: "muscus"</note> signifies green tufts rather than leaves or foliage, with which stones in rushing streams are clothed during the summer; and, to use the word of **Columella** <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella, a 1st-century Roman writer on agriculture.</note>, they "become mossy" <note>original: "muscantur"</note>. However, that which is called *moschos* by the Greeks—and should be designated by the same name by the Latins—is that substance which in our age is ranked among the most precious perfumes. It also has no small use in medicine, such as in *diamuscus* <note>term: <term>diamuscus</term> (an aromatic medicinal powder or cordial containing musk as its primary ingredient)</note>. The apothecary shops <note>original: "officinae"</note> in our time falsely call this substance "moss," no differently than that earlier botanical growth from trees mentioned in **Dioscorides**;
<margin>Musk, not moss; for musk differs in species from moss.</margin>
whereas it ought to be called *musk* and not *moss*, so that by its proper name it might be distinguished from the tufted moss found on stones in rivers and on trees. Since nothing has hitherto...

It appears the name was derived from the new and tender shoots (*stolones*) found on plants; by similarity to these, new follicles full of that perfume grow on the animals that produce musk. ## Chapter XII. On Parsley

<margin>Sweet Parsley</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring a floral and leafy design within a square frame.</image-desc>Some have given parsley <note>original: "Petroselinum"</note> the name **sweet-root** <note>original: "glycydium"</note>; the seed of this plant is by far the most useful part, as the herb itself is somewhat weaker. For what we commonly call parsley today is actually **celery** <term>apium<note>In classical botany, *apium* was a broad category covering celery, smallage, and parsley; the author is distinguishing between the garden celery used as food and the specific "rock parsley" required for medicine.</note></term>, which the ancients called "garden celery." <margin>Andromachus</margin>

<margin>Gentilis believes that Macedonian parsley is that species of celery which some commonly call *macerones*, and the French call *Alexanders* <note>Referring to *Smyrnium olusatrum*, a forgotten pot-herb often used like celery.</note>.</margin>

According to the testimony of **Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire, whose works formed the basis of Western medicine for centuries.</note>, the variety from **Macedonia** is preferred above all others, and especially the choice-grade Macedonian seeds; it excels in this regard because it is extremely bitter and sharp. The seed of our local variety, however, although it might perhaps seem to possess a certain sharpness, is nonetheless entirely lacking in that necessary bitterness. But since we must do without the Macedonian variety, would that we at least had the variety from **Epirus** <note>A region in northwestern Greece and southern Albania.</note>, which in Galen's time—such was the desire to imitate the true item—was brought into Macedonia by way of Thessaloniki so that it could be sold as the Macedonian type. However, the negligence of more recent authors has resulted in us, lacking both the Macedonian and Epirotic types, using the seed of common celery <note>original: "Apij communis"</note> in its place.

First Book. Folio XXIX.

<margin>Galen</margin>
**Galen** <note>The most influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire, whose works formed the basis of Western medicine for centuries.</note>, in his book *On Theriac to Paphilianus* and in his book *On Antidotes*, writes that **Scordion** <note>original: "Scordion"; usually identified as *Teucrium scordium*, or Water Germander. But the negligence of more recent authors has brought it about that we have lost not only the herb itself called Scordium, but even the meaning of the word itself; people have been deceived by the similarity of the name and take **wild garlic** <note>original: "allium sylvestre"</note> in its place. 
<margin>The herb Scordium</margin>
In this they err more than in the matter of parsley <note>original: "petroselino"</note>, which is put into the **Theriac** <term>Theriaca<note>A famous ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including opium and viper flesh.</note></term> not because it fights against poisonous drugs or wild beasts, but for the sake of **dropsy** <term>aquæ intercutis<note>Literally "water under the skin"; a historical term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note></term> and similar diseases. Furthermore, some trustworthy authors have written that the power of Scordium is so great that whatever bodies of the slain in a certain battle had fallen upon it remained uncorrupted for a longer time, especially those parts which touched the herb itself. From this it is believed (with Galen as a witness) that it strongly fights against the poisons of wild beasts and deadly drugs. 
<margin>Galen</margin>
For this reason, we affirm that the Theriac of our times does not provide those effects which the ancient physicians promised...

From this, a most common error has spread: because the word *skordeon* signifies garlic among the Greeks, they take wild garlic instead of scordium—not only in theriac, but in many other medicinal recipes. But wild garlic <note>original: "scorodon agrium"</note> is one thing; the herb scordium is quite another. Therefore, there is a different virtue and a different property in Avicenna’s theriac than there once was in the antidote of **Andromachus** <note>Physician to Emperor Nero and the inventor of the most famous version of Theriac.</note> or **Galen**; unless, perhaps, we believe that the Arabs and Carthaginians, **Al-Ghazali** and Avicenna, were more learned than Galen ever was.

### On the Armenian Stone Chapter XVI.

<margin>These two stones are not found among us. <insert>Dioscorides: Book [5], Chapter 94</insert> <note>This refers to the *De Materia Medica* by Dioscorides, the primary authority on pharmacology in the Renaissance.</note></margin>
The **Armenian stone** <term>lapis armenus<note>Usually identified as azurite, a blue copper carbonate mineral used both as a pigment and a medicine.</note></term>, or *armeniacus*, is categorized among the so-called "florid" colors <note>original: "colores floridi"; a Roman classification for bright, expensive pigments that were often provided by the patron rather than the painter.</note>. Armenia sends this; it is a stone dyed in the manner of chrysocolla <note>original: "chrysocollae"; a term used in antiquity for various green copper minerals like malachite, used for soldering gold.</note>. The best kind is that which is most green, blending its color with blue. It was once sold for thirty coins per pound. Now, a substance similar to sand has been found throughout Spain which receives a similar treatment, which our pharmacists use in place of the true Armenian stone; for this reason, its value has dropped to six denarii. It differs from the blue <note>original: "caeruleo"; here referring to the pigment blue verditer or perhaps lapis lazuli.</note> by a slight brightness, which makes a softer color than the Armenian stone. Without a doubt, that clod which we call **Armenian bole** <term>bolus armenus<note>A medicinal red clay used as an astringent and to treat various ailments; the author is clarifying that this clay is not the same as the "stone."</note></term> is different from the Armenian stone, and should be categorized among the clays.

# On simple medicines

<margin>Avicenna.</margin>
...is attributed to the Greeks. Although **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (980–1037), a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" remained a standard authority in Europe until the 1600s.</note> writes separately about **lapis lazuli** and the **Armenian stone** among other stones, nevertheless almost everything he reports about **lapis lazuli** is written by Greek authors—especially **Dioscorides** and **Galen**—concerning the **Armenian stone**. Nor is it truly surprising that Avicenna wavered regarding the **Armenian stone** (which is even unknown to the physicians of our own age), since he was so uncertain and doubtful regarding the common herb **Hemlock**. 

<margin>On Hemlock.</margin>
He recorded that it consists sometimes of the leaves of a cucumber, sometimes of **mandrake**, according to the opinions of different authors; and he calls it now *fuccara*, now *alpharas*, and occasionally **black henbane**. For in his second book on simple medicines, he describes hemlock under the name *fuccara*; however, in the fourth book, where he treats poisons, he calls hemlock not *fuccara* but *alphaphars*. He even considers it to be <term>Napellus<note>Aconitum napellus, commonly known as monkshood or wolfsbane; one of the most toxic plants in Europe.</note></term>, or a poison which kills a man but does not kill thrushes. Later, he adds the same reason for this phenomenon as Galen provides—not regarding monkshood and thrushes, but rather regarding **hemlock** and starlings <note>original: "sturnis"; Galen famously observed that starlings could eat hemlock seeds without being poisoned due to their specific metabolism, a common trope in Renaissance toxicology to show how poisons affect different species.</note>.

### Concerning Greater Centaury, Chapter XX.

<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
<margin>Chiron the centaur.</margin>
<margin>To others, it seems that Philoctetes was wounded by the fall of an arrow because of a violated oath, and was restored to health by Machaon.</margin>
**Greater centaury** <note>original: "centaurion maius"</note> has jointed stalks, broad and oblong leaves, and a dense root. The root is tender and fragile; it lasts for no more than twelve years. ...its root is recorded by **Dioscorides** <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary pharmacological text for 1,500 years.</note> to be somewhat sweet; and those who know it have confirmed this to be true through experience. The root is vast, heavy, and hard, reaching a length of up to two **cubits** <note>An ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note>; it is full of juice, with a sharp taste, yet turning reddish with a certain astringency and sweetness. It is abundant in **Lycia**, the **Peloponnese**, **Elis**, **Arcadia**, and **Messene**. It also grows most prolifically around **Mount Pholoe**, **Lycia**, and **Smyrna**. 

The appearance of the centaury is so described by **Dioscorides** and **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> that it seems almost to be placed before one's very eyes. If, however, some troublesome critic should ask what kind of herb it is and by what name it is commonly called by our people, **Niccolò Leoniceno** <note>A leading Renaissance medical humanist who corrected many medieval botanical errors.</note> chose to deliberately conceal it; we, however, say it is the **Greater Centaury**, which the common people falsely call **rhapon-** <note>The word is cut off and likely concludes as "rhaponticum," referring to "False Rhubarb," a common misidentification of the time.</note>

# On Simple Medicines

...calls [rhapon]ticum. Everything that is described by **Dioscorides** <note>An ancient Greek physician and author of the most influential herbal of the pre-modern world.</note> regarding **centaury** fits the herb and root commonly called **rhaponticum** <note>A plant often confused with rhubarb in the Renaissance; the author is arguing that this is actually the true "Greater Centaury" of the ancients.</note> so perfectly that no one—unless they were born blind to nature—could fail to recognize it as the true centaury. 

From this, a double error of our current era is detected. First, we accept the herb named centaury by the ancients under the name of rhaponticum. Second, in place of centaury, we frequently employ a common herb in medical practice of which no mention is made by the ancient authors, doing so without any reason or authority. 

It is easy to observe that **centaury** was written by **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath and physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard university textbook for centuries.</note> in place of **cinquefoil** <note>original: "pentaphyllo"; literally "five-leaved," a common medicinal plant.</note>. For **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note>, whom Avicenna seems to have followed most closely, writes as follows in a certain section when reciting the recipe for the **composition of Andromachus** <note>Andromachus was the physician to Emperor Nero; he is famous for inventing "Theriac," a complex "cure-all" antidote.</note>:

<margin>Avicenna.</margin> **Myrrh** <note>original: "Smyrnes"</note>, **saffron**, **ginger**, **rhapontic**, **cinquefoil**, **calamint**, **horehound** <note>original: "prasij"</note>, **parsley**, **French lavender** <note>original: "Stichados"</note>, and the rest. 

Avicenna, imitating this same order, noted it thus: **Myrrh**, **saffron**, **ginger**, **rhubarb** <note>original: "Rhabarbari"</note>, **centaury**, **mountain calamint**, **horehound**, **parsley**, **French lavender**. 

How could it be more clearly demonstrated that centaury was substituted for cinquefoil? This is especially true since he mentions the same centaury in the same description of the **theriac**... <note>original: "theriaces"; a medicinal paste used as an antidote to poison and for various illnesses.</note>

### On simple medicines

(He says) that **turbith** <note>original: *Turbith*; the root of the plant *Ipomoea turpethum*, used in pre-modern medicine as a strong purgative to "purge phlegm."</note> is called by the barbarians <note>In this context, "barbarians" refers to non-Greek medical authorities, specifically the Arabic authors like Avicenna or Rhazes who introduced many "new" drugs to the West.</note> the root of the plant which is called *pityusa* <note>original: *pitiusa*; a type of Spurge (*Euphorbia*). ### On Buckthorn and Currants Chapter XXVIII.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin> <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician whose pharmaceutical manual *De Materia Medica* remained the primary source on herbal medicine for 1,500 years.</note>

...stretching out <note>original: *tendentes*</note>; and it has large, broad, round, green leaves; and it has berries, the flavor of which is sweet with acidity; and it is cold and dry in the second degree <term>Degree: or "mansion" (original: *mansione*), a classification in Galenic medicine used to measure the intensity of a substance's primary qualities—hot, cold, moist, or dry—on a scale of one to four</term>; and the sign of this is its acidity and astringency; and it cools the stomach. Indeed, the fruit is cold and dry in the second degree of the second order; it binds the bowels, and extinguishes yellow bile, as well as the sharp heat of the blood. 

<margin>Concerning Currants among the French.</margin>
For a few years now, the French and Italians have used this fruit in place of **currants** <note>original: *ribes*</note>. It is no wonder that we lack currants and must seek them from distant regions; therefore, we ought to use our red buckthorn in place of currants, and take a double portion of it. For I think that in this time **currants** are entirely unknown, just as are **costus**, **amomum**, **cassia**, and **aromatic reed** <note>referring to *calamum aromaticum*. These were highly prized plants of antiquity whose exact identities were often lost or heavily debated by Renaissance botanists</note>; unless perhaps one were to concede that the **Currant** is the same as our red buckthorn, which is astringent and tart with a certain sweetness.

## Chapter 29: On Spodium.

<margin>What Spodium is.</margin>
<margin>Pharmacists’ errors.</margin>
<margin>Avicenna.</margin>
<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
<margin>Paul of Aegina.</margin>
<margin>Serapion.</margin>
Among the other causes of errors that have occurred in recent centuries, I believe this was not the least: that **Physicians**, knowing nothing of **simple medicines** <term>Simple medicines: also called "simples," these are medicinal drugs consisting of only one ingredient, usually a herb or mineral, as opposed to "compounds."</term>, left the preparation of medications to the judgment of **pharmacists** <note>original: *pharmacopolarum*, literally "drug-sellers."</note>. From this, it happened that they accepted larch resin instead of **turpentine**, and wild garlic in place of the herb **scordium** <note>original: *scordio*, likely Water Germander, known for its garlic-like scent.</note>. Through this same negligence, it has come to pass that for **spodium**—which according to **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> is the root of burnt reeds (though unknown to both us and Avicenna himself)—more recent pharmacists use **burnt ivory**, or the tooth of a burnt elephant.

Moreover, several trustworthy authors have written—and **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary pharmacological text for 1,500 years.</note> especially—that ivory possesses such great power that shavings of ivory applied as an ointment heal **hangnails** <note>original: *digitorum redivias*</note>; for it has an **astringent** <term>Astringent: a substance that causes the contraction of body tissues, often used to stop bleeding or dry up secretions.</term> nature and force. **Paul of Aegina** <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician known for his medical encyclopedia.</note> prepares this remedy not only from elephant teeth (which alone is truly ivory), but also from the shavings of hooves and other bones. And as **Serapion** <note>Likely Serapion the Younger, a 12th-century author whose work on "simples" combined Greek and Arabic medical knowledge.</note> says in chapter 453: "The filings of an elephant’s tooth are styptic; and a plaster made from them cures **whitlows**." <term>Whitlows: original *panaria*, a painful infection or abscess at the end of the finger or toe.</term>

### Chapter 30: On Acacia.

<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral and scrolling vine patterns.</image-desc>
**A**cacia grows in Egypt: for it is (as **Dioscorides** <note>A Greek physician and botanist whose "De Materia Medica" was the foundational text for pharmacology for centuries.</note> says) a woody thorn bush, shrubby, not growing straight or high, with a white flower and a white seed like that of lupins <note>original: *lupinorum*, a type of legume</note> enclosed in pods. The juice is expressed from these pods and dried in the shade; it is black when taken from the mature fruit and reddish when taken from the immature fruit. Some also express the juice from the leaves along with the seed. Furthermore, a gum <note>original: *gummi*, likely Gum Arabic</note> is produced from this thorn bush. Acacia possesses powers of **astringing** <term>Astringent: a substance that causes the contraction of body tissues, typically used to reduce bleeding or secretions.</term> and cooling. The juice of acacia is well-suited for medicines of the eyes; it is also beneficial for **sacred fires** <note>original: *sacris ignibus*, a historical term for erysipelas or various inflammatory skin conditions</note>, chilblains, those ulcers they call **herpes**, and for **hangnails** <note>original: *pterygijs*, referring here to growths or inflammation around the fingernails</note>.

It checks ulcers of the mouth. Its quality is cold in the second degree, and dry and **styptic** <term>Styptic: a specific type of astringent that stops bleeding by contracting the blood vessels.</term> in the third degree. I do not know if France has seen true acacia in this century, because I have heard no one yet who questions whether that which is brought into Europe from **India** and **Egypt**—specifically by the fleet of the **Portuguese King** <margin>The Portuguese.</margin>—is the true acacia. However, our pharmacists <note>original: *pharmacopolae*</note> accept the thickened juice of **sloe berries** <note>original: *prunellorum*, the fruit of the blackthorn (*Prunus spinosa*)</note> reduced into the form of an **electuary** <term>Electuary: a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup.</term> in place of acacia.

<margin>Pliny.</margin>
**Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> writes in his thirty-fourth book—following common opinion—that **cinnabar** <note>original: *cinnabarim*, a bright red mineral (mercury sulfide)</note>, the color of which in paintings perfectly captures the look of blood, is the **blood of a dragon** <note>original: *sanguinem draconis*</note> crushed by the weight of dying elephants, being a mixture of the blood of both animals. He confirms that this cinnabar is indeed useful for antidotes and medicines. However, he rightly rebukes the physicians of his time who used **minium** <term>Minium: a term that historically caused much confusion, as it was applied both to cinnabar (mercury-based) and red lead.</term> instead of this cinnabar, simply because it was also called "cinnabar." For this "cinnabar" which is also called minium is a **poison**, since **quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: liquid mercury, known in Latin as *argentum vivum*.</term> is made from it...

### On Ambergris, Chapter 32.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'A' containing floral and vine patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
If **ambergris** <note>original: *Ambra*; the author is discussing ambergris (the waxy substance from sperm whales) rather than the fossilized tree resin also called amber.</note> is not the **sperm of the whale** <term>Sperma Ceti: literally "seed of the whale." In the Renaissance, many believed ambergris was either the reproductive fluid or the brain matter of whales.</term>, I candidly confess that I do not know what it is. Some say it is the fruit of a tree in the sea; others a gum; others a flowing spring <note>original: *manacor*; likely a Latinization of an Arabic term for a mineral spring or bitumen source.</note> in the sea. Some say it is the liver of a fish, while others say it is sea foam; still others believe it is the dung of a certain animal. Many, such as <margin>Serapion</margin> **Serapion** <note>Serapion the Younger (12th or 13th century), an influential author of a book on "simple" (single-ingredient) medicines.</note> and all the **Arabs** with him, say it is generated in the sea just as mushrooms grow on the land. And they say that when the sea is disturbed by storms, it casts up stones from its bottom, and with them pieces of ambergris. Therefore, what ambergris truly is remains unknown to our **pharmacists** <term>Pharmacopolis: from the Greek for "medicine-seller"; the predecessor to the modern pharmacist.</term> and all physicians. However, it is certain that it is not a poison: for whether it be whale sperm, or a sea mushroom, or foam, it is not a deadly transformation. Let us forgive them these and other errors—though they are indeed worthy of rebuke—since they do not bring about manifest death.

# Book One. Folio XLVIII.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'G' containing a detailed face or mask amidst classical foliage patterns.</image-desc>

The more esteemed Greeks always called the liquid **scammony** <note>original: *scammonium*; the resinous juice obtained from the root of the *Convolvulus scammonia* plant.</note> in the neuter gender; <margin>Dioscorides</margin> however, **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*, the foundational text of Western pharmacology.</note> calls it *scammonia*. The Egyptians call it *sauilum*, and the Romans call it *colophonium* after the region where it is found. Indeed, it is a matter of daily use in medicine, and there is no one who, upon hearing its other name, does not understand that it has an immediate and very great power for **purgations** <term>Purgations: medicinal treatments intended to "cleanse" the body of excess humors, usually by inducing bowel movements.</term>. Everyone knows the liquid hardened from the root of the herb which the apothecary shops sell. This herb grows in many places, but the most highly approved comes from overseas regions, especially Asia and the entire territory of **Colophon** <note>An ancient Greek city in Ionia (modern-day Turkey) famous for its resins.</note>. The name given to it by various nations testifies that it was once associated with that region; while people sought the most excellent scammony and requested it from Colophon in Asia, they gradually caused what was originally a mark of quality to turn into a name and title. <margin>Theophrastus</margin> **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371 – c. 287 BC), a Greek philosopher and the "Father of Botany."</note> mentions scammony in the ninth book of his *Enquiry into Plants* <note>original: *de plantarum historia*</note>, and he first advised that the liquid should be extracted from the root alone. <margin>Dioscorides</margin> Soon after, contrary to what Dioscorides decreed—that there is only one use for the liquid in scammony—our own doctors sometimes also use a decoction of the root in certain cases; others, however, use the juice...

### On Simple Medicines

...when thickened, they intended it to be **scammony** <note>original: *scammonia*</note>. Some Moors <note>The term "Moor" here likely refers to North African herbalists or practitioners of the medieval Arabic medical tradition whose texts influenced European botany.</note>, however, use the juice of a different herb in place of scammony; and while many do not know what that herb is, it is certain that it is not true scammony. Our own physicians approve of the use of this scammony when it is gathered from both the juice of the plant and its root. However, they reject the kind that **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and author of the foundational pharmacological text *De Materia Medica*.</note> extracts from the liquid, or perhaps they simply lack it—such as the kind brought from Mysia in Asia.

In testing its quality, one should not only observe whether it dries when applied to the tongue; for this effect also occurs if it has been adulterated <note>Adulteration: the practice of debasing a product by adding inferior or harmful substances to increase volume or mimic quality.</note> by mixing in the milky sap of the **spurge** plant <note>original: *lactariæ herbæ*; plants of the *Euphorbia* genus, known for their irritating, latex-like white sap.</note>. <margin>The faults and harms of scammony.</margin> Those scammony liquids produced in Syria and Judea are rejected as being foul-smelling, thick, and adulterated with spurge and **vetch** flour <note>original: *erui farina*; flour made from bitter vetch (*Vicia ervilia*), used here as a cheap filler.</note>.

But I do not know which mortal man could truly distinguish such a fraud. I wish that no scammony would ever cross the sea! For as one of the older philosophers argued, it is dangerous to use **purgatives** <term>Purgatives: medicinal treatments intended to "cleanse" the body of excess humors, usually by inducing bowel movements.</term> that are poisonous; indeed, this has often provided an opportunity for treachery regarding inheritance and wills <note>The author suggests that because scammony is so potent and potentially toxic, it was a convenient tool for secret poisonings.</note>. In this regard, the honesty of the apothecary shops is essential. Furthermore, as **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamum (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> writes, scammony "sharpens" all medicines, although it is also held to be harmful to the stomach. I pity the state of human life, which I see daily endangered under the influence of the **Arabs** <note>A reference to the medieval Islamic medical tradition, which made extensive use of scammony; the author expresses a Renaissance-era skepticism toward these later "Arab" additions to classical Greek medicine.</note> in the use of scammony...

# First Book. Page 49.

It generates sharp, stabbing pains, and causes one to fall into dysentery...

...dysentery and **tenesmus** <note>original: *tenasmonem*; a distressing and constant urge to evacuate the bowels, even when they are empty.</note>; it weakens the heart, liver, and stomach. These are the things which the **Arabs** <note>Referring to the great medieval Islamic physicians like Avicenna and Mesue, whose works dominated European medicine for centuries.</note> wrote concerning true, natural, and pure scammony.

<margin>Poisonous scammony.</margin>If, however, you ask me what this "scammony" is that is sold by our **pharmacists** <note>original: *pharmacopolis*; from the Greek, literally "medicine-sellers."</note> as the real thing, I must say that it is not the scammony described by **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), the author of *De Materia Medica*, the primary authority on herbal medicine in the ancient and medieval worlds.</note>. Rather, it is the juice of some herb that yields a milky, sharp sap, belonging to the family of **spurges** <note>original: *Tithymalorum*; a group of plants in the genus *Euphorbia* known for their irritating, latex-like white sap.</note> or "milk-weeds" (as the younger physicians call them). 

For such is the scammony sold by our pharmacists in place of the true variety: indeed, I would hardly believe that any pure and fresh scammony is ever imported. For what I have been able to see so far differs greatly in smell, color, and substance from the qualities of true scammony. But both the Arabs and the Greeks complain that it is **adulterated** <note>Tampered with or mixed with cheaper, often inferior or dangerous substances.</note> in various ways; they note that scammony found in the shops of pharmacists can be deadly when taken internally. Unless, perhaps, we ourselves are beyond this danger, since we never use scammony (or *scammonea*, if you prefer); instead, in place of scammony, we employ **aloe**, **rhubarb**, or other more gentle medicines.

# On Simple Medicines

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
The Romans call **Asphalton** <note>original: *asphalton*; a Greek term for various types of mineral pitch or asphalt.</note> "bitumen." According to **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), the primary ancient authority on the medicinal properties of plants and minerals.</note>, Judean bitumen is superior to all other varieties. It is judged to be pure if it shines with a purple-like luster, is heavy, and possesses a strong, pungent odor. Conversely, it is rejected if it appears dull and black in color, for this indicates it has been **adulterated** <note>Mixed with inferior substances to increase volume.</note> with added pitch. It is found in **Phoenicia, Sidon, and Babylon**.

It is also produced among the **Arverni** <note>A region in central France, modern-day Auvergne.</note> between the city of **Clermont** and a small town the inhabitants call **Pont-du-Château** <note>original: *pontem castrum*.</note>. There, liquid bitumen floats on the surface of springs, which the locals use as a substitute for oil to fuel their lamps. It is likewise produced in the territory of **Agrigento** in Sicily as a liquid; as Dioscorides writes, people there mistakenly call it "Sicilian oil." 

Since it is indeed a type of liquid bitumen, our people simply call it "bitumen." This is the origin of the name for the lake in **Judea** where it is found, called **Lake Asphaltites** <note>Now known as the Dead Sea. In antiquity, large blocks of bitumen were famously harvested from its waters.</note>. The river **Jordan**, flowing from the other lake, **Tiberias** <note>The Sea of Galilee.</note>, empties into this Lake Asphaltites. **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus, the influential Roman physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> recorded that the water in Syria is salty, and for that reason, it is called the **Dead Sea**. 

Judean bitumen is preferred by Dioscorides over all others because its natural properties and medicinal strength are the most effective. This is further evidenced by the testimony of **Strabo** <note>A Greek geographer and historian.</note> in his description of Judea, where he records that even from a distance, by its own power, it [acts upon] the most solid...
<margin>Strabo</margin>

# Whether stags have bones in their hearts
## Chapter XXXVI.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

### On Simple Medicines

<note>original: "vy"; completing the sentence from the previous page</note>vy <note>The text likely reads "heavy odor" (graui odore)</note> odor, is dark in color, and does not easily melt. The power and nature of aloe is to bind from the outside <term>astringent</term>, to induce sleep, to dry, to thicken the body, to loosen the belly, and to purge the stomach. When drunk, it loosens the bowels; indeed, in a weight of three drachms <note>A drachm was a unit of weight roughly equal to 1/8th of an ounce</note>, it purges excellently. 

<margin>Galen, *On Simple Medicine*, in his book *To Paternianus*.</margin>
"Aloe," says **Galen**, "is the juice of a herb that is similar to a squill <note>A bulbous plant in the lily family used in ancient medicine</note>." He says: "We judge the best to be that which is brittle, a clean lump, rich, shiny, pure, and reddish, and very bitter in taste if it is drunk. It both loosens the belly and purges rot <note>putredinem</note>, choler, and phlegm <note>Choler (yellow bile) and phlegm were two of the four humors; excess of these was thought to cause disease</note> when given with oxymel <note>A traditional syrup made of honey and vinegar</note> in a dose of two drachms. It is a great aid for those with stomach and liver ailments." 

<margin>Mesue asserts that aloe opens the veins and causes bleeding, although—to say nothing of Pliny—Dioscorides, Galen, reason, and experience all attest that it stops blood flowing from anywhere, even if it is emitted through coughing.</margin>
And aloe is, as Galen writes in the sixth book of *On Simples*, chapter 23, a drying medicine in the third degree of dryness, and warm in the first extended degree, or the second restrained degree <note>In Galenic medicine, drugs were ranked from 1 to 4 based on how much they heated or dried the body</note>. Beginning his treatment of the harmless variety, he says: "**Ephemeron**—not the one that is harmful and lethal, etc." It is clear from that proposition and division of the argument that there are two types of this genus: one which has the nature of a poison, and the other which has the nature of a remedy.

We leave it now to be sought by the more expert whether those plants which physicians, herbalists, and **pharmacists** <note>original: "pharmacopolę"; literally "drug-sellers."</note> now call **hermodactyls** <note>original: "hermodactylos"; literally "Hermes' fingers." **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of *Natural History*.</note> (as it seems) followed **Dioscorides** <note>The author of *De Materia Medica*, the most influential botanical text of the era.</note>, whom he revered, more closely in the color of the flower. For in **Pliny's** account of this ephemeron, these are the words: "**Ephemeron** has the leaves of a lily, but smaller; a similar stem; and a **blue flower**." These words cannot be reconciled unless they are interpreted to mean a white color <note>The author is struggling with a textual corruption in Pliny; he believes the description of "blue" must be an error for "white" because of his own observations.</note>. Pistachios are commonly named *fistici* by pharmacists, just as pine nuts are called *pineoli*.

### To the most illustrious and most learned man, his father Symphorien Champier, Knight of the Golden Spur and Chief Physician <term>Archiatrus: a title for a high-ranking or court physician</term> to the people of Lorraine, Antoine Champier sends many greetings.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'D' showing a seated figure in a landscape with trees and plants, possibly a botanist or physician studying nature.</image-desc>

Those dictations of yours, most illustrious father, in which you refute the ignorance of the Arabs and teach the pharmacists and younger physicians in how great a darkness of things they are turned about regarding the errors of herbs, fruits, roots, and stones which we use daily—I do not know whether they brought me more pleasure or more pain. For I was wonderfully delighted that those matters upon which the life and health of men depend were brought to light by that man above all whom, after God, I have always most revered and deservedly esteemed most highly. 

Yet I grieved, in turn, for the sake of the human race, because it has suffered this dismal "Muhammadan" <note>original: *mahumeticam*; the author is using religious labels to discredit the medical traditions of the Islamic world, which dominated medieval European medicine</note> rather than Christian sect from the Arabs to rage against it so long with impunity. From these Persians and Arabs, people sometimes buy the hope of life at a high price, even though from that source the most certain death proceeds. Hence it has come to pass, that by the perverse [nature] of some...

...by their judgment, the worst have crept in to replace the best, and the dull to replace the learned. Thus, neglecting the teachings of the best authors, one physician has chosen Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was the standard textbook in Europe for centuries, though criticized by Renaissance humanists.</note> for himself, while another holds tenaciously to a certain Rhazes <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (865–925), another major Persian medical authority.</note>. Another has likewise embraced Arnold <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous medieval Catalan physician.</note>; and indeed, each one is driven by his own madness and ignorance to this point, thinking that he can attain mastery of medicine through such a shortcut. For this reason, an opinion has settled so stubbornly in their minds and is so deeply fixed that they consider it a sin to disagree by even a hair’s breadth <note>original: *latum unguem*; literally "a fingernail's width."</note> from the authority they have proposed to imitate. Entangled in these countless labyrinths of error, they have been unable to reach the knowledge of the truth. Thus it has happened that they provide one remedy in place of another, and one disease is treated as if it were another, until there seems to be more danger from the physician than from the disease itself. I had these things to write to you, most illustrious father, more to comply with your wishes than to offer advice to your fatherly wisdom. Farewell, and love me harmoniously <note>original: *symphoniace*; a wordplay on his father's name, Symphorianus.</note>, as you are accustomed to do.

### Letter.

...concerning simple drugs <term>pharmaca: from the Greek *pharmakon*, meaning both medicine and poison.</term>, so also I might write for you a certain model and, as it were, a sketch of compound medicines, touching very briefly upon all its main points rather than explaining them in full.

<margin>Dioscorides on the Persian fruit <note>original: *persico pomo*; referring to the peach tree (*Prunus persica*), which was believed by the ancients to have been poisonous in its native Persia.</note></margin>

For (as Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and botanist whose *De Materia Medica* was the foundation of Western pharmacology.</note> says), some have reported that there was a deadly tree in Persia which, when later transplanted into Egypt, changed its nature and became healthy and edible.

<margin>Columella.</margin>

Furthermore, a weightier witness and authority on this matter is Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella (4–c. 70 AD), an influential Roman writer on agriculture.</note> in his poem, who, while dealing with annual fruits according to the seasons—after pausing for early figs, apricots <term>armenica: literally "Armenian apples."</term>, and plums <term>damascena: plums originally from Damascus.</term>—immediately added:

*Baskets are packed with fruits which barbarian Persia*
*Had sent; and the story goes they were armed with ancestral poisons:*
*But now, having set aside the death once offered with little distinction,*
*They provide ambrosial juices, having forgotten their harmfulness.*
<note>original: *Stipari calathos pomis que barbara Persis Miserat...* from Columella's *De Re Rustica*, Book X.</note>

<margin>A change of place changes the properties.</margin>

Just as he says here that this tree was once believed to be deadly in Persia, but soon, having lost its power to harm, it produces fruits beloved by all: in the same way, Scammony <note>A purgative resin obtained from the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*.</note> and Turpeth <note>The root of *Operculina turpethum*, used as a strong laxative in medieval medicine.</note> were perhaps once healthy for the Persians and Arabs, but are now deadly and poisonous to the French and Italians. Consequently, the medicines composed from them are destructive, such as the *diaphonicon* of Mesue <note>A date-based laxative electuary attributed to Mesue the Younger, a likely pseudonymous Arabic author whose works were standard in the Middle Ages.</note>, the *Electuary of Juice of Roses* by Nicolaus <note>Nicolaus Salernitanus, author of the *Antidotarium*, a central text for medieval pharmacists.</note>, and other similar preparations.

**Psellus** <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and physician</note> writes to the **Emperor Constantine** as follows: Quinces are very styptic <note>original: "stiptica" — astringent, causing the contraction of body tissues</note>; if one preserves them by cooking them with honey or sugar, they strengthen the stomach and are beneficial in cases of dysentery by suppressing **yellow bile** <note>one of the four humors, associated with heat and irritability</note>, and they gladden the heart.

*   Take one and a half ounces of **cinnamon**; 
*   One ounce of **ginger**—

## On the triphera, which our people call Persian, but I call demonic or furious.

<margin>
Cacodemonic triphera, which they call Persian. <note>original: "Trifera cacodæmonica" — cacodemonic implies "evil spirit," here used by the author to criticize the dangerous nature of the preparation.</note>
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring scrolling vines and floral motifs.</image-desc>
Among the other causes of errors that have occurred in medicine in recent centuries, I believe this was not the least: that younger physicians, knowing nothing about simple medicines <term>simple medicines: "simples" are individual herbs or minerals used as drugs, as opposed to "compounds" which mix many ingredients</term>, left the composition of medicines to the judgment of the ointment-sellers, whom the common people call *aromatarii* <note>original: "aromatarios" — spice-merchants or apothecaries</note>. From this it happened (to say nothing of the rest) that that antidote of dangerous and difficult composition was named "Persian Triphera" <term>triphera: a Latinized form of the Arabic "itrifal," which originates from the Sanskrit "triphala" (three fruits); it was a common category of electuaries in medieval medicine</term> by a certain Persian physician desiring to usurp that name for himself. I, however, being cautious and careful in every medical matter, cannot help but fear that some ingredients were utterly lacking in this triphera, or that spoiled ones were added, which I believe are entirely ignored by pharmacists and younger physicians. 

<margin>
Younger physicians have written very poorly regarding simple medicines.
</margin>

And these things regarding furious nightshade <term>solanum furiosum: likely Belladonna or "Deadly Nightshade," known for its hallucinogenic and lethal properties</term> were written by Theophrastus, which have been rendered here in his own words so that, when compared 
<margin>Dioscorides</margin>

But however the matter stands, this is a plant easy to find and recognize, which they call "nightshade," "sleep-inducing," and "furious" alike. All the ancients report that both plants—those they call sleep-inducing nightshade and also the furious kind—are harmful to the mind. Dioscorides, describing its powers more precisely, warned that swallowing more than twelve of its fruits, which he calls clusters <note>original: "corymbos"</note>, produces ecstasy <note>original: "ecstasin" — from the Greek *ekstasis*, meaning to stand outside oneself; here used to describe a total alienation of the mind or a "trip."</note>, meaning an alienation of the mind and madness; he understands this not as just any simple madness, but specifically what the Greeks call *Ecstasin*, where a person departs from themselves and stands outside their own mind.

<margin>Poisonous Persian Triphera</margin>
Therefore, the "Persian Triphera" <term>Trifera perfica: an ancient "electuary" or paste-medicine, originally from Persian tradition, which often contained many ingredients including opium or toxic herbs</term>, on account of these properties of nightshade, makes and renders men maniacal, fanatical, and displaced from themselves. For in that antidote (as noted in Book 1), the juice of nightshade or *solatrum* is an ingredient. Only a few years ago did this *triphera* come into use among our own people in Lyon <note>original: "Lugdunenses" — the citizens of Lyon, France, a major center for medicine and printing in the Renaissance.</note>. I wish it had never arrived, and that the Persians alone used it! Indeed, we have seen many who took it become fanatical and senseless...

## Book Second

...many simple ingredients enter into it that are contrary to one another, such as nightshade <term>solanum: specifically "sleep-inducing nightshade" or Withania somnifera / Physalis alkekengi, though often confused with lethal varieties</term>, which is cold in the third degree, dry, sleep-inducing, and poisonous. Likewise, one pound of vinegar is added; yet hot ingredients also enter in, such as mace and cubebs <note>Mace is the spice from nutmeg husks; cubebs are a type of peppercorn.
