<margin>Serapio</margin>
Serapio <note>Ibn Sarabi (12th century), an influential Christian physician who wrote in Arabic and was a primary source for medieval herbalism.</note> says that nightshade induces evil side effects and madness, making men feel as if they are drunk for three days, and finally leads to death. And, as Mesue <note>John Mesue (Yuhanna ibn Masawayh), a Persian physician; his "Antidotary" was a standard text for European pharmacists.</note> says, the fruit of nightshade always generates a confusion of the senses. Therefore, one must beware of that "triphera" <note>original: "trifera" — a type of medicinal electuary or preserve, usually containing three types of myrobalan fruits.</note> as if from a roaring lion. Thus, to conclude, we must admit that this Persian Triphera is poisonous, ruinous, and an enemy to human nature.

<header>On Compound Medicines</header>

...they deemed it a sin to change [these old formulas]; but the fault lies much more with our modern physicians—the doctors, I mean—who have basely accepted such defects and, even more basely, have fostered them to this day. For they lacked neither talent nor learning, but rather the will to correct them. Furthermore, most of these errors appear so nakedly that no one is of such dull wit that the defects do not reveal themselves at first glance. Here is an example of what I mean.

In the pills of <term>hermodactyls: "fingers of Hermes," likely meadow saffron or colchicum, used since antiquity for joint pain</term>, there is included <term>turbith: the root of *Operculina turpethum*, an exotic and harsh purgative</term>, which is extremely poisonous and unknown. <margin>Modern physicians.</margin>

In the pills of <term>lapis lazuli: a deep-blue semi-precious stone</term>—or rather, if it be permitted to say so, "pills of the devil"—the stone is poisonous, ruinous, and known only to painters <note>Lapis lazuli was the source of ultramarine pigment; its use as an internal medicine was highly controversial due to its abrasive and toxic qualities.</note>. <term>Hellebore: a plant famous for treating madness but notoriously difficult to dose without causing death</term>, finally, was never actually tested by a true Christian.

In the pills of <term>Armenian stone: a blue copper carbonate, similar to azurite</term> described by Mesue <note>John Mesue, an influential Persian physician whose "Antidotary" was a standard pharmaceutical text in Europe.</note>, a stone is included that is known in Armenia alone, but is found nowhere else. <term>Scammony: a harsh resinous purgative, here referred to by the pharmaceutical name dyagredium</term> is likewise an enemy to the nature of the stomach.

In the pills we call "of <term>mezereon: *Daphne mezereum*, a shrub with highly toxic berries and bark</term>," there are milky substances <note>original: "lacteria" — refers to plants with a milky sap, often highly caustic purgatives</note> and things contrary to nature; and mezereon itself is ruinous.

### Second Book. Folio LXXXVI.

<term>Mesue's</term> <note>original: "Mesuæ" — referring to Mesue the Younger, an influential but semi-mythical 11th-century Arabic medical authority whose works dominated European pharmacy for centuries</note> <term>colocynth: the "bitter apple," a desert vine fruit known for its violent purgative effects</term> is abrasive to the belly and harmful to the limbs; <term>turbith: a purgative root from the East</term> is poisonous, unknown, and (as Mesue himself says) a milky substance. Likewise, <term>xylobalsamum: the wood of the balsam tree</term> is unknown to the French and Italians. In the <term>minor pills of light: "catapotiis lucis minoribus," a specific traditional formula for eye health</term>, there is included <term>carpobalsamum: the fruit of the balsam tree</term>, which has never been known by our people. Likewise, <term>lapis lazuli: a deep-blue semi-precious stone</term> is familiar to painters, but ruinous when used by physicians. 

These things were discovered and put into use by barbarians, Muslims, Persians, Arabs, Carthaginians, and Africans. <note>The author uses "barbarous" in the Renaissance humanist sense, referring to non-Greek and non-Roman sources that "corrupted" classical knowledge.</note> Therefore, most dear reader, act so that this barbarism—which long ago occupied all the good arts—may be exploded and utterly driven out. For this reason, it will be your duty and the duty of others who delight in proper studies to strive to do together with me what I cannot achieve alone. 

Certain men of letters have recently claimed for themselves the praise of having liberated France <note>original: "vindicatæ Galliæ"</note> from the barbarians and the Arabs; let us claim that same praise for ourselves much more justly. <margin>Galen.</margin> **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> teaches the same in the fourth book of his work *On Simple Medicines* <note>original: "De simplicium medicamentorum temperamentis et facultatibus"</note>, chapter four, saying:

### To Whom Curative Medicine is Suited, and in Which Diseases Concoction Must Precede Chapter 2.

# On the Method of Curing Bodies

...medicine casts down, it ought to be carried to the bowels; and thus they are neither drawn out themselves, nor are they an impediment to others. It follows that if the medicine is weak, it cannot prevail over many and copious **humors** <term>humors: the four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern health.</term>: otherwise, an "unformed" or ineffective action would arise from the weaker force—which is impossible for nature—and thus the medicine only moves the humors but does not draw them out. This results in a great disturbance of the whole body. Therefore, medicines should only be attempted, according to the edict of **Hippocrates**, when things are **concocted** <term>concocted: the process where the body's natural heat "ripens" raw humors, making them ready to be expelled.</term>, not raw. **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129 – c. 216 AD), the influential Roman physician whose works dominated medical theory for over a millennium.</note> also teaches this in the first book of his *Commentary on the Aphorisms*, section 23, writing:

> In long-lasting diseases, it is always necessary to wait for concoction: for then we have nature itself assisting the evacuation. Indeed, it seems that after concoction, nature itself distinguishes the humors and expels superfluities. But when nature moves them perfectly, medicine is not needed; if, however, it acts more moderately or weakly, it is necessary to supply what is lacking through medicating, so that the evacuation of the harmful humor happens from both sources: nature indeed expelling, and the medicine drawing it out. For just as humors are not to be diminished before concoction, so too they are not to be eradicated [prematurely] after it.

### Avicenna, Book 3, Treatise 4, Chapter 1: On the Care of Colic

...writes thus: "And it sometimes happens that medicines that draw from the body attract other bad humors to the intestines, and sometimes they even attract pure humors. ...regarding the ulceration of the intestines <note>original: *cerationis intestinorum*; likely referring to the pathology of dysentery described on the previous page.</note>, he says the following: "And if evacuation should be necessary on account of the malice of the humors <term>malice of the humors</term> <note>original: *humoris maliciam*; refers to 'bad' bodily fluids, such as corrupt bile or phlegm, believed to cause disease.</note>, use it with fear and caution. <margin>Leonhart Fuchs</margin>
Leonhart Fuchs <note>A German physician and botanist (1501–1566), famous for his herbal and for his critique of medieval Arabic medicine in favor of original Greek sources.</note> does not approve of the opinion of those who use rhubarb in any way, even when it is roasted <note>original: *torrefacto*; the process of parching the root over heat, which was thought to lessen its laxative effect and increase its ability to stop diarrhea.</note>. For he says that even if these people think they are imitating the example of the ancients in this matter, they are nevertheless deceived in their opinion. For they will find that not one of the ancients—indeed, not even Avicenna, their prince—used rhubarb to move the bowels. 

Nor is that strange, for he says the rhubarb of the ancients was completely different from our own. Hence, since this rhubarb of ours is something other than that which the ancients used, it is inevitable that those who think they are following the ancient example by using our rhubarb are being deceived.

## Chapter IX. For whom evacuation is suitable, and for whom only alteration.

<margin>Galen</margin><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter G with foliate ornamentation and a central mask-like face.</image-desc>Galen, in his explanation of Aphorism 18, Book 2 <note>The *Aphorisms* of Hippocrates were a collection of brief medical truths; Galen wrote extensive commentaries on them to explain their deeper meaning.</note>, writes in this manner: "Repletion" <note>original: *repletio*; a state of being overfilled with food or fluids beyond what the body can process.</note> is defined as more food than is suitable for nature’s measure. Indeed, this is twofold in our bodies: one relates to the large capacity of the vessels, and the other relates to that which does not govern

And they teach that the former is called by another name: **repletion relative to strength** <note>original: *repletio ad uirtutem*; a state where the body's vital forces or "strength" are overwhelmed by the volume of fluids, even if the veins are not physically full</note>.

But how much they have hallucinated in defining it thus, we have already shown more clearly than the midday sun. There is one repletion in quantity, which is called plethora; and another in quality, which is called cacochymia. # Book Three. Folio 104. #

**Galen**, who is usually considered second among the leading physicians, <margin>Galen</margin> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; he was typically ranked second only to Hippocrates</note> is accustomed to mention in the books he wrote regarding fevers, that it is necessary for a physician to know the **temperament** <term>temperament: the unique balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines an individual's health and personality</term> of the human body and the nature of every single thing. This can indeed be understood with quite clear reasoning from the very foundations of the medical art: that is, it is usually easily grasped from the appearance of the body itself, from the arteries and veins, from the prognostic signs found in the urine, from the limbs and their color, the natural motion of the body, age, and sensation. It is also found in the disposition of the mind, habit, exercise, the qualities of the weather, the time of year, the region, the seasons, the humors, the dietary regime, various occurrences, other accidents, and finally, by notable signs.

Yet, there are certain hidden things, and it is less surprising that the causes of these cannot be provided by our natural philosophers than it is that universal causes are established in so many other matters. Why those who are bilious <note>original: *biliosi*; people with an excess of yellow bile, thought to be irritable or "choleric"</note> should crave sharpness is an evident reason; but why one man flees from the smell of garlic or another from cheese is perceived only with difficulty. For certain properties of nature are "blind," known only through experience. For this reason, we have heard among the examples of this that a certain man, early in the morning, offered a **purgative** <term>cathartic: a medicinal substance used to purge the bowels</term>—which had been warmed by the steam of a glowing coal <note>original: *prunæ uapore*; "pruna" can mean a plum or a glowing coal; in this medical context of warming a draught, a hot coal is the likely heat source</note>—to one of the servants in his household who was sick, though not without great difficulty... <margin>Note this story.</margin>

Take half an ounce each of castor <term>castoreum: a secretion from the scent glands of a beaver, frequently used in ancient and medieval medicine to treat nervous disorders</term>, wild rue, pellitory-of-Spain seed <term>pyretrum: a pungent root used as a stimulant</term>, and sweet flag root <term>acorus: an aromatic marsh plant</term>; ten grains of pepper; and one pound of honey-water <term>hydromel: a mixture of honey and water</term>. Let a decoction be made of these until reduced to nine ounces; take three ounces warm in the morning. First, let the bowels be relieved with enemas; then let a purgative medicine be made from aloe, larch agaric <term>agaricus: a wood-growing fungus used as a strong laxative</term>, and polypody fern. Very potent hot ointments made from warming and drying substances should be applied; the bowels should be kept constantly loose."

->For a sore throat or quinsy, according to Archigenes and Antonius Musa.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'A' featuring a seated figure in academic or medical dress, possibly representing the physician Archigenes.</image-desc>

## For those with jaundice.

Those suffering from jaundice <note>original: *arquatos* or *ictericos*; "arquatus" refers to the "bowed" or rainbow-colored appearance of the eyes</note> should be given a potion made from a decoction of ground celery <note>original: *apij*</note>, or maidenhair fern <note>original: *adianthi*</note>, or dock <note>original: *lapathi*</note>, or wild thyme <note>original: *serpilli*</note>. Also, a small cup <term>cyathus: a Roman liquid measure, about 45ml</term> of radish juice <note>original: *raphani*</note> drunk with white wine is very beneficial, as is chicory juice <note>original: *cichorij*</note> with wine. Likewise, one drachm of shavings from a stag’s horn <note>original: *cornu cerui*</note> in white wine is effective. Asclepiades <note>A famous Greek physician who practiced in Rome in the 1st century BCE</note> also used to compel patients to drink salt water for two days for the sake of purging, while rejecting those remedies that stimulate urination.

## For colic, according to Alexander.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a seated figure within a square frame decorated with foliage.</image-desc>
Burn the liver of a wild boar <note>original: *aprinum hepar*</note>; dissolve it and give it to be drunk with wine, and it will be beneficial. Let the potions consist of wormwood and cumin in equal parts, or one drachm of castor <note>original: *castorei*; a pungent secretion from the beaver used to treat nervous and digestive ailments</note>, anise, and pepper with oxymel <term>oxymel: a traditional medical preparation made from honey and vinegar</term>.

## For stones, both of the kidneys and the bladder.

->Book four. Folio CIX.<-

...cleansing the bladder, which also break them <note>The "them" refers to kidney or bladder stones mentioned in the preceding text.</note> apart. 

Take wild rue <note>original: *rutæ agrestis*</note>, wild mallow <note>original: *maluę agrestis*</note>, and celery roots; boil them with wine, press out the liquid, and mix in water. Give two small cups <term>cyathus: a Roman liquid measure, approximately 45ml or 1.5 ounces</term> every morning. These are the signs of stones <note>original: *calculorū*</note> in the kidneys: the urine produced is scanty and sandy, and the urinary passage is obstructed. Therefore, the material cause <note>In Galenic medicine, the "material cause" is the physical substance—in this case, "thick and earthy" fluids—that forms the ailment.</note> for the generation of stones is a thick and earthy humor. The efficient cause <note>The "effectrix" or agent that triggers the formation.</note>, however, is a burning heat of the kidneys or the bladder. Indeed, for stones in the kidneys, one must use medicines that wear them down and cut through them, yet in such a way that they do not cause excessive heating. 

Medicines of this kind include: asparagus roots, maidenhair fern <note>original: *adianthū*</note>, the bark of laurel root, and marshmallow seed <note>original: *altheæ*</note>; also the broth of black chickpeas, squill vinegar <note>original: *scylliticū acetū*; vinegar infused with sea onions, used as a diuretic</note>, and saxifrage <note>original: *saxiphrages*; literally "stone-breaker," a plant traditionally used for urinary stones</note>. Frequent baths should also be used, and after the bath, the patient should drink something from the remedies mentioned above.

### For gout.

Take four ounces <term>uncia: roughly 27 grams</term> each of solid beans and lupins; grind them together and mix with a pound of swine fat <note>original: *adipis suille*; lard</note>. Apply it cold to a hot [inflammation] and hot to a cold [inflammation]. For the same ailment, lentil flour mixed with rose oil is also effective; likewise, stork dung <note>original: *stercus ciconię*</note> mixed with fat.

->On the cures of the ailments of the human body<-

...mixed with pork fat <note>original: *porcino*; likely lard or grease used as a base for ointments</note> cures gout <note>original: *podagram*; specifically refers to gout in the feet</note>. ## For dysentery.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a landscape scene with buildings or ruins in the background and a tree with foliage in the foreground.</image-desc>
By the Latins, dysentery is called *tormen* <term>tormen: a Latin term for "twisting" or griping pains in the bowels, from the verb *torquere*</term>: it is an ulceration of the intestines, sometimes arising from a persistent tenesmus <term>tenesmus: a distressing and constant urge to evacuate the bowels, often with little or no stool</term>, or sometimes from some rupture of the belly. The onset of the disease begins with various bilious excrements; then, in turn, they become bloody, and finally purulent <note>original: *purulenta*; containing or consisting of pus</note>, of the kind that usually flows from carcasses. For these griping pains, the juice of purslane <note>original: *portulacæ*</note> is effective and is a suitable drink for those with dysentery; the cooked purslane itself may also be chewed. Common plantain <note>original: *arnoglossum*; literally "lamb's tongue," a common medicinal weed</note> and a decoction of marshmallow <note>original: *altheæ*</note> root are also suitable, provided an enema <term>clystere: a liquid preparation injected into the rectum</term> of honey-water <term>mellicrato: melicrate, a mixture of honey and water</term> is administered first. Eggs roasted in vinegar and eaten also dry out the discharges of the bowels. Furthermore, the dry dung of dogs that eat bones, drunk with goat's milk, is of great help. Likewise, enemas made from the juice of common plantain, plantain <note>original: *plantaginis*</note>, and honey-water are effective.

# Book Four. Folio CXI.

...another remedy of wonderful effect: in a glass vessel they place six parts of elderflowers <note>original: *sambuci florum*</note>, three parts of dwarf elder <note>original: *ebuli*; also known as danewort</note>, one part of St. John's wort <note>original: *hyperici*</note>, and as much very old oil as is sufficient so that it floats above a proper infusion. Then, having sealed the mouth of the vessel, the mixture is prepared by exposure to continuous sunlight throughout the entire summer. Once it has been sun-treated <note>original: *insolato*; the process of "insolation" was used to infuse the oil with the properties of the herbs using gentle solar heat</note> in this way, they use it where needed; they rub it on carbuncles <term>carbuncle: a cluster of agonizing boils or skin ulcers, a primary symptom of the bubonic plague</term> and all inflammations without end three or four times a day. Others rub it over the entire body, from which the entire force of the sickness is drawn out through a profuse flow of intense sweating.

# On the care of ailments of the human body

## A healing potion for the plague, often tested, and never found to be in vain.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' with floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>
Take two drachms <term>drachm: a unit of weight approximately equal to 3.9 grams</term> of the aforementioned cordial powder, and one drachm of shavings of stag's horn <note>original: *ramenti cornu cerui*; hartshorn was a common source of ammonia in historical medicine</note>. Take one and a half drachms of "holy seed" (as the common people call it) <note>original: *seminis sancti*; likely santonica or wormseed</note> or myrrh, if it can be found; if it cannot, use aloes in its place. This is drunk with the sharpest possible vinegar over a fire as soon as the groin is affected <note>original: *inguina tentantur*; a reference to the swelling of lymph nodes, or buboes, in the groin, which was a primary symptom of the bubonic plague</note>. For the remedy must be ready at hand: for as the sweat breaks out from every part, the venom of the disease is drawn out. And so, near the fire, the limbs must be wiped of the foul sweat with warmed linens, and these cloths must be changed until the stench of the sweat subsides during the rubbing. For it delivers those attacked by the pestilence with marvelous protection; and it is established by clear and common experience that no one who has drunk this potion in a timely manner while fasting will be overcome by this violence.

Fo. CXII.

### Book Four.

...-ache <note>original: *pudendagram*; a term coined from the Latin *pudenda* (shameful parts) and the Greek *agra* (seizure/ache), used here to refer to syphilis</note>: and we say that among epidemics—that is, diseases wandering among the people at large—it ought to be numbered among the purulent diseases: for this disease occurs by divine wrath. Indeed, it is the opinion of the **Blessed Fathers**, who spoke by the inspiration of God, that for many reasons it happens that humans, pressed by the narrow hardships of this life, are scourged by God in manifold ways. Among these, many are seized by God so that, through the scourges, they might rightfully erase the stains of a shameful life through penance: for the sin that prudence does not anticipate or avoid, penance wipes away, which carries us to the harbor of heaven. But because some are so foolish that they do not care to be saved, the Best God rebukes their negligence with lashes, shakes off their drowsiness, and, like a **Good Shepherd**, strives to drive away lethargy and idleness with whips. For this reason, God willed to punish the sin of lust <note>original: *luxuria*; in this context, it refers specifically to sexual immorality or "luxury" in the sense of excess</note> in every law. 

In the Law of Nature, when men progressed from the solemn customs of their fathers toward evil, they no longer offered legitimate honors to God, but instead showed that the zeal they previously held for virtue had turned into a double malice through the deeds they performed. Because of this, they provoked God against them: for many **Angels of God** (as Josephus writes) 
<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 1, Chapter 5.</margin> 
coupling with women, fathered injurious sons who, despising all good because of their confidence in their own strength, are said to have perpetrated deeds similar to those whom the Greeks call **Giants**. Wherefore God condemned not only their malice, but the entire human race; only **Noah** was liberated. 

Likewise, because of lust, God was provoked 
<margin>The same author [Josephus], in the same [book], Chapter 19.</margin> 
against the **Sodomites**, and He resolved to punish their lust, to subvert their city, and to exterminate the entire region at once, so that neither planting nor fruit should ever rise from it again. 

In the Law of Moses, one reads of the prophet **Balaam**, who, after the blessings with which he 
<margin>Numbers 25.</margin> 
blessed the children of Israel, gave counsel to **Balak** on how he might seduce the people through the **Midianite women**, for which a great vengeance followed. 

In the Law of the Gentiles, **Semiramis** <note>The legendary Queen of Babylon, often cited in moral treatises for her alleged incestuous relationship with her son</note>, who had previously founded Babylon and tamed the Indians, finally perished at the hands of her son, to whom she had given herself as a wife. 

If the stain of lust caused men to be scourged by God under the Law of Nature, the Law of Moses, and the superstitious sect of the Gentiles, what is to be said of the **Christian Law**? For in it, Christians are scourged by God so that they may erase the stains of a shameful life through penance. Therefore, in the Law of Grace, during the time of **Charles VIII**, King of the French, God—ever intent on our progress—just as an eagle provoking its chicks to fly, so too did He stir the **French**, **Italians**, **Germans**, **Britons**, **Danes**, **Poles**, **Hungarians**, and **Spaniards**. In order to lead and draw them higher, and so that they might erase the stains of a shameful life through penance, He awakened them with the shameful-ache and rebuked their lust. For this reason, the **Hebrew people** were sent into captivity so many times, and so many times lived in a foreign land: in Egypt under the Pharaohs, and in Babylonia under the Kings of the Assyrians. 

So too were the Christians, in the time of King Charles VIII of the French, worn down by the shameful-ache, by arthritis, and by a scabies worse than that of **Job** or the **Egyptians**, as if by so many hammers of misfortune. They were exposed to the rasp and the file of penance so that they might cease to be filthy. For it is a most grave kind of disease: Josephus writes 
<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 2, Chapter 10.</margin> 
that a similar or even worse disease once existed at the time when **Moses** was rebuking **Pharaoh**. For their bodies were cruelly wounded, being corrupted from within. Thus, it affected many of the Egyptians everywhere...

</margin>

...strength was consumed. Thus says Josephus <note>referring to Flavius Josephus, the Jewish historian mentioned on the previous page</note>. Not a few among the more recent physicians are deluded in thinking that the disease they call *pudendagra* <note>original: *pudendagram*; the "shame-ache" or syphilis</note> is the same as that which the Greeks call *lichen* <note>a Greek term for a skin eruption or "tetter"</note>. Leonard Fuchs—a man otherwise learned—asserts that I once fell into this error (though it is far from the truth), whereas I have always held that this disease is the wrath of God: just as the plagues of Egypt and the boils of Job were; and not by the power of the stars, as astrologers dream, nor from the imbalance of the air, as many physicians think. Therefore, those who call it *lichen*—such as Leoniceno—are deluded in this matter, as are those who say it is *impetigo* <note>a contagious skin infection</note>—as Leonard Fuchs himself falsely imagines—or *mentagra* <note>an eruption on the chin</note>, as most others do. And even if I once wrote that the French Disease (if it ever existed in the past, which we do not believe nor assert) was called *lichen*, I never actually believed that the French Disease or *pudendagra* had ever existed before, but rather that it is a brand-new disease, an act of the wrath of God, and was unknown to the ancients. It is most certain that all those peoples who in former centuries were given over to this vice <note>referring to lust or sexual immorality</note> either succumbed to a new disease or finally perished shamefully from some evil languor. Concerning the cure of *pudendagra*, we write nothing now, for we have written quite extensively about it in our Lyon *Aggregator* <note>Champier's *Aggregator Lugdunensis* (1505), a medical compendium</note>.

<meta>The previous page introduced Symphorien Champier’s "Laboratory," a work intended to correct the pharmacological errors of medieval Arabic and Latin authors by comparing them with ancient Greek authorities. This page begins the specific discussion of "simples"—individual medicinal ingredients—that were unknown to the Greeks but utilized by later practitioners.</meta>

# The Champier Laboratory.

->¶ Simple medicines discovered by the Arabs, unknown to the Greeks, but tested by the Latins.<-

**MANNA**, according to Greek authors, is not a medicine that softens the bowels <note>original: *ventrem*; a reference to a laxative effect</note>, but rather one that binds them. Our modern manna from Briançon, Calabria, or Syria, which loosens the bowels, can be referred to the section on "honey" in the works of Greek authors. ¶ **Sugar** <note>original: *Saccharum*</note> is also classified as a species of honey by both Dioscorides and Galen; they state it solidifies in India and Arabia Felix and is found in reeds, similar in substance to salt. This will be discussed more fully in the following pages. ¶ Regarding **purging cassia** <note>original: *casia fistula*; specifically *Cassia fistula*, the "Golden Shower" tree, used as a laxative</note>, pharmacists must be reminded that while it is mentioned in the books of the Greeks, it is not the variety we use which has the power to soften the belly. For this reason, some more recent authors call it the "pharmacist’s pod" <note>original: *siliqua pharmaceutica*</note>. The Greeks used the name for a certain species of woody cassia <note>likely a type of cinnamon bark</note>. ¶ Regarding **senna**, I say that the Greek authors (I speak of the ancients) make no special mention of it, either because they did not know of it, or perhaps because they did not approve of its use in medicine—even though the Arabs and Latins have strongly approved of it for treating black bile <note>one of the four humors, associated with melancholy</note>. ¶ Truly, it is manifest that the **rhubarb** <note>original: *Rhabarbarum*</note> which pharmacies everywhere now use, and which the Arabs describe and the Latins approve, is different from the one depicted by the ancients. This is clear from its characteristics, which are entirely different from those found in the plant described by the ancients. For the *Rheon* of the ancients (as Dioscorides witnesses in Book 3, Chapter 3) is a black root, similar to Great Centaury but smaller and more red, without scent, spongy or loose, and not heavy. Galen and Pliny do not disagree regarding *rhacoma*, which is brought from the regions above the Black Sea; it is similar to black costus, smaller, and a little more red, without scent, warming to the taste, and astringent. However, the variety now in use by physicians has a very powerful odor and bears no resemblance to black costus. Besides being fragrant, it is not light; rather, the heavier it is, the better it is considered by all physicians. Indeed, the ancients did not use theirs for purging the bowels, but employed it for many other uses. ¶ **Tamarinds** are considered by more recent authors to be the fruit of a wild palm; pharmacies now call them "tamarinds," and indeed, because of the sharpness of their flavor, they are called "sour dates" <note>original: *oxyphœnicas*</note>. They are cold in nature and powerful against yellow bile. There are those who describe its leaves as being similar to those of a willow. I have found no one among the ancient Greeks who recorded anything about this kind. Our pharmacists, however, adulterate them with bitter winter plums, adding vinegar to them and pressing them into a mass. Thus, younger and inexperienced physicians are deceived by the ointment-sellers <note>original: *Seplasiariis*; refers to vendors of perfumes and medicines in ancient Rome</note> and pharmacists. In place of tamarinds, I advise taking winter plums, preserved not with honey, but with a very small amount of the whitest sugar. ¶ **Jujubes**: Galen, in the second chapter of *On Foodstuffs*, regarding "serics"—that is, *Zinzifis* or jujubes—frankly admits that he has nothing to testify regarding them for the preservation of health or the cure of sickness. "For they are," he says, "the food of women." <note>Galen's dismissive comment suggests they were seen as snacks or trivialities rather than potent medicine.</note>

# The Champier Fore-Laboratory.

...and for unruly children, containing little nourishment, and being indigestible. ¶ From **Sebesten** <note>original: *Sebesten*; the fruit of the *Cordia myxa* tree, used as a cough suppressant</note> is made an *Eclegma* <note>a thick, syrupy medicine or linctus</note>, or an electuary of sebesten, a medicine so famous among the Arabic physicians; however, concerning this among the more recent physicians, neither **Dioscorides** nor **Galen** <note>the two primary authorities of ancient Greek medicine</note> made any mention. ¶ Regarding **Camphor**, a medicine so famous among the Arabs, the later physicians, and the pharmacists, neither Dioscorides nor Galen (as far as I have read) made any mention; furthermore, this which we use is often adulterated. Perhaps this study of ours will make the science of medicine appear lowly if we describe those things which more recent physicians are accustomed to announce only by "barbarian" names and beg for only from "barbarians." But—to use the words of **Augustine** <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, a key Christian philosopher</note>—if the Arabs and Barbarians have said anything that is compatible with Christian medicine, it must be taken from them as if from "unjust possessors" <note>This is a reference to a common Renaissance defense for using non-Christian sources, comparing it to the Israelites taking gold from the Egyptians</note>.

->¶ Poisonous and destructive medicines from the sect of the Arabs<-
->once held for the use of Christians.<-

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial "N" depicting a seated figure, likely a scholar or philosopher of antiquity, holding a book within a decorative rectangular frame featuring classical scrollwork.</image-desc>

**N**o physicians of our age, imitating **Mesue** <note>an influential 9th-century Persian physician</note> and the Arabic doctors, err more greatly than in being ignorant of what the root is that the apothecary shops sell as **Turbith** <note>the root of *Operculina turpethum*, used as a drastic purgative</note>. So great is the negligence of our doctors that they disturb almost all sick people with Turbith. However, the Turbith described by **Serapion the Mauritanian** is one thing, but that sought from Mesue is another. In Serapion's writings, Turbith is a fragrant root, whereas in Mesue's writings, it is of the genus of "milky" plants <note>original: *lacteriorum*; plants that produce a latex sap, like spurges</note>. But Turbith will be discussed later. ¶ **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, author of the *Canon of Medicine*</note> writes in the second book of his *Canon*, chapter 502, that **Napellum** <note>Monkshood or Aconite, a highly toxic plant</note> is a destructive poison that kills the one who drinks it; yet, soon forgetting what he wrote, in the same chapter he suggests it be drunk, saying: "It removes *albaras* <note>a skin condition, likely vitiligo or white leprosy</note> when applied as an ointment or when drunk." What, I ask, could have been said or written more absurdly? ¶ Avicenna, Mesue, Serapion, **Al-Farabi**, **Rhazes**, and almost all the Arabs have slipped up because they placed **Mezereon** <note>Daphne mezereum, a toxic shrub</note>, which is called *Chamelea* by the Greeks, among the types of milky spurges. Deceived by the similarity of the name, they attributed many things to it which actually belong to the *Chameleoni* <note>the ground-pine or a similar plant</note>. I believe, however (as we shall show in what follows), that the Arabs erred in their description of Mezereon; it is therefore convenient that we hasten to other matters. ¶ Almost all the Arabs, especially Serapion and Avicenna, err by confusing **Lapis Lazuli** and **Armenian Stone** <note>original: *Lazuli & Armenum*; both are blue minerals, Lapis Lazuli being more precious than the copper-based Armenian stone</note> in the same chapter. It is manifest from Avicenna's own words that he confuses Armenian stone with Lazuli under one and the same heading; for in Book 2, chapter 57, he most clearly teaches this. It is clear from that chapter of Avicenna that almost whatever he reports about Lapis Lazuli, those same things are attributed by the Greeks to the Armenian stone. Indeed, Serapion fell into the same error; for in identifying Lapis Lazuli and explaining its powers, he reports nothing other than what the Greeks handed down concerning the Armenian stone. Hence, since the Arabs note the powers and properties of one in the other, it follows that little or absolutely no trust is to be placed in them. Therefore, let everyone hereafter be truly and [cautiously...]

### ¶ Comparison of the Arabs to the Greeks.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial V with floral motifs.</image-desc>
One must indeed see who stood out more gloriously in medicine. Among the Greeks, everything is pure, learned, and brought forth with the highest choice and judgment; thus you will find nothing worthy of Aristarchus’s correction <note>original: *Aristarchi virgula*; a reference to Aristarchus of Samothrace, a famous ancient critic who used a mark (virgula) to denote spurious or incorrect passages</note>. Among the Arabs, however, besides a certain unorganized and inept style and a "stuttering" of the tongue <note>a common Renaissance critique of the quality of medieval Latin translations of Arabic texts</note>, there are no small errors—as is clear from our own corrections and notes—which are worthy of many marks of disapproval <note>original: *obelis*; the obelus was a mark used by ancient critics to indicate suspected or false text</note>. 

However, it is not that I think the Arabs and the moderns <note>original: *iuniores*; referring to the medieval medical authorities who came after the Greeks</note> should be condemned and rejected entirely. For among them, there are not a few things which I judge to be highly commendable, such as **rhubarb**, their **sugar**, **manna**, **senna**, and **purging cassia** <note>original: *Casia fistula*; a tropical tree fruit used as a laxative</note>. But since very great discernment is needed in reading their books, I believe they should not be set forth unless judgment has first been acquired from the ancients; for in this way, students will easily detect what is bright and what is dark within them. 

¶ The Greeks were earlier in time regarding medicine; the Arabs were much later. The Greeks handed down to us the "seeds," as it were; the Arabs, however, propagated those seeds and, by cultivating them, sometimes defiled them with stains. The Greeks wrote down the rules of medicine; the Arabs did not. The Greeks were more elegant and more subtle. The Arabs, truly, were at times more abundant, and many even added things worthy of memory by their own genius, but they defiled many things with their own barbarity and specific malice. 

For the beginning of all infidelity and malice is from Arabia; furthermore, that land was always pestilential to the human races. So it was with **Muhammad**, so once with **Ham** <note>original: *Cham*; the son of Noah, traditionally associated with the peoples of the Middle East and Africa in early modern geography</note> and his progeny; they introduced the worship of evil demons, while the former [Muhammad] took away what had been established by the wondrous power of God. From Arabia drew their origin **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the most influential medieval philosopher-physician</note>, the most noble of them all, the impious **Averrhoes** <note>Ibn Rushd, known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note>, **Avenzoar** <note>Ibn Zuhr, a physician from al-Andalus</note>, **Algazel** <note>Al-Ghazali, a philosopher and theologian</note>, both **Haly** <note>likely referring to Haly Abbas and Haly Rodoan, two major medical figures</note>, and **Alpharabius** <note>Al-Farabi, known as the "Second Teacher" after Aristotle</note>; for these were supporters of the Muhammadan sect, who abuse the free gifts of God. Therefore, the Apostle [Paul] warned the Corinthians to take care that they not be led astray through empty philosophy, according to the tradition of men, not according to Christ.

<meta>This page continues Champier’s polemic against the "barbaric" influence on medicine. Having previously touched on specific substances like rhubarb and sugar, he now turns to a historical defense of Latin and Greek medical writers, specifically contrasting the eloquence of Roman authors like Celsus and Cato against the medieval Arabic authorities and their later European translators.</meta>

Fo. III.

->The Pre-Workshop of Champier<-
<note>original: *Anteofficina Campegiana*; the "workshop" or "preparatory office" refers to the introductory nature of this text in Champier's medical system</note>

<margin>Quintilian</margin>
...[Cato the Elder] <note>referred to on the previous page</note> attacked Greek learning, philosophers, and physicians with insults; and lest his son be forced to use their services, he left behind his own commentaries on medicine. Cornelius Celsus <note>a Roman encyclopedist known as the "Cicero of physicians" for his elegant Latin</note> was a man most eloquent in the medical art, whom Fabius Quintilian mentions in the tenth book of his *Institutions*, in the first chapter, where he discusses those who wrote in Latin about philosophy. He wrote (he says) quite a lot, following the Sceptics, not without polish and brilliance. Likewise, in the final twelfth chapter, speaking of those who knew and wrote many things, he says: Cornelius Celsus not only wrote about all these arts, but further left behind precepts on military affairs, agriculture, and even medicine—worthy, by his very purpose, for us to believe that he knew all those things. So far Quintilian. ¶ There were also some illustrious Arab physicians, such as Avicenna and Averrhoes; but Celsus and Cato were more ancient in time. Cato and Celsus surpass all the Barbarians, Persians, Arabs, and Phoenicians in the elegance and eloquence of their speech. ¶ Among the Arabs, we have found no one who is to be preferred to Serenus Sammoniacus <note>a Roman polymath and physician</note> for more beautiful merits regarding the Greeks. ¶ Among the Phoenicians, Persians, and Mauritanians, we have found no one who is to be compared to Pliny for more beautiful disciplines. For from the time of Pliny, many wrote in foreign and Arabic tongues, at which time indeed the ferocity of the barbarians invaded Italy, Gaul, and Spain, and destroyed the glory of letters even more than the ornaments of the cities. From this noble slaughter of studies, the meanness of medicine arose, and it became the most inconsistent of all the arts. For it was permitted for anyone to destroy the institutions of others, and it was a matter of glory to snatch something from the midst of (as they say) barbarism. A little while before, due to the ruins of wars, physicians failed among the Greeks and Latins, whose injury resulted in the praise of foreign nations; hence the volumes of Avicenna, Averrhoes, Rhazes, Algazel, Al-Farabi, Serapion, and other barbarians were received in such a great scarcity of resources. Hence came the stunned persuasions of certain men who esteemed only precious foreign and alien things. These same works, the more recent writers—by translating them poorly into Latin and abandoning Roman and Greek dignity—reduced to absurdities with confused names for things; such were Gerard of Cremona, Peter of Abano, Constantine the Monk <note>Constantine the African</note>, Arnaldus de Villanova, and many other barbaric writers of the same ilk.

### ¶ A comparison of the Latins to the Greeks.

<image-desc>A historiated woodcut initial 'P' featuring a scholar seated at a desk or lectern, surrounded by books, appearing to read or write.</image-desc>
After Cadmus, who first discovered letters among the Greeks, there existed the famous Seven Sages of Greece, to whom the former age gave that name (to use the words of Ausonius the Gaul) and the following age did not take it away. Their names are these: Solon of Attica, Chilon of Lacedaemon, Cleobulus of Lindos, Thales of Miletus, Bias of Priene, Pittacus of Mytilene, and Periander of Corinth. After them, indeed, Hippocrates of Cos, Plato of Athens, Aristotle of Stagira, and Galen of Pergamum became famous. These men wisely and healthfully prescribed quite a lot, looking out for the public utility of mortals; from whose treasures medi[cine]...

Fo. III.

->The Pre-Workshop of Champier<-

...medicine <note>original: *cinam*, concluding the word *medicinam* from the previous page</note> of Hippocrates we bring forth; yet it seems that nations follow their own vices: whence Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero</note> mocks them in the presence of Caesar, saying: "Either of the flighty Greeks, or of the monstrous Barbarians." And in his speech *For Flaccus*, he says: "Inborn levity and learned vanity." Indeed, antiquity called the Latins proud, and the Romans grave. Truly, the Greeks affirm that all who speak crudely are called "Barbarians"—which includes all nations except the Greeks and Latins. The Apostle Paul says in his epistles that all those who do not understand one another are Barbarians to each other. And Caesar wished all to be considered Barbarians who did not know how to speak Latin, except for the Greeks and the Gauls, upon whom the Romans bestowed honor. 

Among the Greeks, Hippocrates of Cos was illustrious in the medical art; and among the Romans, Antonius Musa, the personal physician to Augustus, was illustrious. Among the Asians, Galen of Pergamum was illustrious. Among the Romans, Cato the Elder was also illustrious. Paul of Aegina and Alexander of Aphrodisias flourished among the Athenians <note>original: *Atticos*</note>. Among the Latins, Cornelius Celsus and Serenus Sammoniacus flourished. Dioscorides, a military man, was illustrious among the Greeks. Pliny, a knight <note>original: *eques auratus*</note> and distinguished in military discipline, was also illustrious among the Latins. 

However, the bodies of all nations are not equally suited for the perception of wisdom and intelligence; hence the Athenians were considered more ingenious and the Thebans more robust, for the former lived in purer air, and the latter in thicker air <note>This refers to the ancient "Theory of Climates," which suggested that geography and air quality determined a person's temperament and intellect</note>. For this reason, the Germans are called brave, the Italians serious, the Spaniards boastful, the Gauls fierce in arms, the Latins haughty and proud, the Romans grave, the Ligurians vain, the Cretans liars, and the Africans treacherous. For these same reasons, among the Gauls, the Parisians are considered more ingenious, and the Allobroges <note>The people of the Savoy/Dauphiné region, where Champier practiced</note> more robust.

### ¶ Champier’s Warning to the Reader.

[Image: Large decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a landscape with a house and trees.]
**N**o one should think, most dear reader, that I have undertaken this "workshop" <note>original: *officinam*; referring to the title of the work and the production of medical knowledge</note> for the sake of slander or out of a desire for hunting glory; but rather from the love of truth alone, and for the sake of helping mortal men. I have judged it to be of no small benefit to our age—which is blinded regarding true remedies—and to future posterity, if students of the medical art could be led back to a better path in this way. It was by no means done to disparage men who were learned and of great reading (as much as that age allowed), but rather so that readers would not subscribe to their opinions while deceived by the simple authority of a name in all matters. For one must yield to no man's name as much as to the truth. 

Therefore, even if previously through Hermolaus Barbarus, Leoniceno, Marcello of Florence, the Frenchman Ruel, Kopp of Basel, Giovanni Manardi of Ferrara, and the German Leonhart Fuchs—all men most learned in every kind of discipline and most exacting individuals—and through certain other men of great name, not a few errors of the pharmacists, the younger doctors, and the "barbarian" <note>In the Renaissance, "barbarian" was a technical slur for medieval Arabic authors and their Latin translators</note> physicians have been exposed in published books; nevertheless, not all of the errors found here concerning the antidotes <note>medical formulas or recipes</note> of Mesue, Nicolaus, and Copho <note>Three major authorities of the medieval medical curriculum: Masawaih al-Mardini, Nicolaus Praepositus, and Copho of Salerno</note> are explained there. Nor did those authors touch upon them in any particular order, but only as they happened to encounter them. Furthermore, everything here is taught (as they say) more roughly and plainly than in their works. Therefore, so that those devoted to the truth might have all these things arranged in a certain order and gathered as if into a single bundle, I wished to undergo this labor, whatever it may be. As for the stubborn defenders of old ignorance, and those physicians contaminated by the filth of "barbarism" and the Muhammadan sect <note>referring to the Islamic medical tradition, which Champier viewed as a corruption of Greek medicine</note>, along with the whole assembly of sophists, I care nothing for them; for they are entirely lacking in all erudition and judgment; nor [do they possess] anything...

<summary>Champier lists prominent French, Italian, and German humanist physicians before explaining that his work aims to correct the errors of medieval medical authorities like Mesue and Nicolaus by returning to classical truth.</summary>
<keywords>Symphorien Champier, medical humanism, Mesue, Nicolaus Praepositus, Copho, Renaissance medicine, pharmaceutical errors, Leonhart Fuchs, Niccolò Leoniceno</keywords>

### To the most noble, high-born, eloquent, and most learned Doctor of Canon Law, Master Charles de l’Estang <note>original: *Carolus A stagno*; a prominent official in the Diocese of Lyon</note>, Chamberlain of the Church of Lyon: An Epistle from Master Symphorien Champier <note>original: *Symphorianus Campegius*; a prolific French physician and humanist scholar</note>, Chief Physician <note>original: *archiatri*; a title indicating a senior or court physician, in this case to the Duke of Lorraine</note> of the Lorrainers, to whom he dedicates this *Apothecaries' Workshop* <note>original: *Officinam hanc Pharmacopolarum*; referring to the title of the book</note> in perpetuity.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap letter 'E' at the start of the body text, embellished with ornate floral and foliate patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

From this infinite and varied kind of studies, in which the most famous geniuses of our time, O most noble and learned man, have exerted themselves, I would believe that none is more useful for its multifaceted learning, nor more pleasant in its great delight, than this one alone (which this volume now contains). I would further assert, having experienced it myself, that this same work brings so much labor and so much difficulty to its authors that you would not quite know whether readers receive more utility and pleasure, or if the authors undergo more labor and difficulty—provided that they perform the task well. <meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle from Symphorien Champier to Charles de l’Estang. It concludes the description of the book's scope—moving from high philosophy to the practical details of Arabic and medieval medicine—and ends with a formal personal appeal to his patron.</meta>

Header: **Epistle.**

...most brilliant insights <note>original: *clarissima sensa*</note> of grammar, logic, or philosophy, but the entire lineages of the Arab and Punic <note>original: *Poenorum*; referring here to North African or Moorish scholars who influenced medieval medicine</note> physicians. Now, the more obscure meanings of the Arab physicians are explained. The long-standing reading of the Arab and "barbarian" Punic authors is corrected, even against the opinions of many. The often obscure errors of the Arabs are clarified; and not content with these, the authors move on to modern <note>original: *novicios*; referring to "recent" or medieval medical writers compared to the ancient Greeks</note> doctors, then from the moderns to the perfumers <note>term: *Seplasiarios* — specialized sellers of ointments, perfumes, and medicinal pastes in the Roman style</note> and apothecaries. Again, from the apothecaries they investigate the schools of the Empirical surgeons <note>original: *Empiricorum chirurgorum*; those who base their medical practice on observation and experience rather than traditional theory</note>. This book reveals the workshops of the perfumers, such that you could not more justly call any other book a "Proteus" <note>A Greek sea-god known for changing his shape; Champier uses the name here to describe the book’s multifaceted and versatile nature</note> than this one.

To you indeed, most noble and most learned man, I specifically dedicate and name this *Apothecaries' Workshop*. Farewell, most delightful Patron: and (as you already do) continue to favor the learned: continue to champion literature: continue to rescue the Latin language <note>original: *rem Latinam*</note> and the fine arts from the dust of neglect, so that the memory of your name may be shielded from the injury of total oblivion. And love us—as is your custom—harmoniously <note>original: *symphoniace*; a wordplay on the author's first name, Symphorianus</note>.

He ends with a warm plea to his patron, Charles de l’Estang, to continue supporting the humanities and the Latin language.</summary>

### ¶ Rose Aromatic.
<note>original: *Aromaticum rosatum*; a fragrant medicinal powder often used as a base for other compounds or taken to strengthen the heart and stomach.</note>

Take 15 drachms of red roses; 7 drachms of scraped licorice; 3 drachms of wood of aloes [if it can be found] or in its place 3 drachms each of red and white sandalwood; 5 drachms of select cinnamon; 2.5 drachms each of mace and cloves; 2 drachms and 2 scruples each of gum arabic and tragacanth; 1 drachm each of nutmeg, greater cardamom, and galangal; 2 scruples each of spikenard and ambergris; 1 scruple of musk; and as much rose syrup as suffices. Concerning the species <note>The "species" refers to the dry powdered ingredients before they are mixed with syrup into an electuary.</note>.

<margin>
Damask Roses.
</margin>

¶ There are many types of roses: the more fragrant is that which grows in the thickets on the rose bushes. Perfumers <note>term: *pigmentarii* — historically sellers of pigments and perfumes, often functioning as early pharmacists</note> use it for ointments, oils, and medicines. Indeed, all wild plants are considered more potent, because [as they say] for these, the earth is like a mother, whereas for others <insert>the cultivated ones</insert> she is a stepmother. But I would rather give the first praise for scent to the roses which we now everywhere call Damask roses; these are not only twice-bearing <note>original: *biferas*; blooming in both spring and autumn</note>, but bloom almost the whole year round. Places planted with roses are called rose-gardens or *rosetums*, just as we call lily-gardens *liliata*. The Greeks call the rose *Rhodon* <note>original: Ῥόδον</note>; from this are derived *Cynorhodos* <note>the dog-rose</note>, and *rhododaphne* <note>the oleander</note>, and *rhodinum* oil, which our people call rose-oil. ¶ The rose is cold and dry, consisting of an irritating and bitter quality. It helps "hot" heads <note>referring to the theory of Humors, where a 'hot' ailment requires a 'cold' remedy</note> by its smell, but it harms moist heads and triggers catarrhs. When taken internally, it helps those suffering from fevers caused by yellow bile; it strengthens the stomach and liver; yet by its own specific power it harms the testicles. It restrains sharp exhalations so they do not rise to the head.

### ¶ Concerning the Aurea Alexandrina.
<note>The "Golden Alexandrian," a famous multi-ingredient antidote and cordial used in medieval medicine.</note>

<margin>
Error of the more recent doctors.
</margin>

Among the other causes of errors that have occurred in medicine in recent centuries, I think this was not the least: that doctors, knowing nothing of "simples" <note>term: *simplicibus* — single-ingredient medicinal herbs or substances, the building blocks of pharmacy</note>, left the composition of medicines to the judgment of the perfumers. From this it happened [to say nothing of the rest for now] that Nicolaus <note>referring to Nicolaus Praepositus, the 12th-century author of the *Antidotarium Nicolai*, a standard medieval text</note>, through ignorance of simple drugs, gave a name to his antidote "Aurea Alexandrina." He believed it was named after some Alexandrian Muhammadan doctor, rather than after that Greek Macedonian monarch <note>Alexander the Great</note> whose name he wished to usurp for himself, as Nicolaus seemed to believe. I, however—being perhaps too timid and curious in this as in every medical matter—cannot help but fear that Nicolaus was ignorant of certain simple medicines, or did not know their powers, or that they were corrupted in the antidote by the pharmacist...

# The Apothecaries' Workshop

...should be available in the apothecary shops. For these are the simple medicines <note>term: *simplicia*; individual medicinal ingredients, usually plants, used to create "compound" medicines like electuaries or ointments</note>: Fruit of the balsam tree, henbane, Myrrh, opium, balsam, Indian bay leaf, Woody Cassia, Euphorbium, wood of aloes, Rhapontic rhubarb, Wood of the balsam tree, Amomum, parsley, Sweet flag, etc. For these have been found to be missing either in all parts, or certainly in most, which Nicolaus <note>referring to Nicolaus Salernitanus, author of the *Antidotarium Nicolai*, a fundamental 12th-century pharmaceutical text</note> prescribed for his antidote. ¶ In truth, the juice of the balsam <note>original: *opobalsamum*</note> is either not brought to us at all, or if it is, it exists at such a high price that it exceeds the cost of the entire antidote. If we lack the juice of the balsam, we shall also lack the fruit <note>original: *carpobalsamum*</note> and the wood <note>original: *xilobalsamum*</note>. I would hardly believe that pure or fresh Fruit of the Balsam is being imported, as has already been proven in our corrections.

<margin>Amomum.</margin>
¶ In truth, I do not know if Europe has seen "clustered" Amomum—that is, resembling a bunch of grapes <note>original: *botruosum*; from the Greek *botrys*, a cluster of grapes. This refers to a rare eastern spice, likely a species of cardamom or ginger</note>—in this century.

<margin>Henbane.</margin>
¶ Henbane <note>original: *Iusquiamus*</note> is cold in the third degree and dry in the second. The black variety is deadly and poisonous; the red and white varieties are not given without danger. It possesses a death-bringing and sleep-inducing power. And [as Rhazes <note>term: *Razes*; a famous 9th-century Persian physician whose works were central to medieval European medicine</note> writes] all its species intoxicate and produce a stupor.

<margin>Euphorbium.</margin>
¶ Euphorbium <note>The caustic sap of various succulent *Euphorbia* plants</note> is a substance of subtle parts and is powerfully hot. When drunk [as Dioscorides says], its heat burns for a whole day; for that reason, it is mixed with honey when used. It strips the flesh from bones in a single day and separates their fragments from them.

<margin>Myrrh.</margin>
¶ Who can doubt that we lack true myrrh? For I do not know who can distinguish Myrrh from bdellium <note>a cheaper, similar-looking resin from the *Commiphora* genus</note>. Even Galen complains that it is adulterated in various ways, and that the juice of the balsam is found within the best Myrrh, which would be deadly if taken into the body.

<margin>Opium.</margin>
¶ Opium is the gum of the black poppy; it causes *subeth* <note>original: *subeth*; a medieval medical term derived from Arabic for a deep, lethargic stupor</note> and afterwards kills. Mensidenus [as Serapio <note>Serapio the Younger, a 13th-century author on medicinal "simples"</note> reports] said that the benefit of opium lies only in its scent, which causes sleep. In other ways [he says], its use is bad and very dangerous; for it is cold in the fourth degree and dry in the first.

<margin>Indian Bay Leaf.</margin>
¶ Who in our century recognizes *Malabatrum* or "the leaf" <note>original: *folium*; usually refers to the leaf of the Indian bay tree, *Cinnamomum tamala*</note>? In all my life, I have hardly been able to see a single leaf. This was discussed in the first book of our corrections.

<margin>Woody Cassia.</margin>
¶ Who can doubt that we also lack Woody Cassia? When I say Cassia, I mean the aromatic kind, which the shops call "woody" <note>original: *lignea*</note>. I know that the other kind <note>Cassia fistula, or "pudding-pipe tree"</note>, which is now commonly used to soften the bowels, was entirely unknown to the ancients. We have made extensive mention of aromatic cassia in the first book of our corrections.

<margin>Wood of Aloes.</margin>
¶ Wood of aloes, or *agalathon*, is brought from India and Arabia; yet I would hardly believe that it is brought here pure and fresh. We wrote about it in the first book of our corrections.

<margin>Rhapontic Rhubarb.</margin>
<margin>Names for Rhubarb.</margin>
¶ *Rheuponticum* <note>Rhapontic rhubarb</note> is the same as rhubarb. However, in the "Golden Alexander" <note>a famous complex medieval antidote</note>, both rhubarb and *rheuponticum* are included, even though they are the same thing. For what the common crowd of doctors and all the shops now call "rhubarb," and the Phoenicians <note>meaning Arabic-speaking medical authorities</note> call *rauedseni*, Celsus calls "Pontic root," Dioscorides calls *Rha* (and according to some *Rheon*, and others *Rhian*), Pliny calls *Rhecoma*, and Galen (just like Dioscorides) sometimes calls *Rheon*, sometimes *Rhian*, and occasionally *Rheon ponticum*. The ancients did not use it for purging the belly, but mixed it into antidotes and used it for many other purposes, which it is not worth the effort to recount here. ¶ But who would not be simultaneously amazed and annoyed that we lack parsley <note>original: *petroselinum*</note>? For that which is commonly called parsley...

...we call [it], or it is celery <note>original: *apium*; often used interchangeably for parsley or celery in older texts</note>, which was called garden-parsley by the ancients; or whatever it may finally be, it is certain that its seed is not that which the ancients commanded to be mixed into theriac <note>term: *theriaca*; a famous ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients</note> or the "Golden Alexandrine" <note>term: *aurea alexandrina*; a prestigious electuary used as a restorative, named after its inventor, Alexander of Tralles</note>. For, according to Galen, the Macedonian variety is preferred over the others, and among the Macedonian ones, the Eretrian variety is best, being excellent in this regard: that it is extremely bitter and sharp.

<margin>Sweet Flag</margin>
¶ I believe that Sweet Flag <note>original: *Calamus aromaticus*; an aromatic marsh plant</note> is entirely unknown in this time. For what the common people call by that name is a root, not a reed; nor [as I judge] is it the root of that specific reed. Rather, as Manardus <note>Giovanni Manardi (1462–1536), a physician who famously critiqued the errors in medieval pharmacy</note> writes, it is either acorus <note>the common iris or yellow flag</note>—as even Hermolaus Barbarus <note>an influential 15th-century Italian scholar and botanist</note> seemed to suspect in a certain passage—or some other thing unknown to us. Whenever Manardus needed *Acorus*, he was not accustomed to using that common root of unpleasant odor, but rather what is called the aromatic reed. Therefore, do not use the Golden Alexandrine, but leave it to Alexander, its inventor, and to the Muslims, the Arabs, and the Carthaginians.

### ¶ Vinegar of Squill, or Scillitic Vinegar.

<margin>Squill.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative capital letter 'A' featuring a detailed scene within its frame.</image-desc>
Take the scales of the squill <note>term: *squilla*; the sea onion (*Drimia maritima*), used as a powerful diuretic and expectorant</note> and infuse them in vinegar from the beginning of spring until the end of summer in a well-sealed glass vessel. Let it be exposed to the sun's rays and reserved for use. From this is made, with honey, an oxymel of squill <note>term: *oxymel*; a medicinal drink made of vinegar and honey</note> in the form of a syrup, which is effective for many ailments. ¶ The Romans call *Scilla* by the name *Squilla* as well. Squill is of a sharp and burning temperament. It is roasted [says Dioscorides <note>the famous 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*</note>] by being cast into an oven within a lidded earthenware pot. It is taken by casting away all the outermost parts, using that which is most internal. The same is cooked, sliced, even after the first water has been poured off; new water is poured over it until neither bitterness nor sharpness is perceived in the water. It is dried in the shade, and once the squill is covered in "little wheels" <note>original: *rotulas*; thin circular slices</note>, it is then threaded with a cord. It is hung up at intervals so that the slices do not touch each other. We use squill cut and preserved in this way for oil, wine, and vinegar,
<margin>The virtues of Squill.</margin>
which are named "scillitic" after the squill. Against cracks in the feet, the innermost parts of raw squill are applied after being boiled in oil or worked together with resin. Squill boiled in vinegar is smeared on viper bites, and it is given to those in whom we wish to provoke urine. It acts against water collecting under the skin <note>likely referring to edema or dropsy</note>, the inability to retain food in the stomach, and food "floating" in the stomach. It is beneficial for those suffused with bile <note>jaundice</note>, for colic, chronic coughs, asthma, and for those who have difficulty coughing up phlegm, given in the weight of three obols <note>term: *obol*; an ancient unit of weight, roughly 0.5 to 0.7 grams</note> with honey. Being sticky, it moves the bowels. It is equally beneficial when taken boiled. However, it must be avoided and not given to those who have any ulceration of the intestines. When burned to ash, it is used effectively as an ointment for chilblains <note>painful inflammation of small blood vessels in the skin caused by cold</note> and warts.

### ¶ Vinegar of Roses, Rosemary-flowers, Elderberry, and Raisins.

These are made by the infusion of roses, rosemary flowers <note>original: *anthos*; from the Greek for flower, specifically used in pharmacy for rosemary blossoms</note>, and elderflowers in sharp vinegar, leaving it in the sun for forty days or an entire summer. The roses ought not to be fully mature or finished, and the white base <note>original: *extremitas alba*; the bitter white part at the bottom of the petal</note> must be removed. Vinegar of raisins can also be made by infusing raisins in vinegar.

very red, not pale, nor violet-colored, as the roses of the French are now,

¶ "Anthos" <note>original: *Anthos*; from the Greek for "flower"</note> is the flower of Rosemary, which is hot in the second degree, and
dry in the first: however, its excess is not determined by the authorities in terms of degrees. Rosemary has a certain quality of becoming tart:
it restrains the belly <note>meaning it treats diarrhea or loose bowels</note>, and it dries; it helps against coughs and rheum <note>original: *distillationes*; the "dripping" of fluids from the head associated with colds</note>:
it promotes menstruation, whether taken as a drink or as a suppository. The juice has a certain property such that its smoke wards off the plague; and for this reason, in a time of pestilence, it is profitable to frequently fumigate houses with Rosemary, because it makes the altered and corrupt quality of the air better.

<margin>Elder and Dwarf Elder.</margin>
¶ Elder <note>original: *Sabucus*</note> and dwarf elder <note>original: *ebulus*; also known as danewort</note> are of the same virtue, and have a drying power: the virtue of dwarf elder is dry, and it loosens watery humors: both are useful for the bites of venomous animals, and they dissolve [clotted] blood: and they are useful for an old cough, and for shortness of breath: and they are useful for catarrh descending to the throat, and for quinsy <note>term: *squinantia*; a severe inflammation or abscess of the throat</note>, and for the swelling of the uvula: and a decoction of them is useful for stones in the kidneys and for hardness of the spleen: and it has a cleansing, binding, and moderately dissolving power.

<margin>The property of raisins.</margin>
¶ The raisin <note>original: *Passula*; dried grapes or currants</note> is a friend to the liver, and the stomach, and it is beneficial for pains of the intestines, and the kidneys, and the bladder; it nourishes greatly, and is good for the chest and lungs: therefore, we can safely use raisin-water while we are fasting.

# The Apothecaries’ Workshop. Folio 9.

...scammony <note>original: *mica*, likely a fragment of *scammonia*</note>: for which reason one must flee from that kind—which is not white but rather black—as if from a roaring lion. Our preparation, however, purges bile along with phlegm and draws it out through the bowels.

->¶ Concerning the letter M<-
## Sweet Confection of Musk

<margin>
What musk is.
</margin>

Take two drachms <term>drachm: a unit of weight, roughly 1/8th of an ounce</term> each of saffron, Roman leopard's bane <note>original: *doronici Romani*</note>, zedoary <note>a root similar to ginger</note>, wood of aloes (or red sandalwood in its place), and mace. Take two and a half drachms each of choice pearls, silk thread cut with a knife, amber <note>original: *carabe*</note>, white and red coral, and basil. Take one drachm each of white and red behen <note>oriental roots used as tonics</note>, spikenard, and cloves. Take one and a half drachms each of ginger, cubeb, and long pepper. Take one and a half scruples <term>scruple: a small unit of weight, about 1/24th of an ounce</term> of musk. Prepare this with raw honey at four times the weight of all the other ingredients. In the "Confection of Musk" by Mesue <note>Mesue was a famous but semi-legendary Arabic medical authority whose recipes were standard in Europe</note>, there is an ingredient called "leaf" or *malabatrum* <note>Indian bay leaf</note> which is unknown to our people. Musk was named by the Greeks, and in our age it is among the most precious of scents and of no small power in medicine; it seems all the ancient Greeks were ignorant of this kind of fragrance. However, the Greeks do collect "muscus" <note>here referring to tree moss</note> which grows on cedar, white poplar, and oak trees. In both types, that which is more fragrant and whiter is most praised, while that which turns black is condemned. "Moschus" <note>animal musk</note> and "muscus" <note>tree moss</note> differ: animal musk is enclosed in the follicles of certain animals, while tree moss is found on cedar and poplar trees.

## ¶ The New and Improved Confection of Hamech

<margin>
It is useful for illnesses arising from black bile and burnt humors, such as mania, vertigo, forgetfulness, skin spots, leprosy, cancer, and similar conditions.
</margin>

<margin>
Let winter plums be used in place of tamarinds.
</margin>

Take four ounces of yellow myrobalans <note>a plum-like fruit used as a laxative</note>, and two and a half ounces each of Indian chebulic myrobalans and rhubarb. Take one ounce of larch agaric <note>a medicinal fungus</note>, and one and a half ounces of oak polypody <note>a type of fern</note>. Take one ounce each of wormwood and senna. Take one and a half ounces of violets and one ounce of epithymum <note>dodder of thyme, a parasitic plant</note>. Take six drachms each of anise and roses. Take one pound of fumitory juice, sixty plums, and six ounces of raisins with the seeds removed. Infuse all of these in whey <note>original: *aqua casei*, literally "cheese water"</note> and place them in a glass vessel with a narrow, closed opening; leave them there for five days. Then, let them come to a single boil and strain the mixture. In this liquid, dissolve six ounces of cleaned Cassia fistula <note>purging cassia</note>, five ounces of tamarinds, and four ounces of Briançon manna <note>a sweet resin from larch trees</note>. Rub these by hand and strain them, then throw one and a half pounds of sugar over the top. Cook until it has the thickness of honey. Afterward, pulverize the following and add them: half an ounce each of yellow myrobalans, Indian chebulic myrobalans, and senna; four and a half drachms each of belleric myrobalans, emblic myrobalans, and rhubarb; and two drachms each of anise and spikenard. Thus the confection is made. In the recipe by Mesue, one and a half ounces of scammony is added; for this reason his version is to be avoided, as it is extremely harmful to the stomach and the digestion.

# The Apothecaries’ Workshop.

<margin>Cooling Sandalwoods.</margin>
Take one and a half ounces of red roses. Ten drachms <term>drachm: a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</term> of red sandalwood. Six ounces each of white and yellow sandalwood. Seven drachms of Armenian bole <note>a medicinal red clay used as an astringent</note>. Four drachms of spodium made from elephant ivory <note>original: *spodij ex dente elephantis*; calcined ivory used to cool the body</note>. Two drachms of camphor. Five ounces of white wax. One pound of rose oil. Wash the oil and wax, dissolve them over a slow fire, and mix them together. ¶ These cooling sandalwoods are of the third order [of coldness] and the second order of dryness. The red variety is colder than the white and yellow. All of them are beneficial for heart palpitations <note>original: *cardiacæ passioni*</note> accompanied by fever.

---

## White Eye-Salve.

<margin>Ceruse; the harms of ceruse.</margin>
Take ten drachms of washed ceruse <term>ceruse: white lead, a common pigment and medicinal base, though toxic if ingested</term>. Four drachms of starch. Two drachms each of gum arabic and tragacanth. Half a drachm of camphor. Let those ingredients that require it be powdered, and let the gums be dissolved in rose water. Form them into troches <term>troche: a small medicinal lozenge or cake</term>, and when you wish to use them, dissolve them in rose water. ¶ Ceruse is highly regarded, especially that which is made in Rhodes, Corinth, or Sparta. However, as Dioscorides <note>an ancient Greek physician and the father of pharmacology</note> writes, ceruse is lethal and has the harmful nature of a poison. Lead workshops provide ceruse to the people and manufacture it; it has the power to cool, to block, to soften, to fill, and to gently thin [humors]. Furthermore, it suppresses growths and brings wounds to a scar when mixed into waxes, plasters—which they call *liparae* <note>meaning "smooth" or "soothing" ointments</note>—and small medicinal cakes.

---

## Concerning the letter D.
### Diagalanga.

<margin>The nature of galangal.</margin>
Take six drachms each of galangal <note>a root in the ginger family known for its heat</note> and wood of aloes—or in its place, if it cannot be found, red sandalwood. Two drachms each of cloves and mace. One and a half drachms each of ginger, long pepper <note>original: *macropiperis*</note>, cinnamon, and long pepper <note>the text lists long pepper twice, possibly distinguishing between varieties</note>. One drachm each of dried calamint and dried mint. One drachm each of spikenard, celery seed, fennel, anise, and caraway. One and a half drachms of aromatic calamus—or, if you prefer, aromatic acorus <note>both refer to sweet flag, a fragrant wetland plant</note>. Ten ounces of white sugar and enough clarified honey as is sufficient. This preparation is effective against diseases of thick flatulence and acidic gas, strengthens the digestion and the operations of the stomach, and corrects the faults of a cold liver. Galangal is hot and dry in the third order; it is beneficial for those full of phlegm and for moisture in the stomach, aiding its digestion. It helps with colic, creates a pleasant breath, warms the kidneys, increases semen, and dissolves flatulence.

---

## Diacyminum.

Take eight drachms of cumin that has been soaked in vinegar for a day and then dried. Two and a half drachms each of choice cinnamon and cloves. Two drachms each of black pepper <note>original: *melanopiperis*</note> and white ginger.
