...with one scruple <term>scruple: a small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams</term>, one drachm and one scruple each of galangal <note>a root related to ginger used for digestion</note> and calamint, one drachm and one scruple each of ammi <note>also known as Bishop’s weed</note> and lovage, one drachm of long pepper, and one drachm each of spikenard, cardamom, and nutmeg. Prepare this with as much honey as is sufficient. It is effective against coldness of the chest and stomach, and for "winds" <note>original: *ventositates*; referring to gas or flatulence</note> of the skull and the belly. It helps with quartan fevers <note>a form of malaria where fever recurs every four days</note>, aids digestion, and is useful for those with a cough caused by cold humors.

<margin>The properties of Cumin.</margin>
Cumin is hot and dry in the third degree (though some say the second). It promotes urination and disperses gas, especially in the stomach. When drunk, it induces a pale complexion; for this reason, 
<margin>Persius.</margin>
Persius refers to "the grains of pale cumin," and 
<margin>Horace.</margin>
Horace says they "would drink bloodless cumin" <note>original: *biberent exangue cuminum*; ancient authors believed excessive cumin consumption caused a sallow, scholarly paleness</note>. When drunk with wine, it is a remedy against poisons and venomous bites.

### ¶ Diambra.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring foliate patterns.</image-desc> Take four drachms each of choice cinnamon, leopard's bane <note>original: *doronici*; a root used as a heart tonic</note>, cloves, mace, nutmeg, and galangal. One drachm each of spikenard and both large and small cardamom. One and a half drachms of white ginger. Two drachms each of yellow sandalwood, aloeswood <note>a fragrant, resinous wood</note> (or red sandalwood in its place), and long pepper. One and a half drachms of ambergris and half a drachm of musk. Prepare this with rose syrup and rose water. 

Diambra is effective for strengthening the brain; it comforts the powers of the heart, the stomach, and all the "animal" and "spiritual" organs <note>in Galenic medicine, "animal" refers to the brain/nerves and "spiritual" to the heart/lungs</note>. It gladdens the user, warms the digestive organs, and is suitable for the elderly and the weak, as well as for women of a "cold" nature and for ailments of the womb. 

<margin>What is ambergris?</margin>
What ambergris <note>original: *Ambra*</note> actually is remains unknown to our apothecaries and all physicians. However, it is certain that it is not a poison, whether it be "whale sperm," a sea fungus, or sea foam <note>the origin of ambergris, a secretion of sperm whales, was a major mystery in the Renaissance</note>. In any case, it is not a deadly substance; rather, it strengthens the vital and animal spirits through its aromatic quality.

### ¶ Warm Diamargariton.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring scrollwork and floral designs.</image-desc> Take one and a half drachms each of choice cinnamon, cloves, spikenard, galangal, aloeswood (or red sandalwood in its place), licorice, "rose-based" troches <note>original: *diarodon*; medicinal lozenges</note>, and "diaui" troches. Take one drachm each of nutmeg, mace, musky alipta <note>a perfumed medicinal paste</note>, zedoary <note>a root similar to turmeric</note>, rhubarb, and storax calamite <note>a fragrant tree resin</note>. Take one drachm each of shining pearls, ginger, the bone (or cartilage) from a stag's heart <note>original: *ossis, siue cartilaginis de corde cerui*; a rare ingredient believed to cure heart palpitations</note>, and ivory shavings. Take one scruple each of musk, ambergris, cardamom, lovage, and basil seed. Use as much rose honey as is sufficient. 

In this electuary, I have omitted camphor because it is dangerous, and "Byzantine blatta" <note>the operculum of a sea snail used in incense</note> because of its uncertainty; for in medicine, everything ought to be certain. As Hippocrates of Cos said, "The nobility of the subject [the human body] makes us cautious in our experiments." According to the writers Solinus and Ammianus, a type of shell grows primarily in the Indian Sea which conceives pearls from the quality of the dew...

<margin>Pearls are born in Lorraine.</margin>
...which the oysters, thirsting at a certain time of year, swallow through a kind of opening. If the dew they take in is pure, the pearls become a bright white; if it is turbid, they turn somewhat black or pale. Finally, it is believed that they become clearer from the "seed" of the morning air and larger from a more abundant draft of evening air, which makes them darker. If it thunders, the shells clamp shut, and contracting from the distress, they produce "abortive" pearls, which the ancients called small or empty bubbles <note>original: *physemata*</note>. Pearls are also produced that are round on one side and flat on the other; because of this, they are called "drum-pearls" <note>original: *tympania*</note> after the shape of a drum. There are also longer ones, which they call drop-shaped <note>original: *elenchos*</note> due to their tapering length, finishing in a fuller circle like the shape of alabaster jars. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist</note> says that the glory of women is to hang these from their fingers and to wear them by twos and threes in their ears. Pearls are also born on the island of Taprobane <note>modern-day Sri Lanka</note>, in the Persian Gulf of the Red Sea around Arabia, and even on the British shore, as Julius Caesar testified by the inscription placed under a breastplate <note>original: *Thoraci*</note> made of British pearls, which he dedicated to Venus the Mother <note>original: *Veneri genitrici*</note> and placed in her temple. There are also in Lorraine [as I have seen] springs in the Vosges valley <note>original: *valle Vosaga*</note> among the things memorable not to be omitted, so fertile in gems and pearls that almost the greater part of Germany uses these pearls alone. They are not only approved by any experts of the lapidary art, even foreign ones, but are also [and not wrongly] preferred to Arabian and British pearls. Pearls are cold and dry in the second degree. They help with dimness of vision and white spots in the eye; they restrain the menses, clean the teeth, dry out excess moisture, and are beneficial for heart palpitations <note>original: *cardiacæ*</note> and tremors of the heart. They clarify the blood of the heart and—as Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, a 10th-century physician</note> writes—they are balanced in heat, cold, dryness, and moisture. However, Rhazes <note>Al-Razi, a famous Persian physician</note> places them in the second degree of cold and dryness [as we said] with a little subtlety.

## ¶ Cold Diamargariton.
<note>A "diamargariton" is a pearl-based cordial or powder used as a heart tonic.</note>

Take one drachm <term>drachm: a unit of weight, approx. 3.9 grams</term> each of the four "greater cold seeds" <note>traditionally cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon</note>—all cleaned—of purslane seed, white poppy seed, white sandalwood, aloe-wood (or red sandalwood in its place), ginger, red roses, water-lily flowers, borage flowers, and myrtle berries. Take half a drachm each of white and red coral, and three drachms of choice pearls. Mix them together. It is effective for heart palpitations, for those who are sorrowful, and for all weakness of the heart and loathing of the stomach. When prepared warm, it is effective for those with asthma, helps those with difficulty breathing <note>original: *dispnoicis*</note>, and restores those with consumption <note>original: *phthisicos*</note> or those who have been thinned out by long illness.

...one <term>scruple</term> <note>A scruple is a small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams</note> of each of the four major cold seeds <note>original: *quatuor seminum frigidorum maiorum*; these were typically cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon</note>, cleaned; half a scruple each of pearls and the bone from a stag’s heart <note>The "os de corde cervi" was a cartilage-like bone found in the hearts of older deer, prized as a heart tonic</note>; one and a half ounces each of sugar candy and red roses; four grains of musk; and prepare it with as much rose julep <note>A sweet syrup made from rose water and sugar</note> as is sufficient. It is called **Diarodon** <note>From the Greek "dia" (by means of) and "rodon" (rose)</note> from the roses that enter into it. The rose is cold and dry; it strengthens the stomach and the liver, and it is helpful for bloody abscesses at their onset. Its juice [as Rhazes <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (854–925 AD), a Persian physician and philosopher</note> claims] is quite laxative; however, when dried, it is not laxative, but rather more astringent. **Diarodon** is effective for those with jaundice, liver disease, consumption, wasting fevers, heart conditions, and those recovering from chronic or even acute illnesses.

<margin>Dioscorides on asarabacca and camphor.</margin>
For in this composition, asarabacca <note>original: *asarum*; a plant used as an emetic</note> has been removed; for it is [as Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and author of "De Materia Medica"</note> writes] among those things that cause vomiting and expel through the bowels, being hot and dry in the third degree. Camphor is also removed, which is cold and dry in the third degree; it causes wakefulness, is very often adulterated, and is rarely found natural and genuine.

### ¶ Preparation of Calamint (Diacalamentum)

Take of calamint, pennyroyal, hyssop, black pepper, seseli <note>An herb often called "Hartwort"</note>, and parsley, four and a half <term>drachmas</term> <note>A drachma or dram is about 3.9 grams</note> each; of lovage, one and a half drachmas; of celery, one scruple; and of bishop’s weed, thyme, dill <note>original: *aneoti*</note>, anise, cinnamon, and ginger, half a drachma each; and as much honey as is sufficient. **Diacalamentum** is effective for every defect of the chest caused by cold, and especially for those who are in old age. It is also effective for those coughing from a cold cause, and for those suffering from quartan fevers <note>A form of malaria where fever recurs every fourth day</note>, if they use it after eating.

<margin>Calamint. Dioscorides.</margin>
<margin>What Nepeta is.</margin>
¶ Calamint, or *calaminthem*, is called *nepeta* <note>Catmint</note> by the Romans, as Dioscorides writes. In this genus of plants, there is a certain mountain variety: it has leaves like basil <note>original: *ocymi*</note>, of a whitish color, larger and smaller angular branches, and a purple flower. Another variety is similar to pennyroyal, only larger; hence some have called it "wild pennyroyal" because its scent is similar. This is what the Romans call *nepeta*. Finally, there is also a variety similar to wild mint, yet with longer leaves, stems, and branches, larger than all those mentioned before, but less effective and weaker. The leaves of all these have a burning flavor and a sharp taste, and they have a useless root. It grows—this *Nepeta*—in fields, and in rough and watery places. Taken as a drink or applied as a plaster, it helps with the bites of serpents. A decoction of it, when drunk, promotes urine. It is helpful for ruptures, convulsions, and for those who have such difficulty breathing that they can only breathe with a straight neck <note>A condition known as orthopnea</note>, for intestinal cramps, and for the overflow of bile, which they call "cholera." It is also useful against deadly poisons when drunk with wine at the onset of fevers accompanied by shivering and chills. It restores those afflicted with jaundice <note>original: *suffusos felle*; literally "overflowing with gall"</note>. When drunk with salt and honey, it kills intestinal roundworms and pinworms. It likewise kills them when boiled or crushed raw. It is beneficial in the diet of those with leprosy <note>original: *elephantijs*</note> when taken with whey. It kills the fetus in the womb. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (980–1037 AD), the "Prince of Physicians"</note> confuses calamint with oregano.

<margin>Pepper.</margin>
Take six <term>drachms</term> <note>A drachm is about 3.9 grams</note> each of the three peppers <note>original: "trium piperum"; usually referring to black, white, and long pepper</note>; four drachms each of ginger and anise; one and a half drachms each of spikenard, bishop’s weed <note>original: "ameos"</note>, and cinnamon; and one drachm each of celery seed, valerian <note>original: "fizeleos," likely a variant of "phu"</note>, and dried elecampane. Prepare this with clarified honey <note>original: "melle despumato"; honey that has been boiled and skimmed of its foam to make it purer</note>. This **Diatriton Pipereon** <note>From the Greek meaning "made of three peppers"</note> warms the stomach and removes pain caused by raw, phlegmatic moisture; it is effective against acid reflux and aids digestion. ¶ Pepper plants produce berries similar to our juniper bushes. Their pods, which contain the grains, are picked before they open and dried in the sun to make what is called **long pepper**. When they open upon reaching maturity, they reveal **white pepper**, which is then dried in the sun, changing its color and becoming wrinkled <note>This description likely refers to black pepper, as white pepper is typically produced by removing the outer husk</note>. Galen, Paulus <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note>, and Dioscorides make mention of these. It grows frequently in India; and since it is very hot, it is better suited for food in winter than in summer. But we read of this marvel: if you swallow pepper or mustard seeds whole, they do not heat the belly, but if they are ground up, they cause great heat. Pepper is hot and dry in the third degree; it dries out thick and sticky <term>humors</term> <note>The fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to control health</note>, disperses gas, and can irritate the kidneys. Some place it in the fourth degree of heating and drying substances.

### ¶ Simple Diairis.

Take one <term>ounce</term> of Florentine orris <note>The root of the Iris plant</note>; two drachms each of powdered sugar candy and "cold" tragacanth <note>A natural gum used as a binder</note> without camphor. Mix them; let it be made into a powder, or if you prefer, an <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note> by adding honey.

### ¶ Solomon’s Diairis.

<margin>Orris root.</margin>
<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
Take one ounce of Florentine orris; six drachms each of pennyroyal, hyssop, and licorice; four drachms each of tragacanth, sweet almonds, fresh pine nuts, cinnamon, ginger, and pepper; four and a half drachms each of dried figs, fig-flesh <note>original: "carnium," likely referring to the pulp of the dried fruit</note>, dates, and seeded raisins; two and a half drachms of red styrax <note>A fragrant tree resin</note>; and as much honey as is sufficient. It should be taken in the evening with warm wine. **Diairis** <note>A compound named after its primary ingredient, the Iris root</note> is beneficial for those with shortness of breath or coughs, and it restores a lost voice if the loss was caused by cold. Regarding the **Iris**: there are some who call it *lilyrida* or *urania*; the Egyptians call it *Nar*, the Romans call it *marica* root, *gladiolus*, or *consecratrix*. It is named after the similarity to the rainbow in the sky, which the Greeks call *Iris*. This plant is also named Iris for that reason. The most highly prized is the Illyrian and Macedonian iris; our Latin people praise the Florentine variety since they lack the Illyrian and Macedonian types. The nature and power of all of them [as Dioscorides writes] is to warm and to thin out <term>humors</term>. They are useful for coughs and they thin out phlegm that is difficult to cough up. They purge thick and bilious fluids when seven drachms are drunk with honey-water; they also induce sleep, provoke tears, and heal stomach cramps. These same roots, when drunk with vinegar, are useful against the bites of venomous creatures. They benefit those with spleen disorders, those suffering from convulsions, and those in the bouts of fevers or chills accompanied by shivering. They are also useful against feminine incontinence. They induce menstruation when drunk with wine; they are used in [poultices...]

### ¶ Cold Diagragantum.

Take two ounces of white <term>tragacanth</term> <note>original: "dragagāti"; a natural gum obtained from the dried sap of legumes</note>; one ounce and two <term>drachms</term> of gum arabic; half an ounce of starch; two drachms of licorice; three ounces of <term>penidium</term> <note>original: "penidiarum"; a traditional sugar candy made by pulling boiled sugar into sticks</note>; and two drachms each of the "four greater cold seeds" <note>original: "quatuor seminum frigidorum maiorum"; typically referring to the seeds of cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon</note>, cleaned. Add as much violet syrup or violet julep <note>a sweet, medicinal drink</note> as is sufficient. Camphor has been removed from this recipe because it is an enemy to human nature and is almost always adulterated. <margin>Properties of Tragacanth.</margin> ¶ This preparation of tragacanth is effective for every ailment of the chest and lungs caused by heat and dryness, especially for those who are consumptive <note>original: "phthisicis"</note>, feverish <note>original: "hecticis"</note>, suffering from pleurisy, or pneumonia. It is also good for any cough caused by heat and dryness, and for roughness of the tongue and throat. This "cold" tragacanth formula possesses moisture; it helps with coughs and ulcers of the eye by soothing the sharpness of other medicines. It heals roughness of the tongue and throat and loosens the bowels.

### ¶ Diamoron.

Take half a pound of the juice of cultivated mulberries <note>original: "mori Celsi"</note>, one pound of the juice of wild blackberries <note>original: "mori bassi"</note>, half a pound of honey, and three ounces of <term>sapa</term> <note>concentrated grape juice boiled down to a thick syrup</note>. Prepare the juice with the honey and sapa in a bronze or tinned vessel over light coals; let it boil until it is perfectly cooked. Strain it and keep it in a tinned vessel. It is effective for every ailment of the palate; it raises a drooping <term>uvula</term> <note>original: "vuam"</note> and dries out a phlegmatic one. ¶ Mulberries grow both on trees and on brambles. The poet Horace <note>original: "Cas' Horatius"; refers to the Roman poet Quintus Horatius Flaccus</note> believed that eating them after a meal during the summer contributed to health, saying in his *Satires*: "He shall spend healthy summers who finishes his meals with black mulberries, gathered from the tree before the sun becomes oppressive." The mulberry has a wine-like juice in its flesh and three colors: first white, then red, and finally black when ripe. It is among the first to bloom and the first to ripen, but it passes quickly. In temperament, mulberries are moderately warm; their power softens the belly. However, they spoil very quickly in the stomach—regardless of what Horace says—if they are eaten after other foods. They also grow on brambles with a very different skin; these were called *moratha* by Hippocrates. The Greeks graft the mulberry onto chestnut, beech, wild pear, elm, and white poplar trees, which results in white mulberries.

### ¶ **Resumptive electuary, or for restoring**
### **moisture.**

Take six drachms each of roses, licorice, and sugar; two and a half drachms each of gum arabic and tragacanth; one and a half drachms each of white and red sandalwood; three drachms each of white poppy, licorice juice, starch, purslane seed, lettuce seed, and <term>scariola</term> <note>prickly lettuce or endive</note> seed; one drachm each of cloves and <term>spodium</term> <note>original: "Spodij ex dente elephantis"; medicinal powder made from burnt elephant ivory</note>; one and a half drachms of cinnamon; two drachms each of ginger and <term>storax calamite</term> <note>a fragrant resin</note>; five grains of saffron; half an ounce of penidium; three drachms each of citron, melon, cucumber, and gourd seeds; one drachm of quince seed; two drachms each of almonds, pine nuts, and barberry; two drachms each of mallow seed, <term>quince</term> seed <note>original: "seminis coti"</note>, violets, <term>sebesten</term> <note>an Egyptian plum</note>, and water-lily; compound these with violet syrup.

### ¶ Plasters.

We shall say nothing of Plasters, for these do not portend death; for although plasters are of great use in the practice of medicine, and are sometimes substituted <note>original: "permutentur"</note> by younger physicians and apothecaries, yet this substitution is not fatal.

<margin>
Asarabacca.

The harms of Opium according to Nicander and Dioscorides.
Dioscorides.
</margin>
The "Greater Philonium" of Nicolaus, the "Persian Philonium," and "Philoanthropos" <note>Various names for complex sedative confections usually containing opium and henbane</note>, as well as the Philoniums of Mesue and the Son of Zacharias—we leave these aside as if they were the "sons of demons," or of ghosts, or of fauns. Into *Philoanthropos* <note>Literally "Friend of Man"</note> enters the emetic Asarabacca, the burning Euphorbium, Wood Cassia (which is unknown to us), and Carpobalsamum (unknown to the French and Italians). Into the *Greater Philonium* enters Henbane <note>original: "Iasquiamus"</note>, which is poisonous and stupefying, inducing a perpetual sleep; and Opium, in which Nicander <note>A Greek physician and poet</note> recounts—besides the chills recorded by Dioscorides <note>The famous Greek pharmacologist</note>—drowsiness, listlessness, and itching, and the smell of opium throughout the whole body. Other signs are many: a pale face, a fiery color of the lips, small and cold breaths, bluish nails, distorted nostrils, and hollow eyes. He also added that odor which Dioscorides says is given off by the whole body together with sweat, as if evaporating from labor. Into the *Philonium of the Son of Zacharias* there also enter opium, euphorbium, and henbane. Into the other *Philonium*, opium, euphorbium, and henbane also enter. Into the *Persian Philonium*, those sleep-inducing, narcotic, and nature-corrupting things enter in equal order. For a draught of the poppy's liquor, which is opium, is followed by chills and an itching so powerful that a stupor follows; as the poison grows stronger, the itching often becomes so great that he who has drunk it (as Dioscorides says) is stirred up by that annoyance, and furthermore, as has been said, the smell of opium is returned from the whole body.

Clove

Take of cloves, cinnamon, ginger, licorice, and roses, two and a half drachms of each; of aloes-wood (or in its place red sandalwood), galangal, sugar candy, nard, zedoary <note>a root similar to turmeric</note>, and violets, one drachm and one <term>scruple</term> <note>about 1.3 grams</note> of each; of rhubarb, mace, saffron, <term>alipta</term> <note>a medicinal paste or ointment</note>, cyperus, cardamom, basil, lovage, and ivory, half a drachm of each; and as much honey of roses as is sufficient. It is properly effective for those with acid reflux <note>original: "acide eructantibus"</note>, it procures digestion, and it opens the obstruction of the pores and the spiritual passages <note>original: "spiritualium meatuum"; referring to the channels for vital spirits in the body</note>. There is in India a thing similar to peppercorns which is called Clove <note>original: "Gariofilon"</note>, though larger and more easily broken. They say it is produced in an Indian grove; it used to be imported for the sake of its scent, but now for food, like pepper, especially by the peoples of the North. Paulus Ægineta <note>A 7th-century Byzantine physician</note> thinks it should be called *Caryophilon*, not *Gariofilon*.

### ¶ Looth of Pine.

Take thirty <term>drachmas</term> <note>a unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams</note> of pine nuts; half an ounce each of sweet almonds, roasted hazelnuts, <term>tragacanth</term> <note>a natural gum obtained from the dried sap of Middle Eastern legumes</note>, gum arabic, licorice and its juice, starch, maidenhair fern, and blue lily root; thirty-five drachmas of date flesh; four drachmas of bitter almonds; half an ounce each of raisin honey, sugar, and fresh butter; and as much selected honey as is sufficient. This <term>Looth</term> <note>original: "Looth"; an Arabic-derived term for a linctus or electuary, a thick medicinal syrup intended to be taken slowly to soothe the throat</note> of pine is used for a chronic cough, asthma, viscous phlegm, and constriction of the breath. <margin>Spruce differs from pine.</margin> ¶ Spruce <note>original: "picea"</note> differs from pine because it is oilier and has thinner leaves, and because it does not grow as high or as straight as the pine rises. When its roots are burned, the pine does not sprout back, but the spruce does. The <term>pinaster</term> <note>a wild or maritime pine</note> is nothing other than a wild pine of wondrous height that branches from the middle (whereas the pine branches at the top); it yields a more copious resin. It is established from Greek authors that in Europe there are six types of related trees that bear resin: the pine, the pinaster, the spruce, the fir, the larch, and the torch-pine; a seventh, the *piceaster*, can be added in Spain. The pine nut has a certain bitterness and acridity; because of this, it is suitable for those coughing up blood <note>original: "emopicis"</note> and others who need to easily cough up and purge matter from the lungs and chest. As a fruit for eating, however, it is difficult to digest, though suitable for soothing roughness, especially if it has been soaked in water first.

### ¶ Looth of Squill.

Take equal parts of squill <note>original: "squilla"; the sea onion (*Drimia maritima*), used as a stimulant and expectorant</note> juice and clarified honey; cook until it returns to the form of a linctus. Whether <term>Squill</term>—or as Varro calls it, *sqlla*, or Hippocrates *scella*—is a root, a bulb, a sprout, or a fruit, Theophrastus is uncertain. This is because there are those who show it has a double root. However, not every kind is used for its tenderness, but specifically that which is called the *Epimenidian* squill, which has a narrower and smoother leaf than the other kinds, which have very broad leaves. ¶ There are two species of squill used in medicine: the white, which is the male, and the black, which is the female. There is also the *pancration*, which we call the "little squill," which looks like a white lily but with thicker leaves. We have spoken more about squill in the section on squill-vinegar. This Looth of squill is a medicine of great help to those in whom thick, viscous, and "unripe" <note>meaning phlegm that is hard to loosen or expectorate</note> matter abounds in the respiratory organs, making it easy to expel; it also aids difficulty of breathing and pain in the chest and sides. <margin>Two species of Squill.</margin>

Take half an ounce each of cinnamon, dried hyssop, and licorice juice; thirty each of <term>jujubes</term> <note>original: "Iuiubarum"; the red, date-like fruit of the Ziziphus tree, used to soothe the throat</note> and <term>sebestens</term> <note>original: "Sebesten"; a plum-like fruit from the Cordia myxa tree, valued for its mucilaginous properties</note>; two ounces each of seeded raisins, dried figs, and fatty dates; five <term>drachmas</term> <note>a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note> of fenugreek; as much <term>maidenhair fern</term> <note>original: "Capillorum veneris"</note> as the hand can hold; four drachmas each of anise, fennel, <term>iris</term> <note>original: "yreos"; specifically the dried root of the blue lily or Florentine iris</note>, and calamint; and five drachmas of linseed. Afterward, throw in three drachmas each of cleaned pine nuts, almonds, licorice, tragacanth, gum arabic, and starch, and two drachmas of iris. Let them all be kneaded and stirred until the medicine matures and turns white. It is beneficial for a cough and for hoarseness of the voice caused by cold or by thick phlegm contained within the chest and lungs.

## ¶ Looth of Stalks, or of Cabbage.

<margin>Cabbage.</margin>
<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
<margin>Virtue of cabbage.</margin>
<margin>Galen.</margin>
<margin>Cato.</margin>
Take one pound of the juice of stalks, or red cabbage; two drachmas of saffron; and half a pound each of sugar and honey. Mix as is proper, and let it become a <term>Looth</term> <note>a thick, syrupy medicine intended to be licked or dissolved slowly in the mouth</note>. <term>Cato</term> <note>Marcus Porcius Cato (234–149 BC), a Roman statesman who wrote extensively on agriculture and medicine</note> identifies three kinds of cabbage: one with spread leaves and a large stalk; another with curly leaves, which he calls "Apian" or "Selinada"; and a third with small stalks that is smooth and tender—our people call these "stalks," from which we derive the terms "caulicles" or "colicles." By eating cabbage, the senses are cleared. The discourse of <term>Erasistratus</term> <note>a Greek anatomist and royal physician (c. 304–250 BC)</note> maintained that nothing is healthier or more useful for the stomach and nerves than cabbage. Therefore, he ordered it to be given to those with palsy or tremors, and those coughing up blood. Eating cabbage while it is somewhat raw loosens the bowels [as <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>a Greek physician and botanist, author of "De Materia Medica"</note> writes], but it binds them when thoroughly cooked, and even more so if cooked twice. The sharpness of cabbage is greater in the summer and harder on the stomach, even if Erasistratus writes the opposite. According to the decrees of the Greeks, all cabbages loosen the bowels, but wild cabbage is more effective for all purposes than the cultivated variety; yet it is not admitted into the body without some harm. However, sea cabbage, being a participant in saltiness and bitterness, purges the bowels most violently. Cabbage provides little nourishment, but it dispels a hangover and slows drunkenness [as <term>Aristotle</term> reports], for it dries up the vapors [as <term>Galen</term> attests]. If anyone is hard of hearing [Cato says in his *On Agriculture*], let him grind cabbage with wine and drop the expressed warm juice into the ear; he will quickly realize he hears more. Some report that the Roman people used the medicine of cabbage for nearly six hundred years; for physicians had not yet gathered in the city to bring pigments <note>refined drugs or compound medicines</note> with them. Instead, in that age, military men cared for their glorious scars for free with this vegetable <note>original: "olere"; likely referring to "olera" or potherbs/vegetables</note>.

### On the Fox and its nature.

The Fox [as Aristotle writes] is a clever animal and given to evil deeds. It possesses a penis bone <note>original: "virgam ex osse"; the baculum, found in many mammals</note> and mates while lying on the ground. And [as Constantine writes] the fox is said to imitate the barking of dogs out of distress <note>original: "prae angustia," though the context suggests "out of hunger" (fame)</note>; that is, when it is hungry and finds nothing to eat, it feigns death. It lies on its back and draws in its breath with its tongue sticking out. Then, when birds descend carelessly as if to a corpse, it seizes them with an open mouth and devours them. Its dried lung is beneficial for those suffering from asthma, <term>dyspnea</term> <note>difficulty breathing</note>, and shortness of breath, and it strengthens the human lung.

## M

### ¶ Mithridatum.

<margin>The composition of Mithridatum.</margin>
<margin>The death of Mithridates.</margin>
In the chests of Mithridates the Great, King of Pontus and the Persians, after he was defeated, Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus <note>Pompey the Great, the Roman general</note> found a recipe for an antidote written in the king's own hand in a private journal. It was made from two dried walnuts, two figs, and twenty leaves of rue ground together with a grain of salt. Whoever takes this on an empty stomach will not be harmed by any poison on that day. From this it happened [to say nothing of other matters for now] that the noble antidote composed by King Mithridates has had its name usurped by a certain younger physician—not by that King of the Persians and Pontus—who desired to claim the name for himself, as Avicenna and other Arab masters seemed to believe. For that original antidote of King Mithridates was composed of only four ingredients [as was stated], whereas the composition used by the younger doctors and the Arabs is constructed from one hundred and eight or even more <term>simples</term> <note>individual medicinal herbs or substances used as ingredients</note>. For the present, we show only this: that in our age, the younger doctors do not have a certain knowledge of King Mithridates’ recipe. The antidote of King Mithridates contains only four simples; however, that composition of the recent physicians contains one hundred and eight and a bit more, including many things that are unknown to our people and cannot be found by our apothecaries. In this age of ours, these are known neither by the Greeks nor the Latins, let alone the <term>Barbarians</term> <note>non-classical, often Arabic or Germanic, medical authorities</note>. Among these are Myrrh, <term>xylobalsamum</term> <note>the wood or twigs of the balsam tree</note>, turpentine resin, <term>cassia lignea</term> <note>the woody bark of the cassia tree, similar to cinnamon</note>, <term>opobalsamum</term> <note>the sap or juice of the balsam tree</note>, <term>carpobalsamum</term> <note>the fruit or berries of the balsam tree</note>, <term>bdellium</term> <note>a semi-transparent oleo-gum resin</note>, stone parsley, acacia, <term>Lemnian earth</term> <note>a medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos</note>, <term>amomum</term> <note>an aromatic spice related to cardamom</note>, and <term>malabathrum</term> <note>leaves of the cinnamon-laurel tree</note>. We have discussed these at length in the first book of our *Castigations* <note>original: "castigationum"; a work of scholarly corrections or critiques</note>. 

Mithridates, King of Pontus and Armenia, was a very superstitious man. At seventy-five years of age, he always kept philosophers and those most skilled in all the arts with him. When he was besieged by his son Pharnaces and saw that his son was inexorable, being about to die, he is said to have exclaimed: 

-> "Since Pharnaces [he said] commands me to die, I pray to you, gods of our fathers, that one day he himself may hear this voice from his own children." <-

Immediately going down to his wives, concubines, and daughters, he gave poison to them all. When he himself drank it last, he could not be killed by the poison because of the remedies with which he had often blocked his vital organs against harmful juices. Though he paced about in vain, hoping the internal pestilence would finally run through his veins by the movement of his body, it would not take. Finally, he invited a certain Gaulish soldier who was running through the now-broken wall and offered him his throat to be cut. Such was the end Mithridates had, and he left us a very strong proof of his life and his maxim; he was seventy-five years old [as was said].

## N

**Nefrocarticum** <note>original: "Nefrocarticum Nicolai," a kidney-purging remedy attributed to the medieval authority Nicolaus Praepositus</note> is not in use by our apothecaries, nor is it prepared in the workshops. In it are included ingredients that the prudent should be wary of, such as <term>Euphorbium</term> <note>a caustic and highly irritating plant resin</note>, "lynx stone" <note>lapis lyncis, believed in folklore to be fossilized lynx urine, often identified as amber or belemnite fossils</note>, and the stone of a pig's bladder. It also includes ingredients that are not found by our people, such as balsam, myrrh, <term>Cassia lignea</term> <note>an aromatic bark similar to cinnamon</note>, and many others.

## O

¶ **Diuretic Oxymel, or compound oxymel.**

<margin>The nature of honey.</margin>
**T**ake one pound each of the bark of celery and fennel roots; one dram each of parsley, butcher's broom, asparagus, celery seeds, and fenugreek. Let the aforementioned roots and seeds be boiled in twelve pounds of water and one pound of vinegar until half the volume is consumed. Then, with as much honey as is sufficient, let a syrup be made by boiling it to perfection. <term>Oxymel</term> <note>from the Greek for "acid and honey," a traditional medicinal syrup made of honey and vinegar</note> aids digestion, breaks up humors, and purges phlegm; it is given in the morning to disperse phlegm. ¶ Honey is hot and dry in the second degree, composed of thin parts, and is cleansing. It contains a certain acrid quality that must be excreted; it stimulates the belly and promotes urine, but it does not loosen the bowels unless mixed with much water. Skimmed honey <note>original: "dispumatum," honey that has had its impurities boiled off as foam</note> is suitable for the elderly and those of a cold temperament, but it turns to bile in those of a hot temperament. When cooked by itself, it causes less flatulence and is consequently less nourishing.

¶ **Squill Oxymel.**

**T**ake three pounds of skimmed honey and two pounds of <term>squill</term> vinegar <note>vinegar in which the sea onion, *Drimia maritima*, has been steeped</note>. Let it be boiled and skimmed, and prepared as described for diuretic oxymel. It is beneficial for difficulty in breathing, chest pain, and asthma. (The use of squill was discussed in the section on the <term>lohoch</term> <note>a linctus or medicine meant to be licked</note> of squill).

¶ **Simple Oxysaccharum.**

**T**ake one pound of sugar, eight ounces of sour pomegranate juice, and four ounces of vinegar. Place them in a tinned vessel over the fire, stirring until it returns to the consistency of sugar, and store it in an earthenware or tin vessel.

¶ **Compound Oxysaccharum.**

**T**ake one pound—either of all together or of each—of fresh maidenhair fern, hart's tongue fern, ceterach, wall-rue, liverwort, violets, fennel, butcher's broom, asparagus, and couch grass. Infuse the herbs and roots in sour pomegranate juice for three days. Afterward, let them boil slightly; strain and press them out. Then add as much sugar as is required and boil until fully decocted. <term>Oxysaccharum</term> <note>from the Greek for "acid and sugar," a syrup made with sugar instead of honey</note> is effective against <term>synochus</term> <note>a continuous fever</note>, <term>causus</term> <note>a burning, inflammatory fever</note>, and against all acute and very severe illnesses—both the simple and compound varieties, but the simple is more effective. The compound variety is useful in fevers composed of both bile and phlegm.

¶ **On Oil.**

<margin>On oil, from Plato, in the Protagoras.</margin>
**O**il (as Plato writes in his work *Protagoras*) is most beneficial to all trees and herbs, but it is very harmful to the hair of all animals (except for humans). Indeed, he says it benefits human hair and the whole body. Thus, oil is best for the external parts of our body, but worst for the internal parts. For this reason, physicians forbid the use of oil to the sick, nor do they permit its use...

->¶ **Powder Against Worms.**<-

Let a powder be made; let the patient take it in the morning with purslane and grass water.

->¶ **New Rose Remedy.**<-

Take one ounce and two drams each of roses, sugar, and liquorice; two and a half drams of cinnamon; half a dram each of cloves, spikenard, ginger, galangal, nutmeg, zedoary, <term>storax calamita</term> <note>a fragrant resin from the Styrax tree</note>, cardamom, and celery; and as much honey as is sufficient. It is effective for dryness of the heart, liver, and lungs, for it is temperate in nature. It wonderfully aids those weakened by long illness and suppresses <term>diaphoretic sweats</term> <note>excessive or profuse sweating</note>.

->¶ **Rest (Requies).**<-

Take three drams each of roses and violets; eight drams of white poppy; two drams each of endive, lettuce, purslane seeds, <term>psyllium</term> <note>flea-wort seeds, used as a thickening agent</note>, nutmeg, cinnamon, and sugar; one dram each of the three sandalwoods, <term>spodium</term> <note>metallic ash or burnt bone used in pharmacy</note>, and tragacanth; and as much honey as is sufficient. It is called "Rest" because it provides rest and sleep. Opium, mandrake, and henbane have been removed from this recipe, as they are enemies of nature. <note>The author emphasizes safety by excluding strong narcotics commonly used in medieval versions of this recipe.</note>

->¶ **Red Lozenges.**<-

Take three and a half drams each of liquorice, cinnamon, saffron, and roses; one ounce of white poppy; two and a half drams each of saffron, roses, and celery seeds; one and a half drams each of spikenard and violets; one <term>scruple</term> <note>a small unit of apothecary weight, roughly 1.3 grams</note> each of cloves, storax, and anise; and as much honey as is sufficient. These red lozenges, when taken with <term>ptisan</term> <note>a medicinal barley water</note>, check the spitting of blood and soothe acute fevers; however, I do not recommend giving them to those with acute fevers. Before the hour of onset of periodic fevers, it is effective with rose water; it is also useful after <term>phrensy</term> <note>delirium or inflammation of the brain</note> when the cause of wakefulness and dryness of the brain remains. In this composition, henbane and opium have been removed as dangerous, as has myrrh, because good quality myrrh is not found; likewise <term>saffron-magnet lozenges</term> <note>original: "trocisci crocomagnetis"</note> and <term>special mixtures</term> <note>original: "idiocria"</note> are omitted, as they are neglected by our apothecaries.

It bears grains whose flavor is sweet with an underlying acidity. It is cold and dry in the second degree <note>referring to the Galenic system of 'humors' where medicines were classified by degrees of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note>." It cuts off long-standing fluxes and the chronic humors that flow from the womb, as **Dioscorides** <note>a Greek physician and father of pharmacognosy</note> writes. ¶ Rob comforts a "hot" stomach, settles choleric vomiting <note>vomiting caused by an excess of yellow bile</note>, extinguishes thirst, and mitigates the racing of the heart. It also strengthens the heart, binds a choleric stool, and alters the body's condition. Rob of barberry is as effective as rob of currants, and its operation is the same.

### ¶ Syrup of Citron Juice,

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring a serpent-like creature entwined with acanthus leaves and floral motifs.</image-desc>

The **Syrup of Citron Juice** by **Mesue** <note>referring to Mesue the Younger, a likely pseudonymous author of highly influential medieval pharmacy texts</note> is prepared according to his method as follows: Take 12 pounds of the acidic juice of citrons. Cook it in a glass vessel over coals until a third part is consumed, then let it be strained and allowed to rest so that it clarifies. Afterward, take 7 pounds of the clear liquid and pour over it 2 pounds of clear, purified <term>julep</term> <note>a sweet syrup made of sugar and water</note>. Cook this until the julep thickens with clarified sugar that has been cooked to perfection. For every pound of sugar, three and a half pounds of the aforementioned juice ought to be added, as is stated in the syrup of Mesue.

However, it is certain and clear among apothecaries that from each citron fruit, barely one ounce of juice can be extracted after the sediment has settled, as Mesue teaches and commands to be done. Thus, for every pound of sugar or cooked and clarified julep, four and a half pounds of purified and clarified juice are required by Mesue's recipe. Therefore, it must be noted first of all that when Mesue says in the composition of this syrup, "Take 12 pounds of citron juice," and for every pound of juice, 12 fruits are required, that would mean 144 fruits for the entire recipe. Consequently, constructing this syrup of citron juice would result in a syrup of **immense price**. For at the market in **Lyon** <note>original: "Lugdunum," a major European trading hub for medicine and spices</note>, one can barely get four citrons for a single gold coin <note>original: "aureus"</note>. Thus, a pound of this syrup would exceed the price of four gold coins; and yet, from our apothecaries, a pound of the syrup can be had for barely a quarter of a gold coin. You see now how greatly Mesue—the "evangelist" of the younger physicians—is blinded even in the most obvious matters. Thus, through the ignorance of the barbarians, the entire beauty of medicine has perished; which, may the gods grant, we might recover through the studies of all learned men. It would have been better to compose the syrup of citron juice using a decoction of its acidic parts rather than with the juice alone.

This syrup (says **Mesue** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a 9th-century Persian physician influential in the development of pharmacy</note>) is effective in extinguishing inflammations of yellow bile and fevers of violent inflammation, as well as for pestilential fevers. <margin>What citron apples are.</margin>
¶ Citron apples <note>original: "Citrea mala"</note> are highly fragrant, as **Oppian** <note>A 2nd-century Greco-Roman poet who wrote on natural history</note> writes; in Persia, they are produced at all times, for some are picked early while others ripen in the meantime. **Martial** <note>A Roman poet known for his epigrams</note> says in his *Xenia*: "Either these are from the leaves of the Corcyrean garden, or these were the apples of the Massylian dragon." The citron rinds are hot in the first degree and dry at the end of the second. The flesh, however, is hot in the first degree and moist in the second. In the fruit itself, cold and dryness occur in the third degree <note>These "degrees" refer to the Galenic system of humors, used to classify the potency of medicines</note>. The flesh is difficult to digest and produces thick <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituitam"; one of the four bodily humors, believed to cause sluggishness when in excess</note>; for this reason, they should be eaten with honey or sugar. Citron seeds are effective against all poisons, especially the venomous bites of scorpions, whether drunk or applied topically. It fends off the plague, promotes menstruation, and the acidity of the fruit greatly expels yellow bile. The rind aids in the digestion of food and acts against <term>melancholy</term> <note>an excess of black bile, believed to cause sadness and physical ailments</note> and its despondency of spirit. It benefits the stomach when used moderately, for it is difficult to digest if taken immoderately.

### Syrup of Violets.

<margin>The types, species, and properties of violets.</margin>
Take 2 ounces of violets; 8 ounces each of quince seeds and mallow seeds; 20 each of jujubes and <term>sebesten</term> <note>a type of plum-like fruit from the Cordia tree, used as a soothing agent</note>. Boil in the juice of a <term>gourd</term> <note>original: "cucurbitae"; likely referring to a pumpkin or squash</note> or its decoction until a third part is consumed, and with 1 and a half pounds of sugar, let a syrup be made. Syrup of sorrel juice <note>original: "acetosae"</note> is made just like syrup of violet juice. Syrup of <term>verjuice</term> <note>original: "agresta"; the tart, acidic juice of unripe grapes</note> is made like the syrup of citron acidity. ¶ There are several kinds of violets: purple, yellow, saffron-colored, and white. The purple one, growing naturally in sunny and lean places from a rising root, they call "hyacinth." Among the violets, I would place the fragrant flower whose scent is not unlike the **Clove** <note>original: "Carophylo"</note>, from which it rightly took its name among the spices. Violet leaves possess a watery and slightly cold power; their first virtue is that they cool a little; the second is that they soften; and the third is that they soothe hot <term>abscesses</term> <note>original: "apostemata"; painful, inflamed swellings</note> when applied alone or with barley flour. Violets (as **Rhazes** <note>Al-Razi, a celebrated 10th-century Persian physician and chemist</note> says) are cold and sleep-inducing, and they soothe headaches caused by heat. Syrup of violets is beneficial for a "hot" cough and for pleurisy.

<margin>Wormwood.</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial A featuring a tree trunk with leafy branches and architectural pedestal motifs.</image-desc>

Take half a pound <note>original: "lib. dimidiā"</note> of Roman wormwood, two ounces of roses, and three drams of spikenard <note>original: "spicę"</note>. Take one and a half pounds each of fragrant old wine and quince juice. Let them sit for a day and a night in a stone vessel; then let them be cooked until half the volume is consumed. With two pounds of honey, let a syrup be made. It is valuable for loss of appetite, weakness of the stomach, softening of the bowels, and weakness and pain of the liver; for it is a noble and proven remedy. ¶ Wormwood is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. Its juice is a much hotter herb, possessing a significant and notable bitterness, and is especially sharp <term>pontic</term> <note>A term from ancient pharmacology describing a flavor that is both bitter and astringent, named after the Pontus region</note>. Therefore, it cleanses, strengthens, and dries. For this reason, it also drives bilious humors through the lower part of the belly and exhausts them through urine. It wards off hangovers <note>original: "crapulam arcet"</note> and is suitable when drunk to counter inflammations. When drunk with Celtic nard, it cures pains of the belly and stomach, treats jaundice <note>original: "arquatos"; literally "the rainbow-colored ones," referring to the yellowing of the skin</note>, and sharpens the appetite. Its decoction, taken daily in the amount of three cups <note>original: "cyathos"</note>, helps against suffocation from mushrooms if drunk with vinegar.

### ¶ Syrup of Licorice

<margin>Licorice</margin>
Take two ounces of Licorice <note>original: "Liquiriciae"</note>, one ounce of Maidenhair fern <note>original: "Capillorum veneris"</note>, and half an ounce of dried hyssop. Pour four pounds of water over these and let them sit for a day and a night. Then cook the mixture until half remains, adding eight ounces each of honey, sugar, and penidium <note>A form of pulled sugar or barley sugar used to soothe the throat</note>, and five drams of rose water. Let a syrup be made. This syrup benefits an old cough and cleanses the chest and lungs. ¶ The primary virtue of licorice (as Galen writes) is a virtue cooler than the complexion of the human body, as if it were of a lukewarm heat; for this reason, it seems to be of an equal temperament, being moderately moist. Its second virtue is that it soothes, and its third virtue is that it eases the roughness of the throat <note>original: "meri," likely a typo for "arteriae," the windpipe</note> and the bladder, quenches thirst, benefits the lungs, and takes away the burning of urine.

### ¶ Syrup of Hyssop

<margin>The property of Hyssop</margin>
<image-desc>Intricate woodcut initial 'A' with floral motifs against a cross-hatched background.</image-desc>
Take ten drams each of dried Hyssop, celery root, fennel, parsley, and Licorice; half an ounce of pearled barley; three drams each of mallow seed, tragacanth <note>A natural gum obtained from dried sap</note>, and quince seeds; six drams of maidenhair fern; thirty each of jujubes <note>a red, date-like fruit</note> and sebestens <note>a type of plum used in ancient medicine</note>; twenty drams of cleaned raisins; ten each of dried figs and plump dates; and two pounds of penidium. When drunk, it succors the asthmatic; it aids an old cough and catarrh, and kills intestinal worms. Mixed with honey, it performs the same. It is chewed with green figs to loosen the bowels; if mixed with cardamom or iris, it purges most vehemently. It produces a healthy complexion. Combined with wine, it helps with quinsy <note>severe sore throat or tonsillitis</note> when the decoction is used as a gargle. Take twenty drams of epithyme <note>The parasitic "dodder of thyme" plant, highly valued in medieval medicine</note>; fifteen drams each of yellow and Indian myrobalans <note>A plum-like fruit used as a laxative</note>; eight drams each of dodder and fumitory; six drams each of thyme, bugloss (which we call borage), calamint, emblic and belleric myrobalans, licorice, polypody fern, agaric, and Arabian lavender; two drams each of roses, fennel seed, and anise; twenty plums; four ounces of cleaned raisins; and two and a half ounces of tamarinds. With four pounds of sugar and two pounds of rob <note>A thickened fruit juice or syrup concentrate</note>, let a syrup be made. It effectively expels black bile <note>original: "bilem atram"</note> and burnt humors, and purges diseases caused by black bile. It benefits those prone to elephantiasis (which the Arabs call leprosy), those suffering from cancer, malignant wounds, fistulas, scabies, and *saphati* <note>A term for scaly skin eruptions or rashes on the face and head</note>. Epithyme is more powerful in its effects than thyme, being drying and heating in the third degree. Moreover, it purges black bile and helps with spasms. Dioscorides says that when drunk with honey, it purges phlegm and black bile through the bowels. It grows most abundantly in Cappadocia and Pamphylia.

### ¶ Syrup of Agrimony

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' inside a woodcut illustration of a scholar observing a globe with measuring instruments.</image-desc>
Take two ounces each of the roots of celery, fennel, and endive (which our people call scariola); six drams each of licorice, camel grass, dodder, wormwood, and roses; five drams each of maidenhair fern, bedeguar <note>A gall formed on wild roses, used medicinally</note>, bugloss or borage flowers, anise, fennel, and eupatorium (which we call agrimonia <note>original: "agrimoniam"</note>); three drams each of rhubarb <note>original: "rauedseni"</note> and mastic; and a portion of spikenard. Cook these in eight pounds of water until a third remains, and with four pounds of sugar and a sufficient quantity of celery juice and scariola (or endive) juice, let a syrup be made. We have removed *malabatrum* <note>The leaf of the Cinnamomum tamala tree, similar to a bay leaf</note> as it is unknown to our people.

<margin>Properties of the poppy.</margin> Poppy <note>original: "papauer"</note> is quite cold in nature and induces sleep; so much so that if anyone uses it excessively, they will be buried in a very deep sleep, much like those suffering from lethargy. Notable physicians report that when mixed with breast milk and saffron, it relieves those suffering from gout <note>original: "padagricos", referring to podagra</note>. Its juice is deadly; indeed, the juice of the black poppy is named opium.

### ¶ Syrup of Mugwort.

<margin>Properties of Mugwort.</margin> Take two handfuls of mugwort <note>original: "arthemisiae"</note>; one handful each of pennyroyal, calamint, oregano, lemon balm, water pepper, savin, marjoram, germander, St. John's wort <note>original: "perforatae"</note>, ground-pine, feverfew with its flower, lesser centaury, rue, betony, borage; and one handful each of the roots of fennel, celery, parsley, asparagus, butcher's broom, saxifrage, elecampane, dittany, galingale, madder, iris, and peony. Take half an ounce each of juniper berries, lovage, celery seed, anise, black cumin, pellitory, cardamom, and aromatic calamus. Let them be crushed and soaked in a sufficient amount of river water for a day and a night. Afterward, let them be boiled until half the liquid has evaporated. Then, remove them from the fire, rub them together with your hands, and strain the mixture. To the strained liquid, add as much honey and sugar as is required, and boil until it reaches perfection. Finally, add sharp vinegar or squill vinegar <note>vinegar infused with sea onion, used to cut through phlegm</note>, and let it be flavored with cinnamon and spikenard. This syrup is effective for ailments of the womb <note>original: "matricis"</note> caused by corrupt matter and obstructions. ¶ Mugwort is named after the goddess Artemis, or perhaps after Queen Artemisia, though it was formerly called *parthenis*. It heals all the maladies of women. It is said that a traveler who carries this herb tied together with sage will not feel the fatigue of the journey. If anyone suffering from a stomach ailment takes this herb as a pottage and mixes it with almond oil, and then applies this poultice to the stomach, they will be healed of that pain, as Dioscorides writes.

### ¶ Concerning Theriac.

<margin>Galen.</margin> Theriac <note>original: "tyriaca", a famous ancient poly-pharmaceutical "universal" antidote</note> was invented as a defense against poisons. It was named by the Greeks after wild beasts or creatures <note>original: "feris siue beluis", from the Greek *therion*</note>, because this composition was established to counter all venomous beasts. For this reason, the younger physicians are mistaken—especially those following the teachings of the Arabs—who call Theriac (or *Tyriaca*), once a noble antidote, not after beasts, but after "Tyro" <note>likely referring to a misunderstanding of *Tyrus*, the viper</note>. Since they do not have certain knowledge of it, it is no wonder if it does not produce the effects promised by the ancients. Galen, in his book on Theriac addressed to Pamphilianus, says it was so named because of the tranquility <note>Greek: *theriaken* from *ther* (beast), but here Galen or the author may be punning on its soothing effects</note> it usually brings to the sick. Therefore, it is quite surprising that many doctors of our age, looking carelessly at these various interpretations, sometimes read "tyrum" and sometimes "viper" in medical books, believing there to be a difference not just in the names but in the animals themselves. They believed some lozenges <note>original: "trociscos"</note> were made from "tyrus" and others from vipers, even though the *Tyrus* or viper is found everywhere in Narbonne Gaul and Italy, and is commonly called *marassus*. This nomenclature is neither barbaric nor devised without reason; for the name seems to be derived through etymological interpretation from the Marsi people, because the Marsi were most skilled at catching and exhibiting that species.

<margin>Silius.</margin> ¶ Silius Italicus also speaks of the Marsi in his eighth book <note>referring to the epic poem *Punica*</note>:

> They knew how to defeat the fierce; and the Marsian 
> youth fought both by hand and by lulling the water-snakes 
> to sleep, and by dulling the viper’s tooth 
> with a song. <note>original: "Debellare acres norant/ ac Marsica pubes Et bellare manu/ & chelydris cantare soporē, vipereūq[ue] harēbis hebetare/ & carmine dentē."</note>

<margin>Aulus Gellius.</margin> Aulus Gellius indicates the same in the sixteenth book of his *Attic Nights*, chapter eleven, saying: "The race of the Marsi in Italy is said to be descended from Circe."

## ¶ The Great Tryphera.
<note>original: "Trifera magna", a "tryphera" is a type of soft, pleasant-tasting electuary</note>

Take one drachm each of: cloves, cinnamon, galingale, spikenard, zedoary, ginger, storax calamite, aromatic calamus, cyperus, iris, hog's fennel <note>original: "peucedani"</note>, acorus, celtic nard, roses, pepper, anise, celery seed, parsley, fennel, Macedonian parsley, wild carrot <note>original: "dauci"</note>, cumin, and basil. Use as much honey as is sufficient.
<margin>Tryphera is without narcotic opium.</margin>
Removed from this tryphera are narcotic opium, mandrake (which is contrary to nature, sleep-inducing, and deadly), the perilous henbane, and hemlock <note>original: "pimes", likely referring to "pimeleon" or a similar toxic plant</note>. This tryphera is given against stomach pain in men and women with water in which have been boiled seeds of fennel, anise, and mastic. It is given against defects of the womb caused by coldness; if drunk with wine in which mugwort has been boiled, it provokes menstruation. With a decoction of mugwort, eight drachms of white poppy seed can be used in place of opium.

## ¶ The Three Sandalwoods.
<note>original: "Triasandali"</note>

Take one and a half drachms each of: starch, gum arabic, tragacanth, and the seeds of melons, watermelons, cucumbers, gourds, and escarole. Add as much rose syrup as is sufficient. Others take the powder and, with enough sugar, make an electuary in tablets. Camphor is excluded as being adulterous and contrary to nature, whatever Avicenna may say. It is effective against heat of the liver and stomach, for those with consumption <note>original: "phthificis"</note>, and for the "royal disease" <note>jaundice</note>. It is also effective for headaches caused by heat when taken with barley water; indeed, it works for every pain arising from a "hot" cause.
<margin>The virtues of the Three Sandalwoods.</margin>
Sandalwoods are cold in the third degree and dry in the second. They assist with weakness of the stomach and headaches caused by yellow bile.
<margin>Sandalwoods.</margin>
Red sandalwood is colder than the white and yellow varieties. All kinds of sandalwood assist with heart palpitations <note>original: "cardiacae"</note> that occur with fever, when the area of the heart is anointed with them.

### ¶ Troches of *Diaui*, or of Violets.

<margin>Violets.</margin>
Take six drachms of white violet flowers, four drachms of starch, two and a half drachms of white poppy seed, one and a half drachms of Rhubarb, one drachm of plantain seed, and a sufficient amount of rose water. Prepare these in the manner of rose troches. ¶ The primary virtue of violets is slightly cooling; the second is that they are soothing; and the third is that they calm hot swellings <note>original: "apostemata calida", or inflammatory abscesses</note> when applied alone or with barley flour. ### ¶ Troches of Alkekengi.

Take three drachms of Alkekengi <note>the winter cherry or bladder cherry, *Physalis alkekengi*</note> berries, and three and a half drachms each of melon seeds and gourd seeds. ### ¶ Troches of Musked Gallia.

Take five parts of red sandalwood, three parts of amber <note>original: "Ambrę"; likely referring to ambergris, a highly valued aromatic substance</note>, and one part of musk. Add a sufficient amount of tragacanth gum extracted with rose water to incorporate them: let them be made into troches, stamped with a seal, and stored in a glass vessel. This preparation comforts the brain and the heart; <margin>They are used in the preparations for noble men.</margin> it is included in the mixtures of medicines, and it makes the scent of the mouth and body praiseworthy.

### ¶ Troches of Agaric.

Take one part of agaric <note>the larch fungus, *Laricifomes officinalis*, used as a purgative</note> and a third part of rock salt <note>original: "Salis gemmę"</note>, or in place of salt, an equal amount of ginger. Let the troches be made with oxymel <note>original: "syrupo acetoso," a syrup of honey and vinegar</note>. These troches are as effective as agaric itself. We have spoken extensively regarding agaric in the first book of our *Corrections* in chapter 50.

### ¶ Troches of Karabe.

Take six aurei <note>an ancient weight equivalent to a gold coin, roughly 4.5 grams</note> of Karabe <term>Karabe: the Arabic term for yellow amber (succinite), a fossilized resin</term>, and two aurei each of the following: burnt hartshorn, roasted gum arabic, burnt coral, tragacanth, hypocistis <note>a parasitic plant extract used as an astringent</note>, balaustia <note>wild pomegranate flowers</note>, mastic, washed lac <note>a resin secreted by insects</note>, and roasted black poppy. Take one and a half aurei each of frankincense and saffron, and half an ounce of white poppy. Make the troche with psyllium mucilage. These troches cut off the flow of blood from any place of its discharge. Avicenna, along with the entire school of the Arabs, is hallucinating here—seduced, of course, by a fabulous error—thinking that Karabe (which the Greeks call *Electrum* and the Latins call *Succinum*) is the gum of a poplar tree. We spoke of Karabe in the first book of our *Corrections* in the collection of errors near the end of chapter 53. From this preparation, opium has been removed, because it is deadly, stupefying, and contrary to nature.

### ¶ On Ointments.

Ointments, though made from diverse things, have obtained a single scent according to an uncertain author. Previously, each ingredient was fragrant on its own, such as balsam sap <note>original: "opobalsama"</note>, liquid myrrh <note>original: "stacte"</note>, and musk <note>original: "moschos"</note>. The method of making them is twofold, as Pliny says in his thirteenth book: the juice and the body. The former consists of various types of oils, the latter of scents. These are called *stymmata* <note>the thickening or base elements</note> and those are called *hedismata* <note>the aromatic seasonings or scents</note>; and from dry scents come *diapasmata* <note>aromatic dusting powders</note>. The dregs they call *magmata*. These did not exist in the times of the Trojan War. It is reported that Alexander the Great first discovered them after the camps of Darius were captured, when he took a casket of ointments among the rest of the equipment. Nor is it certain when they first penetrated Rome; however, after Antiochus and Asia were defeated in the five hundred and sixty-fifth year of the city, the censors P. Licinius Crassus and Julius Caesar issued an edict that no one should sell "exotic" (meaning foreign) ointments. But later, pleasure was admitted as if it were most honorable, so much so that some wished not only to be smeared with them, but to be thoroughly soaked. We shall say nothing further of ointments for the present, since ointments do not enter through the mouth, nor is their administration fatal.

Take equal parts of each of the following: cinnamon, mastic, spikenard <note>original: "spicæ"; likely *Nardostachys jatamansi*, a fragrant root</note>, and saffron. Add Socotrine aloe <note>a high-quality aloe from the island of Socotra</note> in an amount double that of all the other ingredients combined. According to Galen in the seventh book of the *Method of Healing* <note>original: "terapetice, siue Methodi"</note>, chapter 15, the aloe can even be added in triple the amount. This is a truly sublime medicine: for it is "subtiliating" <note>thinning or refining</note> and able to dissolve bad, thick, and viscous humors. It is also drying to those humors that have soaked into the pores; it is warming, able to open obstructions, and cleansing. Regarding aloe, we have spoken in the first book of our *Corrections*, chapter 51.

### Regarding Z.

Various methods are given for sugar of roses <note>original: "zuccaro, siue saccharo rosato"</note>, sugar of violets, and candied ginger. Rose sugar is sometimes made in the form of a solid confection, and sometimes in the manner of a preserve. In the same way, violet sugar and bugloss sugar <note>made from the oxtongue plant, used to treat melancholy</note> are made just like the rose sugar. For these, consult modern practitioners and apothecaries; for they possess the nature of the ingredients from which they are composed.

## Gleanings of Master Symphorien
->Champier on the Antidotaries of Mesuë and Nicolaus, regarding those<-
->medicines which are not in use among us, and have hardly been<-
->known or explained by our people until now.<-
->¶ The first part of the Gleanings. ¶ Certain matters regarding the<-
->*Adrianum* of Nicolaus, added with no small diligence.<-

Two illustrious geniuses of our age have published commentaries on the *Antidotary* of Mesuë <note>an 8th-century Persian physician</note> and that of Nicolaus <note>Nicolaus Salernitanus, author of a standard 12th-century pharmaceutical text</note>: Christopher de Honestis on the Antidotaries of Mesuë, and Johannes de Sancto Amando on Nicolaus. The former was a Florentine by birth, the latter a Gallo-Belgian. Both of them, if you ask my opinion, brought many things into the light with great learning—even if in a "barbarous" <note>Champier, a humanist, likely refers to their Medieval Latin style</note> tongue—and with much ingenuity, drawn from both Latin and Arabic sources. However, because no one man can know everything, we have noticed many things in the antidotaries of Mesuë and Nicolaus which (I say this with all modesty) are either poorly placed or, if I am not mistaken, falsely interpreted. 

For what [leaving aside Platearius <note>Matthew Platearius, author of *Circa Instans*</note> for now, who did not labor much over this] is the value of that superstitious explanation of the *Adrianum* <note>a complex electuary or compound medicine</note>, which that author invented more cleverly than truly? And even if we grant him everything, what, I ask, is the business of Theban opium, henbane, and Euphorbium <note>a harsh, caustic resin</note> being mixed with precious balsam oil, balsam wood, balsam fruit, rhubarb <note>original: "reupontico"</note>, Costus <note>a fragrant root</note>, malabathrum <note>Indian bay leaf</note>, Macedonian parsley, aromatic calamus, myrrh, amomum, and other things which are found neither in France nor Italy? It seems Christopher, Platearius, and Johannes de Sancto Amando wished to philosophize more deeply than necessary. What does that foul and sleep-inducing opium have to do with balsam? What does Euphorbium have to do with myrrh, malabathrum, and costus? To me, opium is vile, Euphorbium is vile, and henbane is not pleasing to the eyes. But let all these things be dismissed...

...we grind. What will they respond to this? Let Platearius <note>Matthaeus Platearius, a 12th-century physician from the school of Salerno</note> eat henbane <note>original: "hyoscyamum"</note> and spurge <note>original: "Euphorbiū"</note> if he wishes. Let Johannes de Sancto Amando <note>a prominent medieval medical commentator</note> drink opium (if it pleases him), which Christopher <note>likely Christophorus Georgius de Honestis, a 14th-century professor of medicine</note> also recommends; but Champier <note>the author, Symphorien Champier, writing here in the third person as Campegius</note> will not take these: nor will he keep henbane or opium in his possession. We shall therefore send opium, spurge, henbane, and those similar woodland phantoms back to the countryside from whence they came. We, indeed, shall have a decoction of white poppy, or lettuce juice, in place of opium, mandrake <note>original: "Mādragorę"</note>, or henbane: and we affirm that this is how Christian and prudent men ought to use them.

### ¶ On the Acharistum of Nicolaus.

We could hardly endure Nicolaus's Acharistum <note>an "Acharistum" was a type of complex medicinal electuary, the name meaning "thankless" or "unpleasant" due to its strength</note> with a calm mind, in which antidote—by Hercules!—there enter pestiferous opium, suffocating hellebore <note>original: "elleborus"</note>, and ingredients unknown to our Christians. Likewise, costus <note>an aromatic root from India</note>, myrrh, bdellium <note>a semi-transparent tree resin</note>, amomum <note>an aromatic spice from the ginger family</note>, cassia bark <note>original: "Cassia lignea"</note>, sweet flag <note>original: "Calamus aromaticus"</note>, and wood-balsam <note>original: "xilobalsamus"</note>, which are not found among us, nor sold by those who worship Christ.

### ¶ On the Athanasia of Nicolaus and others.

Almost the same things noted about the Acharistum must be said regarding the Athanasia <note>a famous compound medicine, its name meaning "immortality"</note>. In that antidote is henbane seed, the opium rejected above, and likewise malabathrum <note>the dried leaves of the cinnamon tree</note>, myrrh, and costus—all unknown to our people. In the Athanasia of Mesuë <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a famous Persian physician</note>, there similarly enter deadly opium, useless burnt goat's horn, and dangerous henbane seed, as well as myrrh and costus, unknown to us. ¶ In the *Athanasia Minor* of Avicenna <note>the Latinized name of Ibn Sina</note>, one finds costus, cassia bark, and myrrh, of which we have spoken above, and likewise mortal opium.

### ¶ On the Antamarum of Nicolaus.

From the Antamarum of Nicolaus <note>another complex herbal compound</note>, the following are to be rejected: the emetic asarabacca <note>original: "azarum"</note>, wood-balsam (unknown to us), abrasive bitter apple <note>original: "colochintis"</note>, burning spurge, ruinous hellebore <note>original: "veratrum"</note>, and scammony <note>original: "Diagredium," a potent resinous purgative</note>, which is an enemy to the stomach.

### ¶ On the Hemagogue Antidote.

From the hemagogue antidote <note>a medicine intended to provoke or increase menstrual flow</note>, one should cast out emetic asarabacca, ruinous hellebore, amomum, myrrh, and wood-balsam, all unknown to our people.

### ¶ On the Laxative Anise of Nicolaus.

From the laxative anise, one must reject scammony, which is contrary to the nature of the stomach; turpeth <note>original: "Turbith," the root of a plant in the morning glory family; the author here puns on the name, saying it "disturbs" (turbans) men</note>, which is unknown to us; and petty spurge <note>original: "Esula"</note>, an enemy of nature.

### ¶ On the Confection of Alkermes.

From the demonic confection of Alkermes <note>a celebrated cordial or "heart-tonic," originally named for the kermes insects used to dye it red</note>, poisonous lapis lazuli <note>a blue semi-precious stone</note> must be rejected; it is useful to painters, not physicians, and is in fact destructive.

## ¶ To Lord Charles de L’Etang, most elegant 
## among noble men,

You have, my patron—to summarize you in a single verse—these nocturnal labors of ours, which are greater than any praise: we could not have been so easily encouraged to publish these, were it not that this one way now seemed open to me: by which, if we did not seem to repay the gratitude for such great merits toward us, we might at least testify to holding it; for we confess that, in the meantime, we are not even sufficient in giving thanks. Truly, the immense magnitude of the benefits from your house toward us is such that only an immense mind could contain them. Farewell, and love us, as you are accustomed to do.

## ¶ Comparison of pernicious medicines, one to another.

### ¶ Second Part of the Gleanings <note>original: "Racemationum"; a term meaning the gathering of leftover grapes, here used for a collection of medicinal notes</note>.

### ¶ A comparison of Scammony to veratrum, or hellebore.
### Chapter one.

If anyone wishes to compare the powers of veratrum <note>a genus of poisonous plants including white hellebore</note> (or hellebore) and Scammony, he will find them equal—not only as leaders in their malice in corrupting human nature, but also in destroying the strength of brute animals. Scammony has (says Dioscorides <note>a 1st-century Greek physician and botanist, the primary authority on herbs</note>) the power of a liquid, and its nature is to purge bile and phlegm through the lower parts <note>i.e., the bowels</note> when taken with honey-water or plain water. Black hellebore <note>original: "veratrum nigrum"</note> also purges the upper stomach <note>i.e., inducing vomiting</note>, drawing out phlegm and bile; it likewise draws out the menses when applied as a suppository; it kills the fetus in the womb. Scammony indeed (says Dioscorides) also kills the fetus when its juice is applied on wool to the female parts; furthermore, it clears away skin spots <note>original: "pannos"; literally 'cloths' but used for skin discolorations</note> when smeared on with honey or oil.
