The Greeks, believing hellebore <note>original: "veratro"; likely referring to *Helleborus*, used in antiquity for both mental illness and purification</note> to be suitable for the purification of houses, would stand and pray to Apollo and Aesculapius <note>the gods of healing and medicine</note> when they were about to dig it up. They would watch closely for an eagle, for it is said to be a great danger: that bird brings death to those digging if it sees the cutting of the black hellebore. Similarly, Dioscorides <note>a Greek physician and botanist of the 1st century AD</note> says that hellebore must be cut very quickly, for its nature weighs down the head. Therefore, those who dig it prepare themselves by eating garlic and drinking wine, as they may dig more safely in this way.

¶ Serapio <note>likely Serapio the Younger, a 12th-century Arabic medical author</note> says that Scammony <note>original: "Scamonium"; a harsh purgative resin</note> strongly purges the belly, but it harms the stomach and liver, diminishes the appetite for food, and causes nausea and anxiety; it is better for men to beware of it.

¶ White hellebore <note>original: "Veratrum album"</note> induces menstruation, kills the fetus in the womb if applied there, and provokes sneezing. Furthermore, if soaked in honey with polenta, it kills mice; and when cooked with meats, it reduces them <note>likely meaning it breaks down the fibers</note>, as Dioscorides writes.

¶ In Scammony, however (as Mesue <note>an influential 9th-century Persian physician</note> writes), there is a biting "windiness" <note>original: "ventositas"; an excess of the air humor causing gas or pressure</note> that causes stinging in the stomach, nausea, upset, and a painful burning sensation. It possesses both heat and sharpness, making it easily inflamed; for that reason, it causes one to fall into fever and thirst. Because of the "attraction" it exerts and the dilation of the openings of the veins, it causes a flux of the belly <note>diarrhea</note>, since it contains a watery substance that causes the excoriation <note>scraping or stripping away</note> of the bowels; thus it generates sharp pains, leading to dysentery and tenesmus <note>the distressing sensation of needing to evacuate the bowels even when they are empty</note>.

### ¶ A comparison of Euphorbium to Turbith. Chapter II.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring intricate floral patterns and curling vines within a square border.</image-desc>
Now that we have come to the comparison of euphorbium and turbith <note>original: "euphorbij, & turbith"; *Euphorbium* is a caustic resin from spurge; *Turbith* or Turpeth is a purgative root</note>, we find no pharmaceutical or medicine more hot in its operation, more swift, or more sharp than euphorbium. Because of its extreme heat, the local inhabitants are afraid to collect it. They hang vessels (as Dioscorides says) made from washed sheep stomachs in the tree; then, from a distance, they wound the tree with spears. Once struck, the liquid leaps out into the vessels in great abundance, as if from a ruptured jar. Sometimes it shoots out with such force [so great is the impetus] that it hits the ground. This liquid, by its heat, burns for an entire day. 

Turbith possesses heat and dryness in the third degree <note>a classification in the Galenic system of qualities</note> of warming things; it purges phlegm but brings about a weakness of the soul <note>fainting or loss of spirit</note>, according to Abenmesuai <note>Ibn Masawayh, a medieval physician</note>; it weakens the stomach and causes loathing. As Mesue writes, turbith is of the genus of milky plants—even if Serapio claims the contrary. Its use brings dryness, nausea, and burning to the body. 

¶ Euphorbium cannot easily be tested by flavor or taste; for if it is touched to the tongue even once, the heat remains for some time and burns the tongue so severely that any other euphorbium touched to it would seem the same. Indeed, Dioscorides says those who use euphorbium must protect all the flesh around their bones with bandages and wax. 

Regarding Turbith, Serapio writes one thing and Mesue another. The Turbith described by Serapio the Mauritanian <note>meaning from the Maghreb/Moorish region</note> differs in no way from tripolium <note>sea starwort</note>; for all the things Serapio writes about Turbith, Dioscorides and Pliny <note>the Roman naturalist</note> attribute to tripolium. However, according to Mesue, Turbith is of the genus of plants that have milk. But Serapio’s Turbith, which is the same as...

<header>The Apothecaries’ Workshop.</header>

It is clearly evident from the description of Dioscorides’ <term>tripolium</term><note>Sea aster (*Aster tripolium*), used as a diuretic</note> that it is not the <term>Turbith</term><note>Turpeth or "Indian Jalap" (*Operculina turpethum*), a potent root purgative</note> which is now used everywhere in the apothecaries' shops. This is because the root of tripolium is fragrant, whereas the one our pharmacists use is entirely without scent. It is therefore clear from what has been said that both Serapio and Mesue <note>Refers to Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a Persian physician whose works were foundational to European pharmacy</note> have erred. I have written more on this matter in the first book of my *Castigationes* <note>original: "castigationum nostrarum"; likely referring to the author’s "Corrections" or "Critiques" of existing medical texts</note>.

### ¶ A comparison of Spurge, or the "milky herb," to the Colocynth, which pharmacists call Coloquintida
#### Chapter III.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' with floral and classical scrollwork ornaments.</image-desc>
The Romans call <term>Tithymalum</term><note>The Spurge family (*Euphorbia*), known for their irritating milky sap</note> the "milky herb." According to the writings of Dioscorides, there are seven types of spurge; however, all of its varieties possess destructive powers. Its nature and the power of its milky sap is to purge the belly through the lower tracts and to draw out phlegm and bile. When collecting this liquid, the person doing the work must stand with their back to the wind; nor should they touch their hands to their eyes. Before approaching this task, the body—especially the face, neck, and scrotum—must be anointed with fat or oil mixed with wine, as the substance also irritates the throat.

The <term>Colocynthis</term><note>Bitter Apple (*Citrullus colocynthis*), a desert vine with extremely bitter, toxic fruit used as a drastic purgative</note>—which some call "goat-melon," some "Alexandrian," and others "bitter gourd," though the moderns call it <term>Coloquintida</term>—itself draws out phlegm and bile. As Dioscorides says, it kills the fetus in the womb; the colocynth is an enemy to the ventricle or stomach. And as Mesue writes, it harms the heart, stomach, and liver; it is agitating and causes the viscera to churn, making the body's operations difficult. It opens the mouths of the veins so violently that it causes blood to flow, and it strips the lining of the urinary tracts.

Regarding the spurges, and especially their sap, Dioscorides says that when smeared on with oil in the sun, it removes hair. It is also applied to treat warts, <term>thymos</term><note>Warty excrescences resembling thyme sprigs</note>, calluses, <term>condylomata</term><note>Genital or anal skin growths</note>, and <term>impetigines</term><note>Skin eruptions or scabs</note>, for which purposes these harmful substances are applied. Furthermore, when the herb is crushed and mixed with water, it kills fish; all seven aforementioned species of spurge are equally capable of this. The primary virtue of the spurges is that they are "hot and dry" in the fourth degree <note>The highest and most dangerous intensity in the Galenic system of qualities</note>. As Rhazes <note>Al-Razi, a 9th-century Persian polymath and physician</note> writes, all species of spurge burn, loosen the belly, induce nausea, and cause ulcers on the body.

The Colocynth (as Mesue says), and especially that which is not fully developed and ripe, causes the recipient great distress and creates "windiness" <note>original: "ventositatem"; painful gas or bloating</note> with difficulty. For this reason, it purges excessively, draws out blood during the movement, and sometimes even kills. If a single colocynth grows alone on its vine, it will be destructive and a lethal poison. It is composed of earthy, fiery, and "burnt" parts; it draws substances from distant parts of the body and is highly dissolving, cleansing, and cutting. Regarding the spurge, Galen writes in his eighth book on *Simple Medicines* that it is hot and dry in the fourth order; it thins phlegm and yellow bile and provokes vomiting, for all its species possess a sharp and hot power.

### ¶ A comparison of Mandrake to Opium
#### Chapter IV.

There are two kinds of <term>Mandragora</term><note>Mandrake (*Mandragora officinarum*), a plant famous for its sedative, hallucinogenic, and purported magical properties</note>: one male, the other female. The female is black, with leaves that are smaller and narrower than lettuce; these leaves are poisonous and heavy in scent, spreading across the ground. Along the leaves grow fruits equal in size to egg yolks; they are pale and fragrant, containing seeds like those of pears.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of narcotic plants, specifically detailing the physical effects and toxicities of Mandrake and Opium as documented by classical and medieval authorities. It transitions into Chapter V, which compares Henbane and Raging Nightshade.</meta>

<page-num>XXIIII</page-num>
<header>The Apothecaries’ Workshop. Leaf XXIIII.</header>

The fruit of the male and white variety <insert>which some have also called <term>morion</term><note>A term used in antiquity for a narcotic variety of Mandrake or Nightshade, likely *Mandragora officinarum*</note></insert> is twice as large as that of the female. It is yellow, the color of saffron, and possesses a heavy scent. According to Dioscorides, a drink consisting of the weight of two <term>obols</term><note>A small Greek unit of weight; about 0.7 grams</note> of mandrake juice mixed with honeyed water purges phlegm and black bile through vomiting, much in the manner of hellebore. However, when drunk in a larger quantity, it causes death. Applied by itself as a <term>pessary</term><note>original: "appositus"; a medicinal plug for vaginal or rectal use</note> in the weight of half an obol, it draws out the menses and the fetus; placed beneath as a suppository, it induces sleep.

Regarding the drinking of poppy juice, which is <term>opium</term>, Dioscorides writes that its use is followed by chills and a very powerful itching, leading to a deep stupor. Often, as the poison grows stronger, the itching becomes so intense that the one who has swallowed it is stirred by the irritation. Furthermore, the scent of opium is given off from the entire body. 

There follows, upon the drinking of mandrake, first a stupor and languor—as the same Dioscorides writes—and an irresistible necessity for sleep, differing in no way from the disease called <term>lethargy</term><note>In this period, "lethargus" referred to a state of profound, morbid drowsiness or coma</note>. In addition to the chills, stupor, languor, itching, and the scent of opium throughout the body, several other signs are listed by Nicander <note>A Greek poet and physician (2nd century BCE) known for his works on poisons and their antidotes</note> regarding the drinking of opium: a pale face, a fiery color of the lips, shallow and cold breathing, bluish fingernails, distorted nostrils, and sunken eyes accompanied by a sweat, as if evaporating from labor. He asserts that the <term>horned poppy</term><note>Probably *Glaucium flavum*</note>, when taken in food or drink, produces the same results as opium and is cured by the same remedies.

Mandrake first puts a person into a deep, unhealthy sleep. Dioscorides says there is also another kind of mandrake called <term>morion</term>, which grows in shady places and around caves. They say that when a <term>drachma</term><note>A weight roughly equal to 3.4 grams</note> of it is drunk, or taken with pearl barley in a side dish or cake, it produces a state of folly <insert>which they call <term>morofin</term><note>Likely a corruption of the Greek *morosis*, meaning dullness of the senses or stupidity</note></insert>. For he who eats it sleeps in the same posture in which he was eating, lacking all sensation for three or four hours after he has consumed it. Physicians use this when they are about to cut or cauterize <note>original: "secturi, vsturive"; an early reference to surgical anesthesia</note> a part of the body. They say, moreover, that the root is an antidote when drunk with <term>raging nightshade</term><note>Solanum furiosum, often identified as *Atropa belladonna*</note>.

Opium is made from the juice of the poppy, having a power to induce sleep; however, if taken too copiously, Avicenna <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and influential medical authority</note> says it is deadly. Mēnsidēnus <note>Possibly a reference to Mnesitheus of Athens, an ancient medical writer</note> indeed said that the benefit of opium lies only in its scent for the purpose of making one sleep; in all other matters its use is bad and extremely dangerous. For it is cold in the fourth degree and dry in the first degree.

Mandrake, as Avicenna writes, provokes sleep; when put into wine, it causes heavy intoxication. Frequent use of it, as well as its scent, causes <term>apoplexy</term><note>A sudden loss of consciousness or paralysis; here used to describe a narcotic coma</note> and renders a man stunned.

### ¶ A comparison of Henbane to Raging Nightshade. Chapter V.

The Romans call "Raging Nightshade" <term>Solanum furiosum</term>, but we call it <term>morella</term> or <term>solatrum</term>. This nightshade has a leaf like a caterpillar-weed, though larger. A drachma of its root drunk in wine can represent to the soul and mind pleasant visions and various images. Doubling that weight causes a state of <term>Ecstasy</term><note>A state of being "outside oneself" or hallucinating</note> for three days. However, four drachmas will kill a person, as Dioscorides writes.

There are three species of <term>Henbane</term><note>original: "Iusquiami"; the genus *Hyoscyamus*</note>, as Dioscorides writes: one has purple flowers and black seed; another has honey-colored flowers and its seed tends toward redness. The third species is less dangerous; it has fatty leaves full of moisture and white seeds. That variety which has black seeds is destructive, and <insert>as Rhazes <note>Al-Razi (865–925), a Persian physician whose works were central to medieval medicine</note> writes...</insert>

Henbane (if faith is to be placed in Isidore) he calls "insane" <note>original: *insana*</note>; for its use is ruinous; for if it is drunk or eaten, it causes madness and a turbulent image of sleep. For this reason, let no one use henbane, because there is no help in it; instead, it mostly kills. However, the variety that has white seed is less harmful.

### ¶ Chapter VI: A Comparison of Hemlock to Camphor.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' depicting a skull resting on a book beside an hourglass. The inscription within the woodcut reads "THE END CROWNS" <note>original Latin: *FINIS CORONAT*</note>.</image-desc>
<term>Hemlock</term><note>original: *Cicuta*</note> is a poison, the public punishment of the Athenians; it has a harmful seed and leaves like coriander, though thinner and with a heavy smell. There is a cooling power in the seed and leaves, such that if it kills someone, they begin to grow cold from the extremities of their body. The remedy, before it reaches the vital organs, is the warming nature of wine. Indeed, the Athenians increased the fame of hemlock by using its juice for death in public trials and capital punishments. ¶ <term>Camphor</term> [as Rhazes writes] is cold and subtle; and whoever uses it encounters wakefulness; and if it is smoked, it cools the kidneys and the bladder, and generates "cold" illnesses. And [as Meseah says] it is cold and dry in the third degree. And [as Avicenna writes] its use causes gray hair. It is mostly adulterated through alchemy by the distillation of varnish, and it is similar to camphor in smell; for this reason, true camphor is rarely or never sold by our <term>apothecaries</term><note>original: *pharmacopolis*</note>; instead, all camphor found among the <term>perfumers</term><note>original: *Seplasiarios*; specifically refers to sellers of ointments and medicines</note> is adulterated through alchemy. ¶ Hemlock is a lethal and wicked herb; whence some of the Greeks called it <term>Amauralis</term><note>original: *Amauralin*; from the Greek *amaureo*, meaning to obscure or dim</note> after the effect of its wickedness, since that name implies it kills by diminishing and thinning; for by its coldness it extinguishes sensation, and once that is extinguished, the senses are diminished. Its juice brings a darkness to the eyes and dizziness to the head, likewise hiccups, alienation of the mind, intense chilling of the outer parts of the body, and finally a convulsion. Those who have swallowed hemlock are strangled as all spirit in the arteries ceases from movement. ¶ Camphor [as Isaac writes] is brought from the regions of Fansur <note>original: *faffella*; likely a transcription error for Fansur, a famous source of camphor in Sumatra</note> and from the region of Calca; and it is a gum growing in those parts. ¶ There are several species of Camphor according to the regions in which it grows; it is clarified through sublimation and comes out white, and its use hastens gray hairs. Certain people [as Mesarugias says] took six <term>aurei</term><note>literally "gold pieces," used here as a weight equivalent to a gold coin</note> of camphor in three turns, and the ventricle of the stomach was so weakened that it could not digest food. If of true and natural <meta>camphor such things are said...</meta>

## ¶ Chapter VII: A Comparison of Wild Cucumber or Elaterium to Spurge and Spurge Olive.

There are those who call it <term>elaterion</term><note>The concentrated juice of the wild cucumber</note>, or the wandering and wild cucumber. It differs from the cultivated cucumber only by its fruit, which it bears much smaller and similar to oblong acorns. It grows in sandy places. Its juice purges phlegm and bile through both the lower and upper parts <note>original: *per inferna pariter & superna*; meaning it acts as both a laxative and an emetic</note>.

<margin>The properties of Spurge.</margin>
¶ Indeed, <term>Spurge</term><note>original: *Esula*; likely *Euphorbia* species</note> is among those species containing a milky sap, and it is (as <term>Mesue</term><note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, a 9th-century Persian physician</note> says) the purgative of the peasants. When fresh, it is truly bad; the black variety is indeed pernicious—it harms the heart, the liver, and the stomach, bursts the veins, and excoriates the internal organs, leaving behind inflammations and causing one to fall into fevers. As a solution, it draws out phlegm, yellow bile <note>original: *aquam citrinam*</note>, and humors generated from black bile. ¶ <term>Caper Spurge</term><note>original: *Cataputia*; *Euphorbia lathyris*</note> is hot in the third degree and moist in the first. It purges phlegm, secondly yellow bile, and thirdly black bile. The fruit of the caper spurge (says <term>Galen</term><note>A highly influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note>) possesses a cleansing and <term>diaphoretic</term><note>original: *dyaforeticam*; sweat-inducing</note> power; the flower is the same, though in some way weaker. If thirty of its seeds are ground and drunk, they purge yellow bile, phlegm, and watery humors, causing vomiting and a flow from the belly. They loosen the stomach with a powerful attraction and provoke nausea and vomiting. ¶ <term>Elaterium</term> (says <term>Dioscorides</term><note>The primary ancient authority on botany and pharmacology</note>) also draws out the menses and kills the fetus in the womb when applied as a <term>pessary</term><note>original: *appositū*</note>. Elaterium (as <term>Habix</term><note>Likely referring to a medieval Arabic medical authority</note> writes) is much sharper than <term>colocynth</term><note>bitter apple</note> and more bitter than it.

<margin>What Mezereon is.</margin>
¶ Concerning <term>Mezereon</term><note>Daphne mezereum, a toxic shrub</note>, which is called *Chamaelea* by the Greeks, and which <term>Avicenna</term>, Mesue, Serapion, and almost all the Arabs placed among the types of milk-bearing plants: they attribute many things to it that actually belong to the <term>Chameleon plant</term><note>likely *Atractylis gummifera*; the author suggests the Arabic writers were deceived by the similar names</note> (having been deceived by the similarity of the names). We shall say nothing of it for the present, for it is not in use among us.

<margin>Concerning Spurge Laurel.</margin>
¶ Regarding <term>Spurge Laurel</term><note>original: *Laureola*; *Daphne laureola*</note>, which Dioscorides calls *Daphnoides*, it draws out phlegm through the lower parts and causes vomiting; it likewise stirs the menses. Let us leave it aside on account of its poisonous nature and malice. The more skilled herbalists of our age specifically call this "laureola" and show that it rises from the earth with leaves similar to those of the laurel.

### ¶ Champier's Exhortation to the Reader.

It has frequently happened to me in my travels, most beloved reader, that either because of my own illness or that of my kin, I have experienced the various frauds of the physicians who follow the Arabs <note>Symphorien Champier was a humanist who often argued for returning to original Greek medical texts rather than relying on medieval Arabic translations and commentaries</note>. They use certain most vile means, such as <term>Scammony</term><note>a plant resin used as a harsh purgative</note>, colocynth, <term>turbith</term><note>an East Indian root</note>, and <term>asarum</term><note>wild ginger</note>, and other frauds of the Arabs.

# The Apothecaries’ Workshop

<margin>The errors of the Arabian physicians.</margin>
...others selling destructive medicines at exorbitant prices; some, because they do not know how to cure, take up the practice out of greed. Indeed, I have found certain followers of the Arabian sect using this kind of <term>Scammony</term><note>A harsh purgative resin derived from the root of *Convolvulus scammonia*</note> to treat ailments that could be driven away in a few days—or even hours—with <term>Rhubarb</term>, <term>Agaric</term><note>A medicinal fungus, usually the Larch Agaric, used as a gentle purge</note>, <term>Cassia fistula</term><note>The "Golden Shower" tree, whose pulp is a mild laxative</note>, <term>Manna</term>, and other "blessed" medicines. They do this to prolong the sickness for a long time, not without danger to the patient, so that they might keep their patients returning for a long duration and grow old alongside the diseases themselves.

<margin>Why he composed the workshop.</margin>
For this reason, it seemed necessary to me to construct aids for health from every source and to collect our "Apothecary's Workshop" into a brief manual. This way, wherever I might go, I could avoid the dangerous medicines of Scammony, <term>Turbith</term><note>The root of *Operculina turpethum*, another strong purgative</note>, and <term>Colocynth</term><note>The bitter apple, a violent laxative</note>, and escape their traps. With this confidence, I can begin my journey from this time forward, knowing that if any illness falls upon me, those Punics <note>original: *Pœnos*; here used as a derogatory term for North African or "barbarian" medical authorities</note> and Arabs will find no entrance to me, nor will they seize the opportunity.

<margin>Which are the "blessed" medicines.</margin>
Above all, however, I believe one should have ready those things which, when suddenly needed, seem most difficult to find—such as honey, cassia fistula, common oil, and agaric. If these are not at hand, take the violet herb, mallow, pellitory-of-the-wall, and borage, which can be found very quickly. If the treatment happens to require rhubarb, plums, cassia, agaric, and the like, use these; for these are the drugs that a prudent man and a wise physician ought especially to keep with him.

<margin>Poisonous medicines.</margin>
<margin>Colocynth.</margin>
<margin>Turbith.</margin>
<margin>Nightshade.</margin>
<margin>Spurge.</margin>
<margin>Spurge Laurel.</margin>
<margin>Opium.</margin>
<margin>Mandrake.</margin>
<margin>Camphor.</margin>
Let the physician flee from Scammony, <term>Lapis Lazuli</term><note>While a gemstone, it was sometimes used in powdered form as a violent purgative</note>, <term>Armenian Stone</term><note>A blue carbonate of copper, similar to azurite, used as an emetic</note>, the seven types of <term>Tithymallum</term><note>Various species of Spurge (Euphorbia)</note>, <term>Hellebore</term><note>original: *veratrum*</note>, Colocynth, Turbith, Nightshade, Spurge, Spurge Laurel, Opium, Mandrake, the "Camphor of the Alchemists," along with Henbane and <term>Euphorbium</term><note>The caustic resin of the Spurge tree</note>, just as one flees from poisons, the basilisk, the crocodile, the salamander <note>original: *falandram*</note>, the viper, and the <term>sea-beast</term><note>original: *marafum*; possibly referring to a legendary toxic sea creature or a corruption of *marinum*</note>.

<margin>He refutes the barbarians.</margin>
Furthermore, let scholars—and especially those who cannot bear to hear anything unless it is dictated in elegant Latin—not wonder why I have used "barbarous" terms here and there while citing the barbarians themselves. Let them know that I have not done this without cause. For since I wished to refute <term>Rhazes</term><note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (865–925), a Persian polymath</note>, <term>Al-Farabi</term>, <term>Serapion</term>, <term>Mesue</term>, <term>Avicenna</term>, and the other barbarians, I judged it permissible to use the very words they use in their own books. I feared that if I spoke otherwise, I would not seem to be pursuing Latinity so much as trying to attack good authors through a love of words, or reproaching them through false accusations. Furthermore, by quoting their own words, my adversaries cannot claim I lack either diligence or good faith.

<margin>Who should be avoided.</margin>
Moreover, if I have ever used the testimonies of Hippocrates, Galen, and Paul <note>Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century Byzantine physician</note>, I have sometimes used them according to the chapter headings of the "barbarous" editions. I did this so that, in this way, I might satisfy those who lack the new and proper Latin translations. Therefore, let students of the medical profession beware, lest they wander into error because of the ignorance of the Arabs and Punics in medical matters. There is no other cause for this ignorance except that we have defected from the Greeks to the "brothels" <note>original: *lupanaria*; a very harsh metaphor for dens of vice or filth</note> of the Arabs and Barbarians.

<margin>The decrees of the Arabs.</margin>
Since, therefore, those who follow the decrees of the Arabs dwell in great darkness and are easily entangled in infinite webs of error, let students resolve to drink medicine from the Greek fountains rather than from the Arabian puddles. As for their objection that we can produce nothing from our own lands that comforts and warms as effectively as <term>Galangal</term>, <term>Cloves</term>, and <term>Sweet Flag</term>...

He justifies using "barbarous" Arabic terminology only to better refute those authors on their own terms.</summary>

# The Apothecaries’ Workshop. Folio XXVI.

...makes it so: we respond that this happens through our own fault, for we are ignorant of these things. In truth, our palate does not tolerate it because it does not "tickle" the senses unless it is imported from Arabia or India. 

<margin>Magisterial compositions</margin> 
Therefore, perhaps someone will object: "Do you then condemn those 'magisterial' <note>official or authoritative medical recipes</note> compositions of <term>Avicenna</term><note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose 'Canon of Medicine' was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries</note>, <term>Mesue</term><note>A name attributed to influential but poorly identified Arabic medical writers, likely Yuhanna ibn Masawayh</note>, and <term>Serapion</term><note>Yahya ibn Sarafyun, a 9th-century Syriac Christian physician</note>, from which medicines for all diseases are produced?" 

<margin>Good recipes condemned.</margin>
Fair words! <note>original: "bona verba"; an interjection used to urge someone to speak carefully or avoid ill omens</note> I do not condemn the writers, except insofar as they have been ineptly translated into Latin for us; and there is danger in this matter because we may imitate them at our peril. 

<margin>The barbarians wrote for barbarians.</margin>
But I do not condemn anyone's merchandise either. Rather, I say that they wrote for their own ages and for their own people: the Arabs for the Arabs, and the "barbarians" for the barbarians <note>In the Renaissance, scholars often labeled medieval medical writers "barbarians" because of their non-classical Latin style</note>. They wrote specifically for their own climate. 

<margin>Some medicines are suitable for us, others for the Egyptians</margin>
The nettle does not burn, dry, or purge any less in our climate than it does among the Arabs and the most distant Indians. I will say nothing of the fact that these were different eras. Furthermore, we are practicing medicine in Celtic Gaul <note>Modern-day France</note>, not in Arabia, Egypt, or India. It is well known that these nations have a different <term>temperament</term><note>In Galenic medicine, the balance of humors (hot, cold, wet, dry) specific to a person or region</note>, a different sky, and a different celestial orientation. 

Let those who are wealthier than the Gauls have their spices: their <term>musk</term>, <term>balsam</term>, <term>amomum</term><note>An aromatic spice from the ginger family</note>, <term>amber</term>, and <term>aloe-wood</term>. Indeed, if they wish, let them even devour pearls <note>original: "uniones"</note> and gems like Cleopatra <note>Referring to the legend of Cleopatra dissolving a priceless pearl in vinegar to win a bet regarding the cost of a meal</note>, which cost many thousands of gold coins. 

<margin>Hyssop</margin>
Only let them not begrudge the poor their own "vintage"—that is, rosemary, laurel, hyssop, marjoram, myrrh, <term>bugloss</term><note>Anchusa officinalis, also known as oxtongue, used to treat fevers</note>, <term>plantain</term>, and even the pine, the oak, or the commonest grasses of the fields.

->End of the workshop.<-

# The Book of Antidotes of Lord Symphorian
## Champier, Chief Physician of Lorraine
### Divided into three books.

The first book consists of proven remedies <note>original: "experimentorum"; in this context, these are recipes or treatments that have been tested and found effective through practice</note> for the curing of various diseases.

The second book consists of medical secrets for diverse ailments.

The third is titled "The Pills of Heroes and Illustrious Kings." This work is highly useful, both for the treatment of diseases and because of the novelty of the subject matter and the authority of the ancient authors cited.

# Letter.

To the most kind and universally learned man, Lord Martin d’Achaquie <note>Martin d'Achaquie was a doctor of the Faculty of Medicine in Paris and a contemporary of Champier.</note>, most deserving professor of the Apolline art <note>The "Apolline art" refers to medicine, as Apollo was the Greek god of healing</note>, and most eloquent Doctor of the University of Paris, Symphorien Champier, Chief Physician of the Lorrainers, ->sends fondest greetings.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "I" featuring floral and scrollwork patterns, with a small central banner inscribed with "FINIS ROMAE" (The End of Rome).</image-desc> You have anticipated me with your prior goodwill, Martin, most learned of physicians. Even before I had any personal acquaintance with you, you—a man distinguished in both learning and virtue—invited my nephew Jean Champier (physician to the most reverend Lord Cardinal of Tournon) into the circle <note>original: "aleam"; literally "the die" or "hazard," used here to mean the intimate sphere or chance of friendship</note> of your friendship. Since I consider it utterly foreign to human nature, and indeed a sin, not to respond in kind to such affection, I have decided to secure your love for me and my nephew more tightly with this little gift: our *Antidotary* <note>A book of recipes for "antidotes" or medicines</note>. In this work, the secrets and proven remedies <note>original: "experimenta"; practical clinical trials or effective recipes</note> of the ancients are treated. May you hold this as a pledge of our love for you, until such time as we may produce greater works for you that are more fitting for your most illustrious honors. In this book, the remedies of ancient philosophers and physicians are cited, such as those of: Soranus, Asclepiades, Herophilus, Chrysippus, Diocles, Demetrius, Galen, Erasistratus, Empedocles, Apollonius, Democritus, Heraclides, Praxagoras, Philotimus, Themison, Proculus, Parmenides, Thessalus, Tryphon, and Nicander.

Champier presents his "Antidotary" as a gift of gratitude for the friendship shown to his nephew and lists the numerous ancient medical authorities whose recipes are included.</summary>

# Letter. Folio XXVIII.

However, we do not write these things for the sake of historical accuracy, but to drive away the diseases of men. We do not record which diseases were cured by the philosophers themselves, but which ones, and in what manner, they ought to have been cured: so that under the guidance of these same philosophers, through their instruction and example, we may perceive the best method of healing to be clearly expressed. Just as **Xenophon** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and historian</note>, famous for his pleasant wit and a pillar of Greek eloquence, composed the *Education of Cyrus* <note>original: "Paedia Cyri", better known as the *Cyropaedia*, a semi-fictional biography of Cyrus the Great used to illustrate the ideal ruler</note>, which **Africanus** <note>Scipio Africanus, the Roman general</note> approved of so highly that he always kept it in his hands, and which **Marcus Tullius [Cicero]** wore out through constant reading. In that work, the famous Cyrus, King of the Persians, is described not for the sake of historical truth, but as the image of a perfect commander—not as he actually was, but as he ought to have been—so that through the instruction and example of Cyrus, we might perceive the best kind of royal administration clearly expressed.

Therefore, read our *Antidotary* <note>A collection of medicinal recipes or "antidotes"</note>, which I very recently—along with several other volumes corrected with no small diligence—handed over to **Jean Crespin**, a bookseller and most elegant printer, to be shaped upon the striking-anvil of the press <note>original: "excusoria incude"; a metaphorical reference to the printing process</note>, so that they might be published under your name and dedicated especially to you. Farewell, my Martin; receive this little gift, such as it is, with a cheerful countenance and read it through with a happy brow. Live and be well, and love us harmoniously <note>original: "symphoniace"; a playful pun on the author's first name, Symphorien</note>.

<sig>D iiij</sig>

<summary>In this concluding part of his dedicatory letter, Champier explains that his medical text is intended as an idealized guide for healing, similar to how Xenophon’s Cyropaedia served as an idealized guide for leadership. He concludes by presenting the printed work to Martin d’Achaquie as a gift of friendship.</summary>

# Book One of the Antidotary

->The sublime experiments of Lord Symphorien Champier <note>A prominent French physician and humanist (1471–1539)</note> for curing various diseases, illustrated by the authorities of various philosophers.<-

## Book One.

<margin>
Soranus <note>Soranus of Ephesus, a Greek physician of the Methodist school</note> was an Ephesian by nation; he lived in the times of Trajan, Herodian, and Galen; he also wrote books on medicines.
</margin>

->¶ Soranus’s experiment:<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' containing a serpent or dragon-like creature entwined within the letter's curves.</image-desc>
Soranus’s syrup, by which all those suffering from quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where the fever returns every fourth day</note> can be cured. Take two handfuls each of the roots of fennel, parsley, celery, butcher's broom, and asparagus; one handful each of wall germander, hart's-tongue fern, and ground-pine; half an ounce each of bishop's weed, caraway, and capers; three drams of dodder <note>A parasitic climbing plant used as a purgative</note>; two drams each of sandalwood and roses; half a pound of borage juice, and as much sugar as is sufficient. Let a syrup be made, of which the patient should take every morning for eight days. Afterward, if any "digestion" <note>Signs that the "humors" are breaking down</note> appears in the urine, a bloodletting should be performed from the <term>salvatella vein</term> <note>A vein on the back of the hand, located between the ring finger and the little finger</note> of both hands; let the blood be drawn according to the discretion of a good and learned physician and the strength of the patient’s constitution. ¶ You will be amazed by the effect of the juice of the lesser plantain if it is given with <term>mead</term> <note>original: "mulsa"; honey-water</note> two hours before the fever fit begins; I have personally tested this. Furthermore, my own experience says that if the seed of St. John's wort is crushed and given in a wine drink to a quartan fever patient before the fit, it cures the fever.

<margin>
Asclepiades of Prusa <note>A Greek physician who practiced in Rome and favored diet and exercise over harsh drugs</note>, relying more on the help of eloquence and medicine, discovered a new medical method [having exploded the old].
</margin>

->¶ Asclepiades’s experiment for <term>amphimerina</term> <note>A fever that returns daily</note>, which they call a quotidian fever.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' with architectural and foliate patterns.</image-desc>
Take half an ounce of gromwell <note>original: "milij solis"</note>, pulverize it, and boil it with three ounces of white wine; let the patient drink it one hour before the fever fit for three days. ¶ Likewise, the following experiment is effective: Take one ounce each of cleaned raisins, fumitory, bedeguar <note>A gall formed on wild roses</note>, hemp-agrimony, celery root, fennel root bark, maidenhair fern, anise, mastic, and hops. Let them be boiled perfectly, and take three ounces of this decoction every morning. After many days, he would make a laxative decoction with yellow <term>myrobalans</term> <note>A plum-like fruit from India used for its astringent and digestive properties</note>. This is also effective for quartan fever, but then the decoction should be made with Indian and Chebulic myrobalans; for quotidian fever, it should be made with yellow and Chebulic myrobalans.

<margin>
Herophilus <note>An ancient Greek physician often called the father of anatomy</note> [surpassed] all before him.
</margin>

->¶ Herophilus’s experiment for <term>causon</term> <note>original: "caufonide"; a severe, burning inflammatory fever</note>.<-

# On Experiments. Folio XXIX.

The water of a gourd roasted in an oven settles thirst, if given with sugar, and it softens the belly; let the dose of the water be from four to six ounces <note>The original "ctas dam- cijs" is a fragmented OCR of *uncias*, or ounces</note> taken at one time. Purslane wonderfully removes a burning fever <note>original: "febre causonica"</note> if it is ground with barley flour, mixed, and applied to the stomach and the <term>hypochondria</term> <note>The upper part of the abdomen, just below the ribs; ancient doctors believed many "vapors" originated here</note>. Psyllium <note>Also known as fleawort</note> removes these same heats, however great they may be, if it is infused in water for one day and two drams are drunk with sugar or a violet <term>julep</term> <note>A sweet medicinal drink, usually made with syrup or rose/violet water</note>. Ground centaury is also effective, given as a drink before a <term>paroxysm</term> <note>The period when a fever is at its most intense</note> with water of <term>scariola</term> <note>Prickly lettuce, used as a cooling herb</note> or endive.

---

### ¶ Chrysippus’s tested electuary for a cough.

<margin>
Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus of Cnidus (4th century BCE), a Greek physician</note> was a philosopher and physician; he was the first to change the teachings of Hippocrates and Prodicus with what Pliny calls "tumultuous chatter" <note>original: "garrulitatem"</note>.
</margin>

Take three and a half ounces each of linseed and cleaned raisins; two ounces each of cleaned bitter and sweet almonds and pine nuts; three drams each of roasted hazelnuts, <term>iris root</term> <note>original: "yreos"</note>, and select turpentine; one and a half drams each of white frankincense, mastic, and saffron. Let them be ground, and let <term>troches</term> <note>Small medicinal lozenges or cakes</note> be made with goat’s milk; afterward let them be dried, and finally ground again. Let an <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note> be made with honey. The dose is one dram in the morning with a little fine wine, and in the evening, when the patient goes to bed, let them hold a little in the mouth. ¶ But if the cough is accompanied by a "flux from the brain" <note>Catarrh or post-nasal drip</note>, let such a powder be used: Take half an ounce each of <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>A medicinal red clay from Armenia used as an astringent</note>, <term>spodium</term> <note>Ash or metallic oxide, often from zinc or ivory, used to cool the body</note>, gum Arabic, and myrtles. Let a powder be made; let it be given morning and evening before meals, up to three drams every day.

---

### ¶ Diocles’s experiment; it is a secret for asthma.

<margin>
Diocles of Carystus was a follower of Hebrew medicine <note>This likely refers to a specific ancient school or is a period spelling variation</note>; he wrote a letter on good health to Antigonus; Plutarch, Pliny, and Galen cite him several times.
</margin>

Take six drams each of dried hyssop, basil, maidenhair fern, horehound, and scraped licorice. Let them be boiled in a sufficient amount of water until half is consumed; then let it be strained, and a spoonful of honey poured over it, and let it be taken as a drink every morning. ¶ For difficult asthma, let it be given with Armenian bole: to one without a fever, with moderately diluted wine; to one with a fever, with wine heavily diluted with water. He who is not cured by this medicine will not be cured by any other way. Armenian bole does not achieve this through a "manifest quality" <note>A property perceptible by the senses, like heat or cold</note>—since it is cold and dry and is constrictive rather than dilating—but it has this effect from a "property" that our scholars call "hidden" <note>An "occult property" or specific virtue that cannot be explained by the balance of the four humors alone</note>.

---

## ¶ Demetrius of Apamea’s tested remedy for consumption.

<margin>There were two men named Demetrius: one was Attaleus, the other Apameus; this one was a follower of the sect of Herophilus <note>Herophilus was an ancient Greek physician often called the "father of anatomy"</note>.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial A featuring a central tree-like motif with dense foliage, flanked by decorative elements.</image-desc>
Take fresh pine nuts, grind them, and mix with fruit syrup <note>original: "rob"</note> and skimmed honey until it is reduced to the consistency of honey. Let up to three drams of this be administered dissolved in warm water, or let it be licked in the manner of a <term>looth</term> <note>A medicinal syrup or linctus intended to be licked slowly; from the Arabic "la'uq"</note>. ¶ All the ancients agreed on <term>Armenian bole</term> <note>A red medicinal earth or clay</note>, that when taken in a drink it dries the organs of the lungs; thus they do not cough, provided the patient does not err in their diet. An <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note> made from laurel berries with honey works the same way. 
<margin>This man left several books on internal medicine to posterity.</margin>

## ¶ Demetrius Attaleus’s tested remedy for heart palpitations.

Take one <term>scruple</term> <note>A small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams</note> each of red coral powder and saffron; let it be drunk with aromatic wine, for it immediately frees the patient. ¶ Likewise, the acidity of a citron cures a hot tremor of the heart; coriander powder with bugloss water does the same. ¶ Likewise, lemon balm <note>original: "mellissa"</note> does the same when eaten on an empty stomach; because of their entire medicinal property, pearls also contribute much.

## ¶ Erasistratus’s syrup for hoarseness, which clarifies the voice.

<margin>Erasistratus of Chios was a follower of the rationalist sect after Hippocrates; he was born of Aristotle's daughter, as Suidas <note>The author of a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> claims.</margin>

Take one ounce each of endive or <term>scariola</term> <note>Prickly lettuce</note>, maidenhair fern, butcher’s broom, asparagus, raisins, scraped licorice, <term>epithyme</term> <note>Dodder, a parasitic plant</note>, and sweet almonds. Take two drams each of anise seed, fennel, and dried hyssop; take half an ounce each of mallow seed and fleshy dates. Let them all be cooked in two pounds of water until half is consumed. With enough sugar and skimmed honey, let a syrup be made. Let the patient take it every morning and evening, two hours before eating. ¶ Likewise, squill <note>Also known as sea onion</note> boiled with honey is effective. Likewise, garlic, however it is eaten, clarifies the voice.

## ¶ Heraclides of Tarentum’s experiment for dropsy.

<margin>Heraclides of Tarentum wrote many books, as Galen writes in the sixth book of *On the Affected Parts*.</margin>
Take one and a half ounces each of dwarf-elder root, and the leaves and roots of <term>navelwort</term> <note>original: "vmbilici veneris," literally "Venus's navel"</note>. ## ¶ Praxagoras’s experiment for liver pain.

## ¶ Philotimus’s experiment for obstruction and hardness of the spleen.

### ¶ Proculus’s experiment for breaking a kidney stone.

<margin>
Proculus is 
cited by Scri-
bonius Lar-
gus and Celsus 
on folio [X].
</margin>
Take two ounces each of the roots of **asparagus**, **pimpernel**, and **field mallow**: boil them in two <term>pounds</term> <note>original: "libra," a unit of weight roughly equal to 327 grams</note> of water until half the water is consumed. If one drinks four ounces of this decoction every morning, the stone in the kidneys will be broken. ¶ For the same purpose, the following <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note> is effective: Take half an ounce each of the seeds of **fennel**, **celery**, **anise**, **spicknel** <note>original: "meu"</note>, **asarabacca** <note>original: "asari"</note>, **gentian**, **horehound** juice, **iris** <note>original: "yreos"</note>, and **wall germander**; two <term>drachms</term> <note>A unit of weight, about 3.9 grams</note> each of **ginger**, **caraway**, **chamomile flowers**, **cinnamon**, **wild carrot** <note>original: "dauci"</note>, and **spikenard**; and as much **honey** as is sufficient. Let an electuary be made, and let it be taken with a decoction of fennel. And when we wish to make it a laxative, we add one drachm each of **agaric** <note>A medicinal fungus</note> and **rhubarb** per dose.

### ¶ Parmenides’s experiment for dysenteric flux, and also for diarrhea.

<margin>Parmenides</margin>
Take four parts of the ash of **snails** burned with their shells, two parts of **green galls** <note>Growth on oak trees used for their astringent properties</note>, and half a part of **pepper**. Let them be ground very finely and made into a powder. Give this with wine and a decoction of **dried pears**. ¶ Likewise, **milk** boiled with an equal weight of **wild carrot** and administered is a singular protection. ¶ Likewise, **beans** cooked with their skins in water and vinegar and eaten during a time of dysentery are a singular remedy. ¶ Likewise, a drunk decoction of **marshmallow** <note>original: "alteae"</note> helps immediately. ¶ Likewise, the proper and chief cure for dysenteric flux is purgation with **myrobalans** <note>A dried fruit used as a laxative and astringent</note> and **roasted rhubarb**.

If it happens that the womb descends <note>referring to uterine prolapse</note>, then a <term>fumigation</term> <note>The application of medicinal smoke</note> made with **cow dung** is of great benefit.

<header>First Book of the Antidotary.</header>

<margin>
From Scribonius and Varro.
</margin>
**T**ake three <term>drachms</term> <note>A unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams</note> each of **rose oil**, **willow oil**, **chamomile oil**, **poppy oil**, **chicken fat**, **ceruse** <note>white lead pigment, used historically in ointments despite its toxicity</note>, **burnt lead**, and washed **tutty** <note>zinc oxide</note>; with as much **white wax** as is sufficient, let an ointment be made with which the area should be smeared. ¶ Likewise, take an **egg yolk**, a little melted **chicken fat**, a little **rose oil**, and half a <term>scruple</term> <note>A small weight, about 1.3 grams</note> of **saffron**. Let them all be mixed together and kept in a glass vessel in cold water; stir with the finger until it becomes like a ball. With a **feather** <note>original: "pena," used as a soft applicator</note>, let the place of pain be anointed with this.

### ¶ Nicander’s experiment for arthritic pains and gout.

<margin>
Nicander of Colophon was a grammarian and lived in the time of the young Attalus, who defeated the Galatians. He wrote the *Theriaca* concerning remedies against poisons.
</margin>
**T**ake one and a half ounces each of the juice of **motherwort** <note>original: "matricariæ"</note>, **mugwort**, **asphodel** juice, and **sage** juice; one ounce of **houseleek** <note>original: "semperuiuæ"</note> juice; one and a half ounces of **psyllium seed** mucilage; two ounces of **sweet almond oil**; one ounce each of **fenugreek** and **linseed** mucilage and **dill** juice; one and a half ounces of **cabbage** juice; three ounces of **violet oil**; and as much **wax** as is sufficient. Let an ointment be made, and let the places of pain be anointed with it. ¶ Likewise, for pains of the joints, **oil of ribwort plantain** <note>original: "lanceolata"</note> is effective if the place is anointed with it; similarly, **oil of a decoction of squill** <note>a type of sea onion</note> is effective and contributes much to soothing joint pains.

->¶ Thus ends the first book of the Antidotary.<-

¶ A six-line poem by **Josse Bade van Asse** <note>original: "Iodoci Badij Ascēsij," a famous Renaissance printer and scholar</note> in praise of Lord **Symphorien Champier** <note>original: "Sympherianus Caniperius," the author</note>, whom he not undeservedly calls a "complete man" and a priest of **Jove**, **Phoebus**, and **Minerva**: of Jove indeed because of his skill in ancient theology; of Phoebus because of his experience in medicine; and of Minerva because of his exact knowledge of all philosophy. He gives a most beautiful specimen of all these things in these works.

->That nature might unfold new arts to mortals,<-

->"For one man, Symphorien, shall be every man."<-
->"For he, priest of Jove, Phoebus, and myself at once,"<-
->"Will surpass the Thrice-Great Hermes in genius."<-

# Certain Secrets of Champier for Various Ailments.

## Book Second.

¶ A medicine found in the Egyptian city of Jupiter <note>modern-day Luxor/Thebes</note>, which rouses the stomach, soothes windiness, aids digestion, softens the belly <note>acts as a laxative</note>, draws out phlegm and bile, and also cures and soothes faults of the chest, side, liver, spleen, and kidneys.

<margin>A singular medicine called *diaspoleteon* by Oribasius.</margin>
Take one ounce of **cumin** soaked in vinegar for three days, then dried again and ground very finely; seven <term>drachms</term> <note>A unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams</note> of **long, white, or black pepper**; one and a half ounces of fresh **rue** leaves collected a day before; and with **honey** make an <term>electuary</term> <note>A medicinal paste or syrup made by mixing powdered drugs with honey or sugar</note>. It will benefit phlegmatic patients; or [make it] with the juice of **barley water** <note>original: "ptiſanæ"</note> and it will benefit choleric and melancholic patients, as Oribasius <note>a famous 4th-century Greek physician</note> writes. One spoonful is taken morning and evening.

<margin>A golden electuary for various ailments.</margin>
An electuary for dizziness of the head and dimness of the eyes, which also settles catarrh <note>original: "rheumatiſmum"</note> of the throat, removes pain from the chest, eases the lungs, takes away heart pain, disperses pain in the side, heals those with pleurisy, cures those with spleen issues, strengthens the stomach, removes inflammation, heals those with consumption <note>original: "phthiſicos"</note>, dissolves a cough, soothes kidney stones, checks all colic pain, improves a pale complexion, heals those with localized pains <note>original: "methoicos"</note>, and brings down menstruation.

Take one ounce of **round birthwort** <note>original: "ariſtolochiæ rotūdæ"</note>; six drachms of **purging cassia**; one ounce of **cloves**; eight drachms of **storax calamita** <note>a fragrant resin from the *Styrax officinalis* tree</note>; six drachms of **myrrh** (if good can be found, though it is rarely found; and if good, aromatic myrrh cannot be found, put in its place two drachms of **saffron**); six drachms each of **spikenard** and **pellitory-of-Spain** <note>original: "pyretri"</note>; one ounce of **shaved liquorice**; seven drachms of **black pepper**; six drachms of **greater centaury**, which our people call **rhapontic** <note>original: "reuponticum", a species of rhubarb</note>; nine drachms of **gum tragacanth**; six drachms of **peony seeds**; one ounce each of **iris** <note>original: "syreos"</note>, **saxifrage**, and **caper root**; six drachms of **hyssop**; seven drachms of **pennyroyal**; three ounces of **gentian**; four drachms of **marking nut** <note>original: "anacardi"</note>; five drachms of **galbanum**; eight drachms of **turpentine**, or in its place **larch resin**; one ounce of **Macedonian parsley**, or in its place the **common** kind; six drachms of **mastic**; five drachms of **galangal**; eight drachms each of **ivory shavings**, **basil**, and **savory**; six drachms each of **dill seed** and **celery seed**; seven drachms each of **fennel seed** and the **bone from a stag’s heart** <note>A popular medieval remedy, actually the ossified cartilage found in the hearts of older deer</note>; five drachms each of **cardamom** and **red coral**; four drachms of **oregano**; one and a half ounces of **peeled almonds**; eight drachms each of **pine nuts** and **white pepper**; and one <term>scruple</term> <note>A small weight, about 1.3 grams</note> of **choice musk**. First let the dry ingredients be ground, and with **honey** let an electuary be made, of which he should take a quantity the size of a **chestnut** in the morning. It is also effective for those who have drunk poison and for the bite of a serpent; it soothes the pattern of **quartan fever** <note>a fever recurring every third day</note>, clears **quotidian** and **tertian fevers**, and benefits the stomach, spleen, and liver.

# Book of Secrets

<margin>The King of Persia’s purgative for those suffering from melancholy, from Oribasius.</margin>
¶ A <term>purgative</term> <note>a medicine used to cleanse the body of "humors"</note> suitable for melancholic patients, according to Oribasius of Sardis <note>a 4th-century Greek medical compiler and personal physician to the Emperor Julian</note>.

Take one and a half <term>drachms</term> <note>a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note> of **anise**, one drachm of **parsley seed**, half a drachm of **black pepper**, one and a half drachms of **epithyme** <note>a parasitic plant, often called "dodder of thyme," used to purge black bile</note>, and as much **honey** as is sufficient. You shall give one or two spoonfuls according to the strength of the person receiving it. ¶ Another: Take five drachms of **epithyme**, one drachm of **mint**, and one and a half drachms of **green rue**; give this to be drunk with the best **wine** for three days.

---

<margin>The antidote of Philoxenus.</margin>
¶ An <term>antidote</term> <note>in this context, a general internal remedy or "electuary"</note> by the author Philoxenus <note>likely an ancient Greek physician cited in medical compendiums</note> for a long-standing cough, and for all things that are not easily expelled from the chest; it is also effective for <term>empyics</term> <note>those suffering from internal abscesses or pus in the lungs</note> and for blockages of the internal organs.

Take twelve drachms each of **long and round birthwort** <note>original: "aristolochiæ"</note>, twenty-one drachms of **gentian**, nineteen drachms of **dried laurel berries**, twelve drachms each of **rue seed** and **horehound**, and twenty-eight drachms of **smyrnium** <note>a herb similar to celery</note>, or **celery** or **parsley** in its place. Add as much **honey** as is enough to make an antidote. You shall give a dose the size of a hazelnut with **mead** <note>honey-water</note>; it also cleanses a wound, causes it to scar over, and leads it to health.

---

<margin>The electuary of Oribasius</margin>
¶ Another <term>electuary</term> <note>a medicinal paste made with honey</note> by Oribasius of Sardis for those who cough from the chest and lungs.

Take **fatty pine**, especially when it is wrapped in its own resin; boil it in water with **fresh horehound**. To the resulting liquid decoction, add a moderate amount of **honey** and boil it again until it returns to the thickness of honey, and use it.

---

<margin>An electuary for intestinal worms.</margin>
¶ An electuary for **intestinal worms** by Oribasius of Sardis.

Take half an ounce each of **dried wormwood**, **southernwood**, and **cardamom**; six drachms each of **cabbage seed**, **dried mint**, and **lupin seeds**. Let them be powdered and made into an electuary with **honey**. Let the patient take three drachms in the morning with **purslane water**. A <term>plaster</term> <note>a medicated bandage applied to the skin</note> of this kind is also effective: Take **lupins**, **laurel berries**, and **ox gall**, apply them together, and place it upon the navel.

---

<margin>Champier’s painkillers for acute pains in gout and joint disease.</margin>
¶ <term>Anodynes</term> <note>pain-relieving medicines</note> or poultices that return one to a painless state during attacks of **gout** <note>original: "podagra"</note> and **joint disease** <note>original: "artetica"</note>; these have been tested by me many times, especially when the pain is acute with much inflammation of the area caused by "hot matter."

Take one pound of **lentil flour**, three ounces each of **dragon’s blood** <note>a bright red resin obtained from certain plants</note> and **Armenian bole** <note>a medicinal red clay used as an astringent</note>, one drachm of **camphor**, and half a pound of **barley flour**. Let them be tempered with **rose oil** and **vinegar**, and let a <term>cataplasm</term> <note>a warm, moist poultice</note> be made. It should be applied to the painful place by spreading it over a linen cloth, and it should be renewed after it dries.
¶ Also of **plane tree**...

¶ Likewise, green leaves of the **plane tree** <note>original: "Platani"</note>, crushed and applied as a <term>poultice</term> <note>a soft, moist mass of material applied to the body to relieve soreness and inflammation</note>, remove inflammation in the knees and assist those suffering from gout and arthritis. Indeed, Oribasius of Sardis <note>the 4th-century personal physician to Emperor Julian</note> provides another poultice, which is as follows.

<margin>Oribasius’s poultice.</margin>
¶ Take three <term>drachms</term> <note>a unit of weight, about 3.9 grams</note> each of **opium** and **saffron**. Grind them with cow’s or goat’s **milk**, and mix in the soft interior of **bread**. Grind it vigorously, and use it as a poultice with **rose oil** mixed in; place leaves of **beet** or **lettuce** over the top. Likewise, opium ground with saffron and lettuce, mixed with rose oil and applied on a linen cloth, is very effective and soothes pain.

### ¶ For long-standing pains residing in the chest without fever, from Oribasius.

<margin>Oribasius’s electuary for chest pains.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial letter 'A' featuring interlaced vine and leaf motifs in a rectangular frame.</image-desc>Take six <term>ounces</term> each of **fenugreek** and **fat dates**. Let them be boiled down, and when they are cooked, strain them. To their juice, add a generous amount of **honey** and cook over coals until it is moderately thick. Use this well before eating.

### ¶ Lozenges of the King of Bohemia for a catarrhal cough, tested by me many times.

<margin>The King of Bohemia’s lozenges for catarrh.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornate woodcut initial letter 'A' with detailed foliate decorations and scrolls within a square border.</image-desc>Take two drachms of **white frankincense**, one and a half drachms of **Armenian bole** <note>a medicinal red clay from Armenia used as an astringent</note>, one drachm of **cold diadraganth powder** <note>a compound powder based on gum tragacanth</note> without camphor, and two <term>scruples</term> <note>a small unit of weight, 1/3 of a drachm</note> of **diayris powder** <note>a compound powder of iris root</note>. Let the <term>lozenges</term> <note>original: "trocisci," medicinal tablets intended to dissolve in the mouth</note> be formed with **rose honey**. Let the patient hold one in the mouth frequently, long before meals and when going to bed.

### ¶ Lozenges of Oribasius of Sardis for various pains of the head; as soon as you smear the forehead, you will cut off the pain; they work marvelously even if the patients have a fever or suffer from phrenesy.

<margin>Lozenges for various pains of the head.</margin>
**A**ccept eight drachms each of **laurel berries** and **green grapes**, two drachms of **iris**, and one and a half drachms of **opopanax** <note>a medicinal gum resin</note>. Make lozenges with **vinegar**, and when needed, apply them mixed with vinegar and **rose oil**.

### ¶ A lozenge for every type of daily fever, and for false quartan and false tertian fevers, from the tradition of Oribasius.

<margin>For types of quartan and daily fevers.</margin>
**A**ccept two drachms of **Oriental saffron**, two and a half drachms of **pellitory** <note>original: "pyretri," a plant used to induce heat and saliva</note>, two drachms of **oregano**, and three drachms each of **hyssop** and **myrrh** (if good quality can be found). Combine with water and make lozenges of one drachm each. Use with **warm water**.

### ¶ For those spitting up blood.

<margin>The King of the Medes’ purgative for spitting blood.</margin>
**A**ccept three ounces of **purslane**, and one ounce each of **pomegranate flowers** <note>original: "balaustiarum"</note>, the inner membranes found in **acorns**, and **blackberry flowers** or **blackberries**. Boiling these, let the patient especially use two ounces of that decoction for drinking; for it is very effective for these cases, as is the juice of the purslane itself.

# Of Pills or <term>Catapotia</term> <note>from the Greek 'katapotia,' meaning medicines to be swallowed whole</note>

...should be drunk: however, the **fig** <note>original: "ficus"</note> is very effective for the first [stage]. **Marshmallow root** <note>original: "Euisci radix"</note> and **mint** are good for recent eruptions, and two <term>drachms</term> <note>a unit of weight, approximately 3.9 grams</note> of **great centaury** given to those with fever with water; **pomegranates** are also potent, as is the juice of **lentisk** <note>the mastic tree</note> leaves. ¶ For formed blood clots <note>original: "trombos"</note>, **hare's rennet** <note>original: "coagulus leporis"</note> drunk as a potion dissolves them; likewise, lye made from **figs** drunk with water dissolves clots, as does **thyme** or **savory** boiled with vinegar.

## ¶ For a lost voice, from Oribasius of Sardis.

<image-desc>Decorative initial A with floral and foliage patterns.</image-desc>Take **linseed**, **raisins** without seeds, fried **pine nuts**, and peeled **hazelnuts** in equal weights; grind them and administer with raw **honey**: and give one spoonful from that. Likewise, boil **cabbage** juice with honey and give it as an <term>electuary</term> <note>a medicinal paste or syrup</note>.

## ¶ Aurelianus Caelius’s potion for <term>dropsy</term> <note>an old term for edema, or swelling caused by excess fluid</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative initial A depicting a scholar or physician seated at a desk reading a book.</image-desc>Aurelianus, in his book of *Responses or Aids* and in his third book *On Chronic Diseases* <note>original: "cronion"</note>, provides a singular decoction of **squill** <note>original: "scillæ," a sea onion often used as a diuretic</note> for dropsy, which is as follows. Take two pounds of **squill**, cleared of all waste so it is reduced to one pound; it must be cut up and placed in a new earthenware vessel, then three <term>sextarii</term> <note>a Roman measure of volume, roughly a pint</note> of wine added. When these have been boiled down to a third, two spoonfuls of the liquid should be given to the sick person, increasing the dose as the treatment progresses until it reaches one <term>ounce</term>. But this should be given before taking food, with a long interval of time, and after exercise or after anointing the body.

# Book Three.

## ¶ Pill-manual of illustrious men.

## ¶ <term>Catapotia</term> from the invention of Campegius <note>Symphorien Champier, a notable 16th-century French physician</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative initial P containing a human face or portrait.</image-desc>Pills are called *catapotia* because they are swallowed whole by the sick, and not chewed with the teeth or dissolved in liquid and licked; Celsus <note>a Roman medical encyclopedist</note> writes of these in his fifth book, chapter 25.

## ¶ Pills suitable for yellow bile, and for evacuating it.

Take half an ounce of washed **aloe**, one drachm of **rhubarb** <note>original: "Reubarbari"</note>, four grains of **nard** spike—either Celtic [if you cannot find Indian]—and one drachm of **winter plums**: mix with **syrup of violets**: let six pills be formed for every drachm: let the patient take one before dinner, or sometimes three or five, when they go to bed.

## ¶ Pills suitable for phlegmatic people, and for evacuating <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita," one of the four bodily humors believed to cause sluggishness</note>.

Take one drachm of light, white **agaric** <note>a medicinal fungus</note>, one <term>scruple</term> <note>a small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams</note> of **ginger**, three drachms of washed **aloe**, and one scruple of **mastic**: let them be made into pills with **honey of roses**, six to a drachm: give one before dinner, or three, or five, when they go to bed.

### ¶ Pills for black bile, and those that purge it.

Take one <term>drachm</term> <note>a unit of weight, about 3.9 grams</note> each of **oak polypody** <note>original: "polipodij quercini," a type of fern used as a purgative</note> (ensure it is not decayed) and **senna pods** from Syria; half an ounce of **washed aloes**; and half a <term>scruple</term> <note>a small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams</note> of **mastic**. Let them be formed with **syrup of fumitory** <note>original: "syrupo de fumoterra," a plant used to treat "melancholy" or black bile issues</note> into six pills per drachm; give one before dinner.

### ¶ Pills for the head for <term>soda</term> <note>a historical term for a localized, often throbbing headache</note> caused by the stomach’s involvement in matter from yellow bile.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral motifs.</image-desc>
Take one and a half drachms each of **washed aloes** and **pills of simple hiera** <note>original: "yera simplici," a traditional bitter medicinal formula</note>; two drachms of **winter plums**; one drachm of **choice rhubarb**; and half a scruple of **spikenard**. Mix with **syrup of violets**. Let six pills be made per drachm; let the patient take one before dinner, or three when going to bed. 

In the case of *soda* arising from cold matter, it may be made thus: Take one and a half drachms of **white and light agaric** <note>original: "agarici albi," a fungus used as a purgative</note>, three drachms of **washed aloes**, one drachm of **chebulic myrobalans** <note>original: "myrobalanorū, kebulorum," a fruit used in Ayurvedic and medieval medicine for digestion</note>, and half a scruple of **mastic**. Let them be formed with **honey of roses** into six pills per drachm; give as directed above. 

¶ If, however, the *soda* is from matter consisting of black bile, take half an ounce of **washed aloes**, and half a drachm each of **Syrian senna pods** and **oak polypody**; six grains of **mastic**. Mix with **syrup of violets**. Give one before dinner, or three or five when going to bed. Some physicians add **thyme**, **dodder of thyme** <note>original: "epithimum"</note>, and **rhubarb**. If it is caused by the scorching of phlegm <note>original: "adustionem pituitæ"</note>, one scruple of **washed tartar** and one drachm of **white agaric** could be added. **Pantaleon of Vercelli** <note>a 15th-century physician</note> adds **lapis lazuli** (also called azure stone); but beware of using it, for it is a deadly poison. Lapis lazuli is useful only to painters. If **epilepsy** should occur through the stomach's involvement, one might add **peony seeds**, **myrobalans**, **chebulic myrobalans**, **thyme**, and **dodder of thyme**, with a little **white frankincense** and **French lavender** <note>original: "stichados"</note>.

### ¶ Precious pills against thin catarrh descending to the chest.

Take one drachm of **white and light agaric**, half a drachm of **white ginger**, two scruples of **choice oak polypody**, one drachm of **Armenian bole** <note>original: "boli armeni," a medicinal red clay</note>, three and a half drachms of **washed aloes**, two scruples of **liquorice juice**, and four drachms of **yellow myrobalans**. Prepare with **mucilage of tragacanth** made with **rose water**. Let six pills be made per drachm. Give sometimes one before dinner, sometimes three or five when going to bed. You may use these every day by taking one before dinner, or three or four times a week. They are effective against thin <term>catarrh</term> <note>excessive discharge or mucus</note>; they are also effective against thick catarrh, but in that case, they should be formed with **oxymel of squill** <note>a mixture of honey, vinegar, and the sea squill plant</note>, because it cuts through thick phlegm.

### ¶ Pills or lozenges of raisins for every catarrh.

### ¶ Pills of King Philip the Fair of France for dysentery and lienteric flux.
<note>Philip IV (1268–1314). "Lienteric flux" refers to a form of diarrhea where food passes through the body undigested.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' with floral motifs.</image-desc>
Take one <term>drachm</term> <note>about 3.9 grams</note> each of **myrobalans** <note>astringent fruit used in tanning and medicine</note> and **yellow chebulic myrobalans** that have been lightly toasted; one and a half drachms of **toasted rhubarb**; one <term>scruple</term> <note>about 1.3 grams</note> of **mastic** <note>a resin from the pistachio tree</note>; and half a scruple of **red coral powder**. Mix these with **syrup of myrtles** and let six pills be formed for every drachm of the mixture. Let the patient take one before dinner, and sometimes three when going to bed.

### ¶ Cough pills of the King of Majorca for catarrhal flux.
<note>Majorca was an independent kingdom in the 13th and 14th centuries. These pills, called "bechichiæ," are specifically for coughs.</note>

Take one and a half drachms of **frankincense** <note>original: "olibani"</note>; one drachm of **mastic**; four scruples of **Armenian bole** <note>medicinal red clay</note>; one scruple of **cold tragacanth powder** prepared without camphor; and four ounces of **candy sugar** dissolved in **violet water**. Let the pills be formed in the shape of **lupin beans**. Let the patient hold them in the mouth frequently, long after a meal, and also when going to sleep.

### ¶ Pills of the King of Castile for obstruction or blockage of the liver, and for strengthening it.

Take two drachms of **washed aloes**; one and a half drachms of **choice rhubarb**; one scruple each of **spikenard** <note>original: "spicæ"</note> and **ivory spodium** <note>original: "spodij ex dente elephātis," likely calcined ivory used as an absorbent</note>; half a drachm of **powdered rose troches** <note>original: "diarodon," a rose-based medicinal tablet</note>; two scruples of **white and light agaric** <note>a medicinal fungus</note>; half a scruple of **mastic**; one drachm of **powdered senna pods**; and half a drachm of **powdered rhubarb troches**. Prepare this with a **syrup of endive**, which we call **chicory** <note>original: "scariolam"</note>. Let the patient take one pill sometimes before dinner, and sometimes three when going to bed. **Mesue** <note>an influential 9th-century Persian physician</note> says that aloes is harmful to the liver, which goes against the opinion of **Dioscorides** <note>a 1st-century Greek physician</note> and other Greek authorities; therefore, we say that Mesue is not to be believed on this point.

Let the ingredients that need pulverizing be ground to a powder. Then, with **syrup of citron juice** or **lemon syrup**, let a mass for pills be formed, from which six pills are made per drachm. <header>On blessed medicines</header>

...sometimes three when going to bed, sometimes one in the morning during winter and spring, and in times of plague, one every morning. These pills preserve one from the plague, and they have been tested in **Pannonia** <note>a Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>, and throughout all **Germany**, and many times by me in **Lorraine**.

¶ **Mastic pills** which cleanse the stomach and correct a corrupted appetite; they are effective where there is weakness of the stomach caused by the corruption of the <term>humors</term> <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient doctors believed had to be balanced for health</note>; it is also a medicine for a diseased womb.

Take half an **ounce** of **mastic**; ten **drachms** <note>a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note> of washed and select **aloes**; three and a half drachms of light **white agaric** <note>a medicinal fungus found on larch trees, used as a purgative</note>; and prepare them with the juice of **mugwort** <note>original: "arthemesiæ"</note>. These pills can be taken at any time, for they cleanse and regulate the stomach. These were the invention of **Peter of Abano** <note>Petrus de Abano (c. 1250–1316), a famous Italian physician and philosopher known for reconciling Arabic medicine with Greek philosophy</note>.

¶ **Pills of the King of the Britons**, which may be called **houndstongue pills**, for all catarrhal diseases <note>illnesses involving excess mucus</note>, for <term>coryza</term> <note>the common cold or nasal congestion</note>, and for a catarrhal cough.

Take eight drachms of **white frankincense**; one and a half ounces each of **white poppy juice** and **lettuce juice**; one and a half drachms of **saffron**; and half an ounce of **houndstongue roots** <note>original: "cinoglossæ"</note>. Let pills be made and administered. Some people add **opium** and **henbane**, but because of their violent effects, we have used poppy and lettuce juice in their place. Regarding **myrrh**, because none could be found of good quality, we have made no mention of it. These pills are among the secrets of medicine and are not known by many.

## On Cathartics and blessed medicines, and why it is beneficial for everyone that the belly be favorable, according to Galen, Oribasius of Sardis, and Paul of Aegina.

<margin>Galen</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral patterns and scrolling vines within a square border.</image-desc>

From the beginning, it has always been the view of the ancients that for the sake of health, a **productive belly** <note>original: "venter fecundus"; referring to regular bowel movements</note> should be ensured daily, and a blameless discharge of urine should be produced according to the intake of food or drink. But if these things do not occur, then it is necessary to use those things which expel them and ensure the compliance of the belly and the urine. However, for those with healthy bodies, it is superfluous to give a <term>cathartic</term> <note>a strong laxative or purgative</note>; for indeed (as **Galen** writes) they are afflicted by twisting pains and excessive aches, and the purging becomes difficult; those who are healthy suffer distress even more quickly. In the sick, however, it is harmful if they are not emptied. Therefore, it is necessary to take precautions so that at the first onset of spring, **epileptics**, **asthmatics**, **phlegmatic** individuals, and **arthritics** <note>original: "artetici"; those suffering from joint pain</note> are purged. In long-lasting illnesses...
