<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature and effects of wine, transitioning from the medical views of the Arabs (Avicenna, Rhazes, and Averrhoes) to a detailed survey of classical Greek and Roman philosophical and poetic attitudes toward wine consumption, dilution, and abstinence.</meta>

# On the nature of wine according to the Philosophers. Folio 46.

We call no one a "drunkard" of sweet wine, because sweet wine possesses no flavor proper to wine itself, but renders it entirely alien. Therefore, one who is gripped by a desire for sweet wine is more truly called a lover of sweet things, rather than a lover of wine. <margin>The opinion of Athenaeus.</margin> ¶ Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the *Deipnosophistae* (The Banquet of the Learned), a major source for ancient food and drink.</note> writes that Troezenian wine induces sterility in those who drink it, just as wine in Achaia causes miscarriage.

¶ It is also worth knowing that just as theorists in music assert that the sesquialter ratio <note>original: "hemiolium," a 3:2 ratio</note> creates a harmony through the fifth; the double ratio <note>original: "displasium," a 2:1 ratio</note> creates that which is through all <note>the octave</note>; while the harmony through the fourth consists of the sesquitertian ratio <note>original: "epitrito," a 4:3 ratio</note>. In a similar way, the "Dionysian harmonicists" <margin>Dionysius on music.</margin> established three harmonies for mixing wine with water: through the fifth, the third, and the fourth. Thus, those drinking in harmony might drink five parts, or three, or even four. For the sesquialter ratio <note>the musical fifth</note> arises where there are two parts of wine to three parts of water. <margin>On the mixing of wine with water.</margin> The double ratio <note>the octave</note> is with two parts water added to one of wine; the sesquitertian <note>the fourth</note> is when one part of wine is poured with three parts of water. This frugality in drinking was recognized as very suitable for the "Centenary" dinners of the Romans, in which it was a crime to spend more than a hundred bronze coins, as Septimius Florens writes.

<margin>Plato’s opinion from the Cratylus.</margin>
¶ Let us add that point of Plato’s from the *Cratylus*: that the Greeks call wine <term>oinos</term> <note>Plato suggests a pun here between *oinos* (wine) and *oiesis* (opinion/belief) + *nous* (mind)</note> because it fills the mind with the vanity of estimations and opinions, or perhaps from its "benefit" <note>original: "emolumento"</note>. This is confirmed by the Homeric line: "you will feel a helping aid, if you drink." <margin>The Cypriot poet.</margin> To these, the Cypriot poet <note>Likely referring to Eubulus, often cited in Athenaeus</note> adds his vote: "The gods made wine for Menelaus as the most excellent thing for dispelling cares." He then continues: "To those who are sensible," he says, "I offer only three cups: the first to Health, the second to Love and Pleasure, and finally the third to Sleep. When those called wise have drained this, they soon take their leave. The fourth cup, I think, is certainly not ours, but belongs to violence." <note>original: "iniuriae"</note>

¶ A moderate use of wine is entirely praised, which was so strictly observed among the ancients that Hesiod <margin>Hesiod</margin> writes: "Three parts of water, and it is right to add a fourth of wine." <note>A very diluted 3:1 mixture.</note> And he orders this to be done even during festivals when the soul is made merry. Athenaeus <margin>Athenaeus</margin> also says that the Greeks were accustomed to drink two cups of wine diluted with five of water, or one to three. The ancient Greeks added the unmixed wine to the water, not the water to the wine, so that the smallest amount of wine would mix more easily, as the author Theophrastus <margin>Theophrastus.</margin> states. <margin>Panyasis. Three drinks.</margin> ¶ Panyasis, in what he wrote regarding side-dishes, assigns the first drink to the Graces, the Seasons, and Dionysus; the second to Venus and again to Dionysus; and the third to insolence <note>original: "probro"</note> and ruin. But in antiquity they drank to the number and memory of friends—some according to the number of the Graces <note>three</note>, some according to the Muses <note>nine</note>.

<margin>Plato’s law on abstinence from wine.</margin>
¶ Plato, 그 monarch of philosophers, orders in the *Laws* that boys abstain from wine until the age of eighteen, as it is not necessary to "add fire to fire." Then, until forty, they should use it moderately. After that age, one may invite himself to drink a bit more to relieve the weariness of life. Furthermore, all slaves, women, magistrates, and orators who consult for the state should abstain, as should spouses on the first day of their marriage; for the rest of the time they should be moderate when they are free for the task. It is harmful to be heavy with wine, and drinking makes people lazy. Aristotle also seems to prove this when he says that the offspring of drunkards is infertile; it was likewise forbidden to Roman women and slaves.

<margin>Cicero’s precept on wine.</margin>
¶ Cicero prohibits wine for the sick in the fourth book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, because (he says) it rarely helps and very often harms; it is better not to use it than to run into obvious danger in the hope of doubtful health. The Epizephyrian Locrians (as Athenaeus is the authority) considered it a capital offense to use wine according to the law of Zaleucus, just as today the Saracens <note>A term used by Renaissance writers for Muslims.</note> do, not so much from the law of Muhammad as from the ancient custom of the nation and the Arabs.

<margin>Alexander of Aphrodisias’s problem.</margin>
¶ Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A Peripatetic philosopher who lived around 200 AD.</note> says in his *Problems* that water-drinkers are sharper in sight and the other senses; for copious wine greatly obstructs the senses in their spiritual pathways. Finally, in our own doctrine, there is no swifter path to attaining high virtues than...

# Aphorisms on the nature of wine

<margin>The utility of wine. Mnefitheus the physician. Socrates.</margin>
...abstinence from wine and meat; since in many places in the sacred volumes, divine wisdom is compared to water.
¶ The philosopher Mnefitheus <note>A 4th-century BC Greek physician known for his dietary rules</note> says that wine taken in moderation adds strength to both soul and body; but quite the opposite happens when it is taken beyond measure. For this reason, they call Dionysus <note>Bacchus, the god of wine</note> a "physician," and they say that one of his Nymphs is named Hygieia <note>the personification of Health</note> after health itself. Socrates, in the works of Plato, praises wine taken moderately at a banquet, because just as a rain from Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note> gently dewing the plants makes them more vigorous than a violent downpour, so too moderate unmixed wine <note>original: "merum"</note> arouses virtue and makes the mind more eager for its duties, whereas immoderate wine overwhelms it. Nor indeed were funeral preparations <term>pollincturae</term> <note>The ritual washing and preparation of a body for burial</note> and funeral feasts invented for any other reason than that, through the restorative power of wine and food, the longing for the deceased and the resulting sadness might be suppressed.

<margin>Commendation of wine by Asclepiades the physician.</margin>
¶ Asclepiades <note>A famous Greek physician who practiced in Rome</note>, a very celebrated man among physicians, greatly commended wine and did not deny it to the sick. He said its nature was very close to that of the gods; Homer even dedicated a book to its praises and virtues, saying the gods gave wine to humans to drive away cares. For bodies wasted by hunger or consumed by medicinal purges, it is most healthful, and it is an enemy to all inflammations. Generally, however, infrequent and brief drinking is safe, according to that oracle of Hippocrates: "To thirst for nothing, or to drink nothing, follows no reason." For in this matter, we indulge more in pleasure or habit than in necessity.

<margin>Julius Viator, a Roman knight</margin>
¶ Julius Viator, a Roman knight, taught that a man could lack drink entirely; because of a disease under the skin <note>likely dropsy or edema</note>, he gradually accustomed himself to drinking absolutely nothing. It is fitting, above all, that men master the belly; without this, it is impossible to say or do anything beautiful. Frugality is the mistress of the counsels of the wise. Whosoever of those philosophizing forge anything, it is fitting above all that they master the belly.

<margin>Plutarch</margin>
¶ For wine (as Plutarch writes) and meat indeed make for greater physical strength, but they impede the actions of the mind. And if we wish to choose a man for war by whom we may be most preserved, let us choose him who is least indulgent in wine, sleep, and food; or if, at death, we wish to commend our children and virgins to someone, let us commit them to a man of this sort, and not to a slave.

<margin>Concerning famous men who were devoted to wine: Lysander, Demetrius, Holofernes, Alexander.</margin>
¶ We read that wine obscured the distinguished virtues of many. We read in Athenaeus that, first of all, Antiochus the Great <note>Ruler of the Seleucid Empire</note> used to sleep for whole days because of his drunkenness and was only awakened in the evening. Lysander, the leader of the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, a man otherwise frugal in all other matters, was nevertheless devoted to wine. Among the lovers of wine was also Demetrius, who was a hostage at Rome. Likewise Holofernes, King of Cappadocia, and Alexander the Macedonian. As was said above, Alexander would sleep for two days and as many nights from drunkenness; for this reason, he was "unwarlike" in matters of love <note>meaning he lacked sexual vigor or interest</note>, because (according to Aristotle) the semen <note>original: "genitura"</note> of drunkards is watery. For that Darius <note>Darius the Great of Persia</note> who overthrew the Magi, it was inscribed in his funeral epitaph: "I was able both to drink much wine and to carry it well." Dionysius the Younger, the tyrant <note>of Syracuse</note>, was also a drunkard, from which his eyes were ruined; he offered a golden crown to those drinking <note>in a competition</note>, which the philosopher Xenocrates won. Alexander even invited the Indians—who were known as the greatest drinkers—to a prize-winning contest. A certain man is said to have drunk "choas" <note>an ancient Greek unit of liquid measure, roughly 3 liters</note>, won a talent <note>a massive sum of money</note>, and lived for only two days afterward. Mithridates...

# F. XLVII.

### From the philosophers, poets, and orators.

Likewise, he proposed a silver talent <note>A high unit of currency in the ancient world</note> as a prize for gluttony <note>original: "polyphagiæ"</note> and excessive drinking <note>original: "polypotiæ"</note>. Among all the heroes, Nestor is depicted by Homer as a drinker, and Agamemnon is similarly criticized by Achilles. To touch upon the poets as well, and other learned men, the lyric poets Anacreon and Alcaeus, and the comic playwright Aristophanes, wrote much while in a state of drunkenness; so too did Aeschylus, about whom a critic mockingly said: "O Aeschylus, if you do what is fitting, you do it without knowing it." Yet, the opposite often occurs among poets. Horace wrote that he "abstained from bread <note>Ceres</note> and wine <note>Bacchus</note>," and Juvenal mentions "knowing no wine during the whole of December." And according to Pliny, the painter Protogenes, while painting the *Ialysus* <note>a famous painting of a local hero of Rhodes</note>, lived for many days on nothing but soaked lupines. Minos, about to receive the law from Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, practiced the highest abstinence for nine days in a cavern, as told by Homer. Among the Hebrews, there were Moses and Elijah, and among us, Christ fasted for forty days.

¶ They say that King Romulus, having been invited to a dinner, did not drink much there because he had business to attend to the next day. They said to him, "Romulus, if all men did that, wine would become cheaper." He replied, "On the contrary, it would be dear, if everyone drank as much as they wanted; for I have drunk as much as I wanted."

¶ Seneca, in his work *On Tranquility of Life*, testifies that they called Bacchus "Liber" <note>the Free One</note> because he frees the mind from the slavery of cares, expels the cold, and invites sleep. But when drunk too copiously, he disturbs the head and harms the stomach. For this reason, Pliny says quite rightly that it can be said: "Nothing is more useful for the strength of the body, yet nothing more ruinous to its pleasures, if moderation is lacking." From this flows the monstrous lust of drunkenness: paleness, sagging cheeks, ulcers of the eyes, trembling hands that spill full vessels, and what constitutes an immediate punishment—frenzied dreams and nightly restlessness. From this comes foul breath, the forgetting of all things, and the death of memory; for the vapor weakens the brain and softens the limbs. Hence Aristotle, in his book *On Sleep*, warns that wine should not be given to children or nurses.

¶ We find in history that the wife of Egnatius Metellus, because she had drunk wine from the vat, was beaten to death with a club by her husband, and he was acquitted of the killing by Romulus. And Fabius Maximus writes in his annals of a matron who had unsealed the caskets in which the keys to the wine cellar were kept, and was forced by her own family to die of starvation. From this arose the custom of relatives giving a kiss to women: so they might know if they had drunk strong wine <note>original: "temetum," which was then the name for wine</note>.

¶ The Egyptian kings also had a certain fixed measure of wine to drink, by which they could neither be burdened nor become intoxicated. For to kings (as it says in the Proverbs of Solomon) wine should be given least of all, because nothing is secret where drunkenness reigns; lest by chance they drink and forget judgments, and change the cause of their sons and the poor. For this reason, Plautus wittily said: "Wine is a deceitful wrestler; it catches the feet first." There is a celebrated saying of a wise man over the table: "The first cup pertains to thirst, the second to cheerfulness, the third to pleasure, the fourth to madness." Hence, drunkenness is a voluntary form of insanity.

***

# Disputation on Bloodletting

## A summary disputation by Master Symphorien Champier, Chief Physician to the Lorraines, which teaches through which parts of the body blood should be let in cases of internal inflammation, especially in pleurisy <note>An inflammation of the lining of the lungs.</note>.

<margin>
The harmony of the four humors.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a stylized plant with a central flower or fruit and spreading leaves, set against a hatched background within a square border.</image-desc>Just as the world is composed with wonderful skill, so too man is seen to consist of four elements: blood, phlegm, and both types of bile, the black as well as the yellow. For blood is likened to air, phlegm to water, yellow bile to fire, and the bile which is called "black" is likened to earth. Furthermore, in taste, blood is sweet, phlegm is salty, yellow bile is bitter, and black bile is sharp.

<margin>
The generation and origin of the humors.
</margin>

The source of the blood is the heart; from blood comes the spirit <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" or *pneuma* was a subtle substance that carried life and sensation through the body.</note>. Blood flows through the right side of the heart, while the spirit springs forth through the left. Yellow bile originates from the liver, black bile from the spleen, and phlegm from the brain. Blood is truly hot and moist; phlegm is cold and moist; yellow bile is hot and dry at the same time; and black bile is dry with coldness.

<margin>
Hippocrates.
</margin>

The reason that some men are cheerful and others are sad is found in these elements, as Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> says: for those who have the purest blood are generally smiling in appearance, florid in body, and sometimes of a charming complexion.

<margin>
The four complexions.
</margin>

However, in those whom yellow bile overflows, they are agile, light of mind, quick-witted, and prone to anger. Those who abound in black bile are sluggish, faint-hearted, and timid; whereas the phlegmatic are slow and cold. The schools of physicians surmise that from an abundance of sweet phlegm flows a great deal of sleep, just as hunger arises from acidic humors, thirst from salty ones, and the interruption of thirst from raw ones.

<margin>
Blood is the most excellent among the humors.
</margin>

Among the humors, blood is judged to be by far the most excellent. Indeed, it is the material of the spirits upon which life chiefly depends, as well as the operation of the vegetative power <note>The biological faculty responsible for growth and nutrition.</note> and the animal power. Therefore, it is held to be the treasure of nature and (as Plato says) the food of the flesh and the entire body; if it perishes, death follows immediately. Those, therefore, who study the letting of blood should propose one main thing to themselves: it is necessary that they consider which conditions of the body require evacuation, and then the other: which are those that require the withdrawal of blood, since blood is the fuel of the spirit and the treasure of life.

<margin>
What blood is, and what spirit is.
</margin>

For there are many conditions that require evacuation, but not the letting of blood; but we, for the sake of brevity, shall speak of blood-

It emphasizes blood as the most vital humor and the source of the body's life-giving "spirits."</summary>

<meta>The previous page introduced the author, Symphorien Champier, and established the foundational theory of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) as the basis for medical treatment. # On Pleurisy. Leaf XLVIII.

We intend to teach regarding bloodletting <note>original: "sanguinis missione"</note> in pleurisy <note>Inflammation of the membranes surrounding the lungs, causing sharp chest pain.</note> as it pertains to the disease. We shall soon discuss which veins ought to be cut; for there has been much inquiry into these matters. It is asked whether it matters not at all which vein one chooses to cut in cases of pleurisy, or whether it matters a great deal, as was the view of Galen <note>A highly influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD).</note> and nearly every most distinguished physician—that is, whether this vein or that should be chosen, and from which side it should be lanced.

<margin>A question of the moderns.</margin> Therefore, the "neoterics" <note>Referring to the "modern" doctors of the Renaissance era.</note> and the novice physicians have raised such a question: whether, in the beginning of pleurisy, blood should be drawn from the opposite side <note>original: "ex aduersi parte"</note>, so that if the right side is affected, blood should be let from the left arm at the onset. To this question, the more recent doctors who are fond of the Arabic doctrine and follow Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath (c. 980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> respond and contend that in inflammations of the internal members and viscera, the vein on the side opposite to the affected part must be lanced.

<margin>The response of Hippocrates.</margin> This is argued even though the testimonies of Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BC).</note>, Galen, and Oribasius of Sardis <note>A 4th-century Greek medical compiler.</note> suggest that the vein which is directly in line <note>original: "e directo," meaning on the same side as the pain.</note> with the ailment is the one to be cut.

<margin>Galen. Oribasius.</margin> All the Arabs are beholden to this opinion [of bleeding the opposite side], as can be seen in their books, whom the entire chorus of younger physicians has imitated. Chief among them is that other Solomon, Avenzoar <note>Ibn Zuhr (1094–1162), a famous Arab physician from Al-Andalus (modern Spain).</note>, an Arab by origin, even if he was a Spaniard born in Seville. He mentions certain people of his time who held different views and offered sophisticated arguments—whether these were legitimate or not, our colleague Brissot <note>Pierre Brissot (1478–1522), a French physician who sparked a massive controversy by advocating for the "Greek" method of bleeding the same side as the ailment.</note> does not know. For, as Brissot says, truth can be gathered from both true and false premises, and both rightly and wrongly.

<margin>Brissot of Paris.</margin> This Avenzoar draws blood only from the opposite side; he brings forth neither reason nor any other evidence than the practice of his own father. "I believe most certainly," says Avenzoar, "that this [bleeding the same side] is entirely the death of the patient."

<margin>Avenzoar, called the "Wise" among the Arabs.</margin> Avenzoar "believes most certainly," yet he does not know this through either reason or experience. Brissot, however, as he asserts, had frequent experience in this matter: that bleeding the same side brings great and sudden relief.

<margin>The author's experience in pleurisy.</margin> Indeed, in this year of 1531, in the presence of René Villatery, a most expert apothecary, I myself had an experience here in Lyon <note>original: "Lugdunum"</note> with a certain merchant suffering from pleurisy. I let blood from the direct side, and he was quickly cured and made healthy. Avenzoar believes this to be the total death of the sick man, but one should rather say *why* he believed it.

Brissot says we should not revile him so foully, yet it is easy to rebuke his words or certainly to despise them. For Avenzoar believed it impossible for anyone to be perfectly cured of pleurisy before the sixtieth day; yet if the cause is evacuated, the disease does not last so long, and after the cure, there is no fear of a relapse—something that must be feared in Avenzoar's way of healing.

<margin>Opinion of Rhazes on bloodletting.</margin> Rhazes <note>Al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian physician and philosopher.</note> in the ninth book to Al-Mansur says: where the body is very full, bleed from the arm of the opposite side from the affected part; but in another place, especially in the *Book of Divisions*, he feels otherwise and contradicts himself.

Johannes Mesue <note>Refers to a popular medical text attributed to a "Masawaih," likely a 13th-century Latin compilation.</note>, to add something further, distinguishes by the beginning of the illness, whether the matter is flowing or has already flowed. Likewise, he considers whether the fullness is greater or lesser, and whether it affects the whole or a part.

<margin>Opinion of Mesue. Opinion of Avicenna.</margin> Avicenna, without determination, first bleeds from the leg on the same side, then from the arm of the opposite side twice—first from the basilic vein <note>A large vein in the arm, often used for bloodletting.</note>, then from the "median" or "black" vein—and after some days from the arm of the affected side; finally, he applies cupping glasses to the side. But how far he wanders from the path of truth in this matter...

<summary>This page discusses the 16th-century medical controversy between the "Arabic" method of bleeding the side opposite a pleurisy infection and the "Greek" method of bleeding the same side. The author, Symphorien Champier, cites his own successful clinical experience in Lyon to support the Greek method over the traditional Arabic authorities like Avicenna and Avenzoar.</summary>

# On the cutting of a vein in pleurisy.

...how the Arabs have deviated, we shall show most clearly. First of all,
<margin>The opinion of the Arabs.</margin>
the authority of the ancients explodes and convicts this perverse opinion of the Arabs, the Carthaginians <note>original: "Pœnorum"; here referring to North African/Arabic medical writers</note>, and the more recent authors, for the ancients teach that in all inflammations of the internal viscera, the vein which is directly on the side of the affected place <note>original: "e directo loci affecti"; meaning the same side of the body</note> must be cut.

### ¶ The first opinion, which is that of Hippocrates.

<margin>Book 1 on the method of diet.</margin>
<margin>Book 1 on diseases.</margin>
<margin>Book 6 of the Epidemics.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'H' featuring floral patterns and scrollwork.</image-desc>
Hippocrates, in the fourth book of *On the Method of Diet in Acute Diseases*, writing on the treatment of pleurisy and pneumonia <note>original: "peripneumoniæ"; inflammation of the lungs</note>, writes to this effect: If the pain extends to the upper parts, such as the collarbone <note>original: "iugulum"</note>, the breast, or the arm, one ought to cut the internal vein of the arm <note>likely the basilic vein</note> from that side, namely, which has been affected by the pain. Hippocrates teaches the same in the first book of *On Diseases*, where he speaks again of pneumonia and pleurisy, saying thus: It will be beneficial to pierce the splenic vein <note>original: "Lienarem venam"</note> of this hand, or the hepatic vein <note>original: "iocinoralem"; the liver vein</note>, on whichever side the disease may be; and thus the pain of the side and other parts is relieved. This same point Hippocrates confirms in the sixth book of the *Epidemics*, saying: It is appropriate to purge the pain nearest the cavity; but it is proper to divide, or cut, the vessel <note>original: "ventriculum," here used in an older sense for a blood vessel or chamber</note> of the blood.

### ¶ The second opinion, that of Galen.

<margin>Book on the constitution of the art.</margin>
<margin>Galen's book on Phlebotomy.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'G' containing a seated figure or cherub amidst foliage.</image-desc>
Galen, in the book *On the Constitution of the Art of Medicine*, chapter seven, begins: "Since evacuation is best and easiest when performed from the veins more adjacent to and common with the suffering part." These are his words. To this sentiment are added those things written by the same Galen in the book *On Phlebotomy* <note>The practice of opening a vein to draw blood.</note> in this manner: Revulsion <note>The medical theory of drawing "bad humors" away from an affected area.</note> performed on the same side <note>original: "e directo"</note> quickly shows evident benefit; but on the opposite side, not at all. For evacuation of blood from the left hand greatly aids a poorly affected spleen. But truly, thereafter even in pleurisy patients, a vein-cutting performed on the same side as the affected part has very often shown the most immediate utility. From the opposite
<margin>The words of Galen.</margin>
hand, however, the benefit is either not great, or certainly slow; yet blood let from the same side has often soothed the most violent pains of the eyes within a single day. And a little later: Indeed, a vein-cutting performed on the same side as the affected parts sometimes brings such evident and even sudden utility that the sick themselves and their kinsfolk often remain stunned.
<margin>13. Method of Healing.</margin>
The same author also in the thirteenth book of *The Therapeutic Method*, chapter five, seeking through which places blood ought to be diminished at the beginning of inflammations, says: It is better, therefore, when parts which are in the habit of attracting a <term>phlegmon</term> <note>A localized inflammation or abscess.</note> have begun to do so, to divert it to the nostrils; in like manner, when these parts suffer so, one should also cut the humeral vein <note>original: "humeralem"; likely the cephalic vein</note> in the hand. If that is not visible, the middle vein; where the liver, chest, lung, or heart are so affected, the internal vein, and indeed always...

Fo. XLIX.

# On cutting a vein in pleurisy,

...in all things which are on the direct side. Where inflammation <note>original: "phlegmon"</note> invades the liver, use those veins which are in the right hand; where it invades the spleen, the opposite. Likewise, Galen in the second book of
<margin>Galen, book 2 to Glaucon.</margin>
*To Glaucon*, chapter 7, confirms the aforementioned things, teaching thus: "And indeed if the right part of the uterus has been affected, you shall draw blood from the right hand and leg. But if the left is affected, from the members which are on that direct side." The same Galen
<margin>In the book On Presage.</margin>
discusses this in the book *On Presage Confirmed by Experience*, saying: "In patients with pleurisy <note>inflammation of the membranes around the lungs</note>, the drawing of blood from the vein on the direct side of the sufferer frequently shows great and most evident utility. But from the opposite hand, the benefit is either entirely obscure or merely something to be hoped for." Regarding these testimonies of Hippocrates and Galen, what could be clearer? What, finally, could be more evident? So much so that no one of sound mind can evade the truth here.

### ¶ The third opinion, which is that of Oribasius of Sardis.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a seated figure, likely a scholar or physician, within a circular frame surrounded by ornate scrollwork and floral patterns.</image-desc>
<margin>Oribasius to Eustathius.</margin>
Oribasius of Sardis, Chief Physician to Julian Caesar, writes thus in his
*Compendium of Medicine* addressed to Eustathius: "For one suffering in the
spleen, the vein must be cut in the left hand, near the little finger <note>original: "digitum minorchicum"</note>, or from the left arm, specifically the vein closest to the
elbow. For those with pleurisy, however, the blood must be taken from the side itself
which is in pain. For pains of the eyes,
<margin>From Oribasius.</margin>
it helps magnificently if the cephalic vein <note>original: "capitalis," the "head vein" in the arm</note> is cut from the arm on the side that hurts most." These are the words of Oribasius. If, therefore, these words
of Oribasius are true, it follows that in inflammations of the internal viscera,
<margin>The author's explanation.</margin>
and especially in pleurisy, there is no need for a "retraction" <note>pulling the humors away</note> of the humors through very distant parts, or from the opposite side (as our moderns say) or by "diversion." Rather, the vein must soon be cut which is near and common to the affected side. For all the remaining parts, being stronger, have deposited their superfluities <note>excess fluids or "humors"</note> into the affected place as if into a weaker part. Because of this, in the opposite part or one far distant, there is no superfluity which can flow further toward the affected part, for the sake of which a retraction or diversion ought to be made; since all the superfluity that was in the whole body has already flowed down to the affected part. There is no reason for the
<margin>Objections of the Arabs.</margin>
Arabs and North Africans <note>original: "Poeni"</note> to object to Oribasius on the grounds of "commotion of the humors"—the idea that by cutting the vein on the affected side, a greater rush of humors is made toward the sick part. The humors do indeed run and flow, but not into the sick part; they flow *outward* <note>out of the body through the cut</note>, which is useful and not at all contrary to nature. As for it not flowing into the sick part: how could a weaker part pull from the stronger ones when,
<margin>Galen, On Natural Faculties, book 3.</margin>
as Galen reports in the third book of *On Natural Faculties*, if two men are equally hungry, one does not snatch bread from the hand of the other unless he is the more powerful? Truly, the "pulling" would be greatest when there is no superfluity in the stronger parts which they might deposit of their own accord. Therefore, since the stronger parts cannot receive from the weaker parts (since no deficiency occurs in the strong to make them "pull"), nor can the affected part repel the humors from itself as if it were weaker than the rest—for otherwise an action would proceed from the weaker to the stronger, which is impossible in nature. It remains, then, that the physician must evacuate that which has already flowed into the sick part. He cannot do this by any other means than by
cutting the vein facing the affected side directly, which shares a connection with the sick part.
<margin>Antispastica</margin>
This evacuation is rightly called *Antispastica* <note>a term for "revulsive" or "counter-pulling" evacuation, here used to justify direct relief</note>: for nothing... <note>catchword: "uca," likely part of "vacuat," meaning "empties"</note>

<summary>This page uses the authority of Oribasius and Galen to argue that bloodletting for pleurisy and internal inflammation should be performed on the same side as the pain. The author explains that humors naturally settle in "weak" (diseased) areas, and bleeding those areas directly is the most effective way to drain the excess.</summary>

<margin>
Celsus’s opinion on the cutting of a vein.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'A' featuring floral motifs and a scroll with the Latin motto "FINIS CORONAT" (The end crowns the work).</image-desc>Furthermore, let us discuss whether the drawing back performed through nearby parts has the power to later refill the neighboring part; for most believe the crux of the matter lies here, as Rhazes, Avenzoar, and Avicenna think. Therefore, the cutting of a vein <term>venesection</term> causes the humors <note>the bodily fluids that doctors believed governed health</note> to flow down, but only until they rest. And before Avicenna, Cornelius Celsus—who was considered the "Latin Hippocrates"—says: "Nor am I unaware that some say blood should be let as far as possible from the place where it causes harm; for in this way, they say, the course of the matter <note>the harmful fluids</note> is diverted, whereas in the other way [bleeding nearby] it is called forth into the very part that is burdened. But this is false: for it exhausts the nearest place first; blood follows from further parts only as far as it is emitted from where it was suppressed; because it is not pulled, it does not even come." And a little later: "Blood is also sometimes diverted when, breaking out in one part, it is let out in another: for it stops flowing where we wish, once obstacles are put in place that prevent it, by giving it another path." Thus says Celsus.

<margin>
The author’s explanation.
</margin>

It is established, therefore, in an inflammation <note>phlegmon</note> where blood must be let, that one should always counter its generation with <term>antispastic</term> <note>drawing away or derivative</note> bloodletting, performed especially sharply through nearby parts and at the onset. For it stops the expulsion carried out by the common veins of the whole body by drawing it away, and also evacuates by pulling back. Nor do we command blood to be attracted to the painful spot, but rather to be drawn from it in the opposite direction, even if nothing prevents it from reaching the most distant parts. We call it forth with bindings, frictions, and cupping glasses, but not by the letting of blood, which is dedicated to evacuation; this cannot be done except through nearby parts.

<margin>
Galen.
</margin>

Indeed, Galen always [taught] during the beginnings of inflammations, where blood was to be simultaneously drawn back and evacuated, as he had said in his book *On the Cutting of a Vein*; he prescribes the same reasoning in the second book of *The Art of Healing to Glaucon*, adding the reason why veins of this sort should be cut: "For these,"

<margin>
Galen, book 13 of the Method.
</margin>

(he says) "are closer and more directly aligned with the suffering members." But perhaps someone from the "Arab sect" might say: Galen in the thirteenth book of *Therapeutics* <note>The Method of Healing</note> says, "You shall always make the diversion toward the parts that are most distant." We shall respond that this passage should be understood as referring to the drawing away that is done with purging medicines, friction, and exercise, not with the letting of blood.

But on the contrary, it does not; for this species of withdrawal evacuates the most and the swiftest from the place suffering inflammation. For first, the worse blood gives way to the drawing from the neighboring parts, and quickly the corrupted blood flows forth from the transmitting parts, with the help of the impulse of the excretory faculty turning that way. Since the laboring part strives to unload itself into the chosen and cut vein—as it is the most closely related and shares a connection with it—it is necessary (if a significant quantity is present) for part of the humor to flow back into the nearest vein, which has the greatest association with the specific vein of the sick place. Therefore, this cutting of the vein will most powerfully draw the humor away from the inflammation and its specific vein when it unloads itself into the cut vein." Because of this, Galen in book 3 of *On Crises*, chapter 3 and the last, teaches that in the favorable crises of an inflammation, the blood ought to flow in a direct line. But these things should suffice to refute this most manifest error of both the Arabs and the North Africans <note>original: "Pœnorum," referring to the medical school of Salerno and North African translators like Constantine</note>, as well as more recent doctors. Those who love the truth from their heart will desire nothing more; as for the rest, who have already grown old in that error as if stuck on the rocks of the Sirens <note>a mythological reference to a dangerous attraction one cannot escape</note>, I do not delay for them, since not even the Gods will persuade them otherwise. But if scholars desire to know more of this matter, let them read our *Apologetic Disputation*, which we recently wrote at Lyon against Andrea Turini on behalf of our colleague Matteo Curzio. If they desire even more, let them read Pierre Brissot, a most learned physician and philosopher, and also Andrea Pischinensis himself, and Curzio, and Leonhart Fuchs, the chief physician to the Margrave of Brandenburg.

# On administering wine to those with fevers

## A Question on the Administration of Wine in Fevers, Published by Jacobus Sylvius of Amiens.

### Whether wine can be safely given to sick patients during fevers.

For nine days now, a certain patient in Lyon <note>original: "Lugduni"</note>—a man of great authority among all people, who before this illness was most abundantly endowed with all gifts of nature, intellect, and fortune—had been struggling with a continuous tertian fever <term>febre tertiana continua</term> <note>a malaria-like fever that recurs every third day but remains constant in the intervals</note>. He was sixty-five years old. For about thirty years of his healthy life, he had been accustomed to a strong and noble wine, and quite pure, with no detriment to his health. He thirsted for that same wine in a marvelous way: he most dutifully and earnestly begged and entreated his servants, parents, and friends—who were staying close to him out of a desire to visit, help, and console him—that they might offer him a little wine, specifically a weak wine <term>oligophoron</term> <note>a light, thin wine with little "body" or alcoholic potency</note> diluted with much water, at least on the day when the fever was milder, and even then only during his meal.

Not long afterward, when four very famous physicians and I had gathered to visit him according to custom, that matter was put forward by the family for consultation. Two of the physicians, most renowned in this city, denied that it should be given, fearing that if they tried to extinguish the fire with oil, as it were, it might stir up a heat that could later be overcome by no coldness. I, on the contrary, moved by the reasoning of Symphorianus Camperius <note>Symphorien Champier, a famous French physician and humanist in Lyon</note> and Hieronymus Montuus <note>Jérôme de Monteux, a prominent 16th-century medical writer</note>—physicians who are entirely the most learned after Hippocrates and Galen—and combined with long experience, agreed that it should be given. I did so because the indications taken from his strength <term>virtute</term> <note>the patient's vital force or "virtue"</note>, age, habit, the cause of the disease, the impulse of nature, and his mind <note>his psychological state or "animus"</note> strongly recommended it. I shall briefly explain how much force each of these things has, not only in preserving health, but also in driving out disease.

So that this matter may be completed more briefly, I will bring forward passages from Hippocrates and Galen by which what I have decided may become very clear, especially from the ninth book of Galen's *Method of Medicine* <note>original: "methodi"</note>. Let us investigate whether wine is considered necessary for the sick by a physician, or not. For I say that it is often extremely necessary. So much so, that almost all things administered around the patient are done for the sake of that one thing; sometimes it is moderately necessary, and sometimes it contributes very little to finding remedies. These are the words of Galen, specifically when the patient is very robust or weak, which must be considered more or less by the physician. The same author says not long after: Three faculties <term>facultates</term> of different types govern the living being <note>original: "animal"</note>, each distributed to the whole body from its own particular source, as it were; these Plato calls "souls." One of these is the **natural** faculty, necessary for nourishing the living being, established in the liver as its source, and dispersed through the veins into the whole body. The second is the **vital** faculty, located in the heart, the source of innate heat, and common to the whole body through the arteries. The third is the **animal** <note>the "psychic" faculty, from 'anima'</note> or **reasoning** faculty, which has obtained its home in the brain, the principle of the faculties of the soul...

<summary>This page recounts a medical consultation in Lyon where Jacobus Sylvius argues, against his peers, that a 65-year-old fever patient should be allowed diluted wine based on his lifelong habits and Galenic theory. Sylvius begins a theoretical defense using Galen's concept of the three "souls" or faculties (natural, vital, and animal) that govern the human body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument for administering wine to a patient with a persistent fever. ->Fo. LI.<-
->**Question**<-

[...the soul is the] author of the [faculties], presiding also over voluntary actions and the senses, transmitting movement and sensation through the nerves into the whole animal. Therefore, to preserve these faculties is clearly nothing other than to preserve life, since if any of them are lost, the rest must necessarily perish along with them. From these words of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was the primary authority on medicine in the Renaissance.</note>, it is plain that the "indication" <term>indication</term> <note>a symptom or circumstance that points to the correct treatment</note> taken from the patient's vital forces <term>vires</term> <note>the innate strength or energy of the body's systems</note> carries the greatest weight in healing. For this reason, these forces must either be preserved by the physician or so nurtured that they are not cast down. 

I would add, based on the same author, that no evacuation <note>referring to bloodletting or purging</note> can be rightly established by a physician unless he learns the proper amount from the patient's strength. If the magnitude or length of the disease, or an immoderate evacuation, should cast down these strengths, no one would ever deny they must be restored. Furthermore, just as scents hold the first place for quickly restoring the vital forces, wine holds the second. For wine nourishes the whole body most rapidly and effectively (Galen, *Aphorisms* 18, book 2, and *Aphorisms* 11, book 2). "Whoever," he says, "needs the swiftest addition [of strength], a liquid remedy such as wine is best for recovering the forces; where it is needed even faster, it is done through smell." For it is easier to be filled by drink than by food (*Aphorisms* 11, book 2). Moreover, the drinking of wine dissolves the "hunger of the chest" <note>original: "famem thoracis," a classical term for a specific type of sinking feeling or sharp hunger in the upper body</note> (*Aphorisms* 21, book 2).

To this belongs what is written by Galen in several other places, such as in his book *On the Soul's Dependence on the Body's Temperament*: "Wine, when drunk in moderation, greatly aids digestion <term>coctio</term> <note>the "cooking" or processing of food by the body's internal heat</note>, distribution, the making of blood, and nutrition." This occurs because wine increases the natural heat. Galen (book 7 of *The Method of Medicine*) notes that this heat is indeed the very substance of the bodily powers <note>original: "virtutũ est substantia"</note> (book 2 of *On the Art of Healing, to Glaucon*). To this, we add that for wine to be assimilated into the body, it requires the least amount of "digestion," which is why it nourishes and strengthens so quickly (Galen, book 1 of *On Temperaments*). For it is characteristic of wine to be rapidly transformed by the body (book 3 of *On Temperaments*).

But perhaps someone here might say: "Since wine nourishes more and more readily than other things (according to Galen in his *Introduction to Pulses*), yet during a disease—and especially during its peak—fuller food is not appropriate (as Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BC), whose Aphorisms were foundational medical texts.</note> testifies in *Aphorism* 8, part 1)." When the disease is at its height, one must use the thinnest diet (*Aphorism* 10, part 1). For the more carefully you attend to strengthening the vital forces, the more you increase the disease (Galen, book 1 of *On Crises*, and in his commentary on the *Aphorisms*, book 1). 

Since this objection is of no weight, you may learn the reason from this: the whole state of the fever seemed to have [stabilized], since clouds and "suspensions" <term>eneoremata</term> <note>original: "eneoremata"; cloudy substances seen floating in the middle of a urine sample, used by Renaissance doctors to judge the progress of a disease</note> always appeared in the yellowish urine. But nevertheless, on the ninth day, the fever began to grow milder, and on that and subsequent days, the urine was passed in great volume, so much so that there was a strong suspicion that the feverishness would gradually cease through the urine. 

Furthermore, while thick and red wines provide much nourishment to the body, the "watery" wines <term>aquosa</term> <note>light, thin, or highly diluted wines</note> which we had decided to use provide very little. For watery wines (which is how he names white and thin wines) have a nature similar to water; therefore, they provoke urine and provide minimal nutrition (Galen, *Aphorisms*, book 2). For watery things are quickly excreted through the urine (Galen, *Aphorisms* 18, book 2). Watery wines of thin consistency move the urine and bring very little nourishment to the body (Galen, book *On Good Humors*). Nor is there cause for you to claim that a body otherwise occupied by feverish heat is further heated by the drinking of watery wine, since watery wines actually cool the body imperceptibly (Galen, book *On Good Humors*). Indeed, no white wine is truly "hot" (Galen).

He distinguishes these medicinal, diuretic wines from heavy red wines, which would be inappropriate for a sick patient.</summary>

### On Administering Wine to Those Suffering from Fever

...method. Did he not provide the same food to the sick person during the onset of the fever, and even in the midst of the <term>accession</term> <note>The periodic onset or worsening of fever symptoms.</note> itself? He gave a small amount of bread soaked in diluted wine <note>original: "vinum diluto pane"</note> for them to eat, specifically because of the weakness of their strength—those vital forces from which Hippocrates taught us to take the entire method of establishing a diet, alongside the nature of the disease. 

But why do I use unnecessary witnesses in such an obvious matter? Since Hippocrates himself, in his book *On the Regimen in Acute Diseases*, gives wine not only in daily fevers but even in acute ones, as Galen testifies in the eighth book of his *Method of Healing*. It seems to me to be the right time now to prove that wine should not have been denied even to this age—that is, to old age. For the <term>temperament</term> <note>The balance of the four qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—that determines a person's health.</note> of old age is cold and dry, according to Galen in the first book of *Temperaments* and the eighth book of *On Preserving Health*. Since old age creeps upon men by consuming that very moisture which is most abundant in children, in its place succeeds a dryness which coldness readily follows as a companion; for the heat leaves because it is deprived of the familiar and suitable moisture that cherished it. 

Therefore, the dryness and coldness of old age must be corrected by things that are hot and moist (Galen, *On Preserving Health*, book 8). But wine is the most hot and most moist of substances (Galen, book 1 of the same). Therefore, it is most opportune for correcting the coldness and dryness of the elderly. Added to this is the fact that wine is the most easily and quickly digested <note>original: "coquitur," literally "cooked" or "concocted" by the body's internal heat.</note> of all things: it is distributed into the blood and transformed into nourishment. The body of the elderly needs all these things, as it possesses in the highest degree those weak faculties by which these processes are accomplished. 

However, we chose a "watery" wine, as it is one which nourishes and heats the least—or more truly, it might even cool—lest the heat of a more potent wine should intensify this feverish heat. Its moisture, however, would break the "acrimony" or sharpness of the fever. For a moist diet benefits all those with fever (Aphorism 16, book 1). Wine is beneficial to the elderly because it warms all their members (Galen, book 8, *Health*). Just as wine is most hostile to children, so it is most friendly to the elderly (ibid.). 

But perhaps you will object that the <term>indication</term> <note>A symptom or circumstance that points to the correct treatment.</note> taken from age should be of "likes" <note>Treating like with like, as opposed to opposites.</note> rather than "contraries," as Hippocrates suggests in the aphorism just mentioned, and Galen in his commentary on the same, and in the books on preserving health and the method of healing. In those places, he explains the aphorism briefly. Furthermore, at the end of the eighth book of the *Method*, you indeed seem to speak the truth if I were intending to preserve the temperament of that age, rather than change it—especially since old age is an enemy to life, which consists of heat and moisture. For this reason, some have even wished to call old age itself a disease (Galen, book 5, *On Preserving Health*).

Lest I make your ears deaf with hateful prolixity, I must now move to the other indications by which I would contend that wine should be offered to a febrile elder. For there is an indication of "likes" derived from habit or <term>consuetudo</term> <note>The patient's lifelong habits or lifestyle.</note> (Galen, at the end of the eighth book of *Method*). Therefore, it is primarily harmful to have given things contrary to habit, since habit produces an "acquired" or "second" nature in our bodies. It is from this habit that we take the indication of "likes" (Galen, book 1, *On Preserving Health*). The same point is made in various places by Galen and Hippocrates: "Custom everywhere agrees with nature." Hence it was beautifully said that "custom is an accessory nature" (Galen, *On the Motion of Muscles*). Custom is acquired nature (Galen, book 2, *Temperaments* and *On Continuous Dissolution*). Natures always rejoice in accustomed things (Galen, book 8, *Method*). It is no small thing, and not to be lightly regarded in the discovery of remedies...

<summary>The author argues that wine is an essential remedy for elderly fever patients because it counters the cold, dry temperament of old age and respects the patient's lifelong habits, which act as a "second nature."</summary>

## Question.

...just as we should not think that habit is to be ignored for preserving health, as Galen says in the ninth book of his *Method of Healing* <note>original: "Methodi Medendi"</note>. It is more useful for old men to be exercised in their accustomed work, even if it is moderately harmful. Galen, in the eighth book of *On Preserving Health* <note>original: "De Sanitate Tuenda"</note>, says: Those who are accustomed to bearing their usual labors, even if they are weak and old, bear them more strongly than unaccustomed strong and young men. Hippocrates, in the second book of *Aphorisms*, writes: Things that have been customary for a long time, even if they are of a worse nature, usually trouble one less than unaccustomed things. In the commentary on this, Galen teaches that food and drink create an "acquired nature" <note>An "acquired nature" refers to the idea that the body adapts its biology to its habitual environment and diet over time.</note>. Likewise, Hippocrates, in the second book of *On the Regimen in Acute Diseases*, in the chapter on habit, concludes: If habit must be preserved in the diet of the healthy, since it cannot be suddenly changed without great disadvantage to health, how much more so in the sick? He implies (as Galen interprets) that the sick are harmed more by a change of habit than the healthy, and those even more so who are tormented by acute diseases. For this reason, he did not wish to change habit during a disease. For this reason also, Hippocrates adds that a bad <term>regimen</term> <note>A prescribed course of diet and way of life.</note> in food and drink, provided it is familiar and accustomed, is safer than if a sudden transformation is made into another, even a better one. 

I could bring forward nearly infinite other examples from various books of Galen—and especially from the one he wrote *On Habit*—from Hippocrates, and finally from many other most learned writers, by which I could make plain to you that habit has a great power in preserving the life of man, if I did not think these would be sufficient for you. Furthermore, if one must ever pass from accustomed things to unaccustomed ones, as Hippocrates orders in the second book of *Aphorisms* (because a single habit is dangerous), one should attempt to change those things which are harmful in young men, even if they have been accustomed to them from childhood. This is because their strength can endure a moderately made change and perceive some benefit for the rest of their lives from a better habit. But in old men, do not try it; for even if they could change a habit gradually over a long time, you would sweat in vain, because time is not sufficient for them to enjoy the better habit. 

Galen, in the eighth book of *On Preserving Health*, asks: Do you see with how much danger to life you attempt to change a habit of <term>drinking</term> <note>The original term "thorixis" refers to the deep drinking of wine, often for medical or social reasons.</note> that has been firm since youth in a sixty-year-old, and to do so suddenly? Especially since, beyond that, he would be quite weak from an acute disease. What if I now grant that the custom of generous and pure wine <note>original: "vini generosi & meri"</note> kept by him until now should be changed? Since that wine, being immoderately hot, would not suit a "hot" ailment <note>In Galenic medicine, a fever was considered a "hot" disease, and treatments were usually "cool."</note>, you should not change it entirely during the disease, nor suddenly, if you listen to Galen; rather, something must be granted to custom (Hippocrates, *Aphorisms*, book 1). From these things, I think it is clear even to a child that—taking the <term>indication</term> <note>A sign or symptom that points to a specific treatment.</note> from habit—watery wine, or at least wine quite diluted and used sparingly during meals for the pleasant warmth of the body, should not have been denied. 

The greatest dignity belongs to the <term>forces</term> <note>The vital powers or "vires" that sustain life.</note> themselves, since living itself consists in their preservation; for it is necessary that life be either the forces themselves or their actions. But nothing can be prior to life itself in the body of a living being, because it is not possible to be healthy without life. Therefore, the first power of all to be guarded in men is strength (Galen, book 9). By these words of Galen, etc. Should we prove that watery wine is most opportune for this man to remove the cause of the disease?

# On Administering Wine to Those Suffering from Fever

Galen says they are bilious <note>That is, suffering from an excess of yellow bile.</note>. Therefore, if we remove this abundance of yellow bile from the body, we remove the fever. It will be removed either partly by medicines or partly by a suitable diet—that is, by prohibiting bile from being produced or by expelling that which has already been produced. But indeed, wine mitigates and breaks the sharpness of bitter bile; furthermore, it evacuates it through sweats and urine. Galen, book 1, *On Preserving Health* <note>original: "De Sanitate Tuenda"</note>. If all wines provide this, unless they are thick and harsh, watery wines especially move the urine. Galen, book 12, *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "Methodi Medendi"</note>. Thin, watery wine forces the urine to be passed quickly. Galen, book 1, *On the Natural Faculties* <note>original: "De Facultatibus Naturalibus"</note>. 

But you might object: "Even if wine stirs the urine and extrudes bile through it or through sweats, it still increases the fever by its own heat." Let it be that wine heats (although I would prove that white and especially watery wines are so far from heating that they even secretly cool), yet you cannot immediately conclude that it is not a remedy for the cause of a bilious fever. For a drink of unmixed wine dissolves pains of the eyes, as Hippocrates says in the *Aphorisms*. Furthermore, those medicines administered for the sake of purging bile are hot. For every purging medicine is hot in its power, as Galen says in his commentary on the *Aphorisms*. I admit all things of this kind increase the fever, but while they evacuate the cause of the fever, they provide much more benefit than they cause harm by increasing the fever; for once the cause is removed, the fever promptly slips away.

<margin>From the impulse of nature.</margin>
¶ There remains the final indication proposed to us, taken from the impulse of nature itself, by which we contend the drinking of wine was also required for this feverish patient. Since if it is necessary to lead things out of the body, one must lead them where nature most tends through suitable places, as seemed best to Hippocrates in *Aphorisms*, book 1, aphorism 21. Also, where a disease is not fully judged at the <term>crisis</term> <note>In ancient medicine, the "crisis" was the turning point of a disease where nature either overcame the illness or succumbed to it.</note>, it is fitting for us to supply that which is lacking. Galen, in the commentary on *Aphorisms*, book 1, aphorism 20. Nature, however, in this case attempted a crisis through sweats and urine on the seventh day, but imperfectly; for neither of these resolved the fever, since the sweat was neither copious nor did it flow from the whole body, nor did a greater force of urine appear than in the following days.

¶ Therefore, nature had to be helped by the physician, so that what remained of the feverish matter might be excreted either through urine (which I hoped, above all else, would happen), or through sweats (which I almost despaired of, because neither urine nor bowels were suppressed, nor did a shivering fit precede it), or through both. Furthermore, watery wine is accustomed to provide all these things abundantly, as is partly clear from what has been said, and will become clearer than the sun from what is to be said. Why, then, do we not give this patient wine to drink? For such wine, as much as anything else, <term>concocts</term> <note>Concoction refers to the "ripening" or "cooking" of raw humors by the body's heat so they can be expelled.</note> half-raw humors, promotes sweat and urine, and brings about sleep. Galen, book 4, *On Preserving Health*. This last gift is especially necessary for us in acute fevers, since insomnia and the inability to sleep are their companions. These symptoms miraculously lay low one's strength and cause the body to dry out. Therefore Galen, in book 1 of *To Glaucon*, chapter 5, says: "You shall undoubtedly give thin white wine, and especially to those who do not sleep, if they do not suffer from headaches and there are no throbbings in the temples." Although watery and subtle wines, besides not harming the head, soothe headaches and cool the body imperceptibly. Galen, in the book *On Good Juices* <note>original: "De Euchymia"</note>. Wine is beneficial for old men because it warms all their limbs and purges the serum of the blood through the urine. Galen, book 4, *On Preserving Health*.

<summary>The author argues that thin, watery wine is an effective treatment for bilious fevers because it helps the body expel excess bile through urine and sweat, assisting nature in reaching a "crisis." Despite wine's inherent heat, its ability to purge the cause of the fever and induce sleep makes it more beneficial than harmful for the patient.</summary>
<keywords>wine, fever, yellow bile, Galen, Hippocrates, crisis, sweat, urine, concoction, insomnia, humoral theory</keywords>

## Question

¶ But you might object that wine is not suitable for those who are "choleric" <note>Those with a "hot and dry" temperament, dominated by yellow bile.</note>—whether by nature or by an acquired imbalance—citing Galen in his book *On Good Juices* <note>original: "De Euchymia"</note>. You might confirm this through Hippocrates in the sixth book of *Epidemics* <note>original: "Epidemion"</note>—whether the author is Hippocrates himself or his son Thessalus—who prohibits wine for those with hot temperaments, and this not only when they have a fever, but even during health. As he says: "In a hot nature, there should be cooling, the drinking of water, and rest." Such men he calls *bitter-bilious* <note>original: "picrocholos"</note> from an abundance of bitter bile in the first book of *On the Regimen in Acute Diseases* <note>original: "De Ratione Victus in Morbis Acutis"</note>, and Galen does the same in the eighth book of *The Method of Healing* <note>original: "Methodi Medendi"</note>.

¶ But Galen himself unties this "knot" <note>Meaning a difficult logical or medical problem.</note> a little later in the same book. Regarding a hot nature, he [Galen] advises cooling, water-drinking, and rest, unless perhaps (as some prefer) you say he is advising such temperaments to use water more copiously than wine. These are the words of Galen.

¶ You yourself are aware that I grant wine to all temperaments of this kind, provided that it is "watery" in both appearance and strength. For such a wine is more useful for everything than plain water, seeing as it aids in concoction <note>The internal "cooking" or digestion of food and humors.</note> and provokes both urine and sweat. Galen mentions this in the eighth book of *The Method of Healing* shortly before the previous reference, where he speaks of "daily fevers" <note>original: "febribus diarijs"</note> in bitter-bilious people. If you mix water with this wine, you strip away all suspicion of harm. For wine helps the water to penetrate the body, and it mitigates thirst more promptly than either one could do on its own. Galen, book 1, *On Simple Medicines* <note>original: "Simplicium"</note>. How much this effect is to be desired in acute, hot diseases is manifest to everyone.

¶ Lastly, Hippocrates advises in the seventh book of *Epidemics* that one should gratify the sick in matters of purges, food, drink, and in the things they see or touch, and in other things—provided they do not do much harm. Galen teaches that Hippocrates did not advise this merely to be "nice" to the patient, but so that he might consult the patient’s benefit more successfully. For a slightly "worse" drink or food that is more pleasant is to be preferred over "better" foods that are less pleasant, as stated in the *Aphorisms*, book 2, aphorism 38. For whatever things are taken with pleasure, the stomach embraces and digests more fully; just as it flees from things that are displeasing, which leads to nausea, gas, and "fluctuations" <note>A term for an upset or "sloshing" stomach.</note>.

¶ I omit the fact that a patient is freed from great mental distress—which was tormenting him greatly with the desire for the thing he craved—when those assisting him are obedient to his mind and exhibit what he requested without delay, provided the thing is free from harm or carries the minimal amount of inconvenience.

¶ I pass over the fact that wine is granted in daily and quartan fevers by the common consensus of physicians. Nor is there any reason why I should produce a longer discourse on the proposed subject, lest the "Question" grow into a full-sized volume.

---

# Handbook of the Christian Physician

<margin>
What virtue is according to Plato.
</margin>
¶ Virtue, according to Plato, is the health of the soul, and vice its sickness. Virtue is a good habit, or a quality resulting from good habits, while vice is a bad one. ¶ Just as the body gradually returns to its former vigor when illness is driven away by the use of good food and frequent abstinence from bad things, so too the soul generates, strengthens, increases, and preserves virtue within itself by fleeing evil deeds and practicing good ones.

<margin>
On the care of the soul according to Plato.
</margin>
¶ When you see the body sick with diseases of the soul: treat the soul. And when you see the soul suffering from a defect of the limbs and the flesh: heal the body. For all things, whether good or evil (according to Plato), flow from the soul into the body and the whole person. He therefore commands that the soul be treated first and most of all, if the entire body is to be well. <note>Champier is referencing the Platonic idea of psychosomatic unity—that the mind and body are inextricably linked.</note>

¶ In any disease, when the medicine does not overcome the quality of the "bad humor," it turns into that humor itself, disturbs the body, diminishes strength, and increases the weight of the affliction. <note>humor: In ancient and Renaissance medicine, health was determined by the balance of four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>

What is the cause of disease.

Printed at Lyon by Jean Crespin,
... One thousand five hundred thirty-two [1532] ...
2 volumes. 112, 56 folios. <note>Folios (ff.) refer to the number of individual leaves in a book, rather than numbered pages.</note>

It was to respond to these *Castigations*, <note>Castigations: from the Latin "castigatio," meaning corrections or reprimands.</note> in which he believed himself to be under attack, that Michael Servetus published his book in Paris in 1537, titled: *The Complete Account of Syrups*. <note>Michael Servetus was a Spanish physician and theologian; his book on syrups was a major medical text of the era, though he is now best known for being executed for heresy.</note>
